docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
One household's cashflow books, built so every recorded fact can be proven rather than trusted — an evidence-first journal where changes are appended and balances are recomputation, never edited states.

The books prove themselves: every correction and removal is its own appended record carrying what changed, each row carries a hashed self-check, and re-landing the same movement stores it once (A correction is recorded, not typed) — judge any change near the journal against this property first.

Rule-occurrence confirmation can double-book: a group confirm skips an occurrence a real booking already covers, while the same occurrence confirmed by its own address commits again (A covered rule occurrence double-books when confirmed directly by its own address) — aligning that check across both confirm doors is the highest-value fix.

The removal ritual is not uniform: the expect remove door takes an id and deletes without showing the row or asking for a yes (The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming), one door away from the identical guarded operation.

Which side wins when a retraction record no longer matches the live books is decided nowhere (Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?) — an owner ruling is pending, and until then the keeper facing the refusal has no recovery door.

Next: read the SWOT analysis for the evidence behind each point and the product summary for the capability map. Verification: six objections were raised during the analysis and all six carry resolved markers at their target versions — no fact stands contested; the vault holds no separate coverage or run record.

docs.title: actors
docs.text:
A business actor of the analyzed system: the person, role or external party its behavior serves or involves — documented in business prose and linked to the processes they act in and the rules, data and sensitivities they have a stake in.

The actors' story:

Only two named parties move through this product, and their difference is the whole design. The owner keeps the books; the anticipated payer stands on the other side of every promise the books are not allowed to record. One is a role, the other an external counterparty — and the product treats them so differently that the split explains the register, the confirmation desk and the future-date refusals all at once.

The owner is the single pair of hands: she states payments and income in whatever precision the moment allows, and every guard in the product exists to protect her. Rejections before an entry is accepted, the rehearsal run that previews balances without storing, the confirmations and retractions that ask for a stated yes — all of it shields one accountable person from a balance she cannot stand behind. Her care-about links run across the ledger, the register, the confirmation desk, corrections, retractions and the standing rules; no other actor touches any of that ground.

The anticipated payer is deliberately less visible. A rent due Friday or a salary expected next week is a promise, not a fact, and the counterparty may never deliver — so the promise parks in the expected register as an open item while the books stay quiet. When an owner statement carries a future date, the intake redirects it there rather than booking it as if the money had already moved. The payer appears in the movement, confirmation and correction processes precisely as that open promise, and keeps its own date honesty rules.

What the two facts agree on: nothing reaches the journaled books without the owner's action. The payer never records anything alone; their role is to be the reason promises exist, and to stay visible as an open item until the money lands and the owner confirms it. The census is complete — 2 actor facts, both read this pass.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The counterparty behind a future-dated movement: the bill not yet due or the income not yet arrived, parked in the expected register as a promise.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A future-dated movement is a promise, not a fact — a rent due Friday, a salary expected next week. The counterparty on the other side may or may not deliver, which is exactly why the register keeps the promise separate from the books: if the payer never materializes, the never-moved money still shows where it was expected. The owner's future-dated statement redirects to this register so the books record realized movements only, and the promise side stays visible as open items awaiting confirmation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The one person keeping personal cashflow books; states real payments and income into the ledger and is accountable for their balances.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The household bookkeeper: the person who noticed money actually moved and states the movement in the books, in whatever precision the moment gives. A full set of details, a quick shorthand breath, or field-by-field answers all work. The books exist for this person's decisions, so a wrong balance misleads them twice: once now in the projection preview, once later in every report built on the chain. Rejections, rehearsal runs and the cancel path all exist to protect this single pair of hands from recording something the books cannot stand behind.

docs.title: A booking off its rule s mark is recorded as an exception an on mark one supersedes the occurrence
A booking off its rule's mark is recorded as an exception, an on-mark one supersedes the occurrence
Title
docs.text: A booking off its rule's mark is recorded as an exception, an on-mark one supersedes the occurrence

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When a movement booked from a standing rule's occurrence drifts outside the rule's amount tolerance or day window, the occurrence is recorded as an exception so it stops nagging as open; a booking that matches the rule on category, amount and date closes the occurrence by superseding it, needing no separate record.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Committing a rule occurrence that drifted (amount or date outside the window) records an exception; a covering commit clears the occurrence automatically.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A standing rule's occurrence stays visible as an unconfirmed promise until the books can account for it. Once money is booked for that occurrence, one of two things decides whether the promise needs a goodbye note: if the booking matches the rule — same category, essentially the same amount, within a few days of the occurrence — the promise is simply superseded by the real entry and vanishes from the open list on its own, nothing extra to store. If the booking drifted — a different amount, or too far from the planned day — the occurrence is marked as an exception, so the open list lets it go rather than showing a promise the owner already handled differently in real life. Either way the occurrence never lingers unconfirmed after money has moved.

docs.title: A confirmation never lands ahead of the real day
A confirmation never lands ahead of the real day
Title
docs.text: A confirmation never lands ahead of the real day

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A movement whose day has not yet arrived is not confirmed into the books; confirmation waits until the movement is real, or the owner states its true landing date.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Confirming is refused for anything still in the future — a promise without its landing cannot become a book fact, at any of the confirm doors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Confirmation is the moment a promise becomes a fact, and only a fact can carry balances. So every confirm door refuses money that has not moved yet, each with its own etiquette: a promised row dated ahead is refused outright, leaving the promise untouched and pointing at the edit desk for real changes; a group confirmation quietly skips its future members and commits only the landed ones; a standing-rule occurrence dated ahead opens the questions only to let the owner write the day the money actually arrived — a landing date in the future is refused there too, since a movement can never lie ahead of today. The books would be wrong the moment they recorded it: balances would claim money moving before it did.

docs.title: A correction is recorded not typed
A correction is recorded, not typed
Rule Statement
docs.text: Correcting a posted entry appends a corrective record to the books and never alters an existing row in place.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every fix lands as a new appended corrective record, so the books keep a replayable account of what changed instead of silently absorbing it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the owner fixes a wrong amount, description, category or day on a posted entry, the repair is written down as its own record and the old content is retired behind it. Nothing is overwritten. This is what makes every correction auditable later: the books can always show what the entry said before the fix and what it says now, from the records alone. Only an intentional, named act of repair produces such a record — a failed edit, an abandoned walk or an unknown address writes nothing at all.

Title
docs.text: A hidden occurrence still answers to its own address

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A projected occurrence stays reachable by its own address from 35 days before the ledger's anchor to 400 days ahead even when the projection stopped showing it — suppressed, superseded or edited-out instances all resolve — while a paused rule's occurrences resolve as unknown.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The instance address lookup walks the standing rules' own schedule, not the listed rows, so suppressing or superseding an occurrence hides the list row without retiring the address.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When the owner deletes a promising-looking occurrence, the projection obeys and the row disappears. But the promise never retires: typing that occurrence's address later still finds it, because the books look it up against the rules' own freshly expanded schedule rather than the visible list. An occurrence quietly taken over by a real booking behaves the same way — unseen in the list, alive at the door. The one thing that makes an instance unknown is pausing or ending the whole standing rule.

The owner who deletes an occurrence and later re-confirms it by its remembered address therefore meets a live booking door where the view showed nothing. That gap is what makes the double-booking harm behind A covered rule occurrence double-books when confirmed directly by its own address reachable even after a deliberate suppression.

docs.title: A landed open item confirms as it was promised
A landed open item confirms as it was promised
Title
docs.text: A landed open item confirms as it was promised

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: An expected or projected movement whose day has arrived is confirmed exactly as it was stated when promised — no questions, no corrections, one commit.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Landed open items commit with zero prompts; every detail was already stated when the promise was made.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When an owner opens an open item whose date has arrived — a single promised row, one occurrence of a standing rule, or a landed member of a group — the books ask nothing. The description, day, category and amount recorded at promise time become the realized movement verbatim. Only a movement that is still in the future walks the owner through the details again, because that case lets the real day differ from the planned one. The zero-prompt path is deliberate: a confirmation is the moment "I promised this, and it happened", and re-litigating the promise would only invite typos into a record the owner has already vetted.

docs.title: A landed promise corrects into the books
A landed promise corrects into the books
Title
docs.text: A landed promise corrects into the books

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Correcting an expected entry whose day has arrived commits it into the books in the same act, with the promise retired behind the landed row.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: On a landed promise, edit and confirmation are one action: the restated content posts to the books and the open entry is retired, rather than the promise being rewritten and confirmed separately.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the owner edits a promise whose day has already come — or confirms a landed promise by pressing Enter through its prefilled fields — the restated content enters the books at once as a landed fact, and the promise is retired as part of the same record. There is no intermediate state where the promise stands rewritten and unconfirmed: either the whole act lands, or a failed attempt leaves the promise open exactly as it was. This keeps the promise register honest on its side of the cut: the moment a promise's day has arrived, the only correct place for it is the books, and its open entry stops mattering.

docs.title: A paused schedule stops anticipating without losing its place
A paused schedule stops anticipating without losing its place
Title
docs.text: A paused schedule stops anticipating without losing its place

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Pausing a standing rule stops all new anticipation for it while keeping the rule stored intact; resuming restores anticipation from the same stored rule.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Pausing a standing schedule silences its future anticipation only — the rule keeps every field, its history and its identity for later resume.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An owner going through a change — an ended subscription, a rent holiday — does not want the forecast to keep promising that payment. Pausing tells the planner to stop anticipating that schedule, and the expansion of schedules to anticipated entries skips a paused schedule entirely. What pausing never does is erase: the description, the amount, the rhythm, the window and the history of exempted dates all stay exactly as the owner left them, so a later resume brings the schedule back as a whole. A schedule may also be paused twice or resumed twice — the owner is told the schedule is already in that state rather than being deceived into thinking something changed.

docs.title: A payment habit mixing income and expense is never one pattern
A payment habit mixing income and expense is never one pattern
Title
docs.text: A payment habit mixing income and expense is never one pattern

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A group of payments whose occurrences include both incoming and outgoing amounts produces no proposal, even when their dates fall perfectly into a rhythm.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Money in and money out are different habits: one repeating group whose amounts swing between credit and debit is refused outright as a single schedule, however regular its timing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The detector groups by name and category, and under the same name an account may both receive money and spend it — a payment service that settles inflows and takes fees, a category that carries both reimbursements and costs. Seeing one standing schedule in that mix would anticipate the wrong direction half the time.

So the books hold a line here: before any varying-amount proposal is considered, every occurrence in the group must carry the same direction of money. The moment both directions appear, the group exits detection entirely — no proposal, no amount, no rhythm, regardless of how clean the dates look.

The owner experiences the line as silence: a payment that both pays and charges simply never appears in the review list, and if they want a rule for one direction, that direction must stand alone under its own name.

docs.title: A projection never writes a store
A projection never writes a store
Rule Statement
docs.text: A view-level projection of promised or past movements — including the open confirmation list — computes everything at view time and writes no stored item anywhere.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The projection walk (and with it the confirm picker's backlog) is read-only by design: no store is written from a view.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The confirmation backlog does not exist as a store — it is computed every time the owner looks. The projection walk that powers both the ledger view and the confirm picker boots from committed data, overlays promises and rule occurrences, and hands back rows for display; through all of that it deliberately writes nothing. A promise is never moved, never marked seen, never retired just because it appeared on a screen; only a confirmation commits the change. The owner can therefore browse the backlog as often as they like — looking never books anything.

docs.title: A proposal s amount becomes never negative
A proposal lands where the history last showed it
Title
docs.text: A proposal lands where the history last showed it

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A proposal's start is defined as the settled payment's first occurrence and a monthly or yearly rhythm takes its day or month from the last occurrence, so the schedule lands on the rhythm the history actually showed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The schedule's anchor and landing day are read from the history, not guessed: the first time the payment appeared starts the schedule, and the most recent occurrence fixes the day it now lands on.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When history shows a payment repeating, the proposal must say when the schedule begins and where in the cycle it lands. Both are read from the very rows the detection trusted: the earliest settled occurrence becomes the start — for weekly rhythms, its weekday is the anchor every future instance snaps to — and for monthly or yearly rhythms, the day and month come from the most recent occurrence, so the schedule reflects how the payment currently falls rather than an old date it has since outgrown.

The consequence the owner sees is a proposal whose calendar already matches their history: adopting it with Enter keeps exactly that landing day. Nothing in the flow invents a date; a rhythm the history never showed — days the payment never fell on — cannot enter the form.

An owner who disagrees with the landing day does not argue with the proposal; they type a different value in the form, and the schedule takes theirs.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A rehearsal of a movement shows exactly what would be recorded, including the projected balances, and stores nothing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The dry-run path validates, projects the checking balance, and always ends without touching the journal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Before trusting the books with a statement, the owner can watch the entry happen in rehearsal: the same checks run, the resulting checking balance is computed from the same predecessor the real write would chain from, and the would-be record is shown in full. The rehearsal can never half-happen — whatever it shows, nothing is stored and the books stand exactly as before. Only the checking account is projected in the preview, even for a movement that would move savings too.

docs.title: A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood
A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood
Title
docs.text: A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Every retraction of a committed entry is written as one journal record that carries the victim's exact prior content, appended like any other change; an unknown target records nothing at all.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The retraction appends one pre-image-carrying delete record — never an in-place removal — and an unknown id appends nothing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A wrong entry comes out of the books the same way every other change goes in: as one additional written record, not an edit of what is already there. The record names its victim and carries the victim's state as it stood at the moment of retraction — its day, its words, its category, its account movements, everything joined to it. Because that prior state rides the record itself, the books can be rebuilt from scratch at any time and still show exactly what was removed and when.

Two edges protect the owner at the write. If the address turns out not to exist, nothing is written at all — a mistaken retraction leaves no trace in the journal. And the record itself must match the entry as it currently stands before the removal happens: if the books' actual content disagrees with what the retraction claims, the rebuild stops loudly rather than silently reproducing an inconsistency.

The promised-entry path is different by design: a promise was never in the books, so dropping it simply removes it from the register of future movements — no journal record is owed for a promise that never landed.

docs.title: A retraction only writes after a stated yes
A retraction only writes after a stated yes
Title
docs.text: A retraction only writes after a stated yes

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: The books never change from a retract attempt unless the owner, seeing the printed entry, types an affirmative answer; a bare Enter or any other word cancels and nothing is written.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every retraction path shows the victim first and demands a typed yes; Enter alone or silence on the picker cancels with the books untouched.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner picks an entry to retract; nothing about that intent touches the books yet. First the exact entry is printed — day, words, category, amount — so what would go is never a guess. Only a stated answer in the affirmative carries the retraction through; pressing Enter by reflex, answering with any other word, or giving no answer at all on the pick-from-recent step ends the attempt with the books exactly as they were. The cancel itself is announced, so the owner knows nothing happened.

The rule governs the committed-entry and promised-entry paths equally, and the group and rule-occurrence paths carry the same shape: a printed subject and a stated confirmation, each with its own cancel answer. The one exception is the standalone remove door on the promises register, which drops a promise without showing it or asking — a door this rule does not hold shut.

Nothing here protects against a later change of heart on content; the guarantee is only that a retraction is what the owner, informed and asked, chose to do.

docs.title: A schedule with an existing equal is never re proposed
A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed
Title
docs.text: A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A payment whose description and category already name an existing recurrence rule produces no detection proposal, regardless of how regularly it still repeats.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Detection excludes what the books already anticipate: an existing rule for the same payment silences any new proposal for it, so the owner is never offered a duplicate schedule.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Once the owner has formalized a repeating payment, the detector stops suggesting it. The comparison is deliberately simple — the payment's name and its category together decide whether a rule already covers that ground — so a rule adopted weeks ago keeps its payment quiet in every later detection run, even as the payment keeps arriving.

The practical effect is that the proposal list stays a to-do list. It shrinks as the owner adopts, and it never grows back with items they have already handled. An owner who removed or paused a rule will see the payment resurface in detection again, which is the honest reading: without an active formalization, the repeating payment is once more an observation, not a schedule.

docs.title: A standing rule leaves the books only on a stated yes
A standing rule leaves the books only on a stated yes
Title
docs.text: A standing rule leaves the books only on a stated yes

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A standing rule is removed from the store only after the owner sees the rule about to go and types an explicit yes; anything else cancels and stores nothing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Removing a standing schedule shows the owner exactly which schedule they are dismissing and waits for a typed confirmation before touching the store.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Removing a standing schedule is permanent — removal does not pause it. So the owner is shown the rule's own summary, description, amount, category, rhythm and window, and asked to confirm by typing an affirmative word. Anything other than that word cancels the whole removal and the owner is told plainly that nothing was removed. The rule then leaves the store entirely rather than fading into an inactive state.

docs.title: A steady amount payment proposes its median
A steady-amount payment proposes its median
Rule Statement
docs.text: When at least the minimum count of a payment's occurrences carry amounts within five percent (or half a euro) of the group's median and their dates fall into a regular rhythm, the proposal names that median as the amount.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The first tier of detection trusts amounts that barely moved: the median of the steady occurrences becomes the anticipated amount, and the rhythm is read from their dates.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Most repeating payments are subscriptions and rent: the same figure month after month. For these, detection checks whether a solid majority of the occurrences stayed within a narrow band around the middle value, then reads the rhythm off their dates. If the dates keep their spacing, the proposal carries the median as the amount and nothing about the spread is shown — the price is treated as steady.

The rhythm reading itself is forgiving in business terms: payments that arrive every few days, about a week, about a fortnight, about a month or about a year apart all qualify, judged on the typical gap the dates show. A payment that skips an occurrence once still counts as its rhythm — one long gap does not break the pattern.

When the steady occurrences fail the date check, the payment is not discarded; the detector falls through to its wider reading, where varying amounts may still complete a clean rhythm.

docs.title: A timely varying amount payment proposes its median with its spread
A timely varying-amount payment proposes its median with its spread
Title
docs.text: A timely varying-amount payment proposes its median with its spread

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When a payment's dates fall into a regular rhythm but its amounts vary beyond the steady band, a proposal is still made — with the median as nominal amount and the observed low-to-high range attached — provided every amount carries the same sign.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The second tier handles budget-style payments that arrive on time for changing figures: the timing is trusted, the median becomes the anticipated amount, and the observed range is shown honestly instead of hidden.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Some payments keep their appointment but not their price: the owner confirms a budget figure, then books what was really spent. Detection does not throw these away; it reads the rhythm from all their dates and proposes the middle value as the amount, attaching the observed low and high so the owner sees the spread at a glance in the review table.

One guardrail holds before any of this: the payment may not swing between income and expense. A group whose amounts mix money in and money out is not one payment habit and produces nothing. Deliberately absent is any limit on how far the amounts may wander — a wide spread is surfaced honestly in the range rather than rejected, and since nothing is created without the owner's review, a noisy proposal costs only a glance.

The steady-band rule gives way to this one exactly when the steady band fails: if the steady occurrences themselves already carry a clean rhythm, this tier is never consulted.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When the stated category names a movement between the owner's own accounts, the amount leaves the checking account and arrives in savings mirrored, so both running balances shift by the same entry.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The transfer category carries a mirrored posting: checking gets the amount, savings the opposite — one entry, both balances.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Moving money between two of one's own accounts is not spending and not income — nothing enters or leaves the household. The books record it as one entry that touches both: the checking account carries the stated amount and the savings account its mirror image. The running balances of both accounts shift with that single entry, so the household total is unchanged while the split between the accounts follows the actual move.

docs.title: A weekly rhythm stands on its snapped weekday anchor
A weekly rhythm stands on its snapped weekday anchor

docs.text: A weekly rhythm stands on its snapped weekday anchor

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A weekly or biweekly schedule's start date is snapped forward to the chosen weekday before the rule is stored, and every later occurrence keeps that weekday for the schedule's life.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An owner naming a weekday gets a schedule that always lands on that weekday — the start date moves forward to the first such day rather than keeping a mismatched anchor.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When a subscription or rent repeats on a particular weekday, the owner names that weekday, and the schedule's own start date follows the word, not the calendar coincidence of the day it was typed. A start of the tenth that the owner pins to Friday becomes the first Friday on or after the tenth; every instance the forecast anticipates falls on a Friday from then on. A bare weekday name produces the next such weekday on or after the anchor; a full date typed as the anchor stands for itself, its own weekday being the anchor already. No weekday and no start means there is nothing to stand a weekly rhythm on — the rule is refused until the owner provides the anchor.

docs.title: A zero amount promise is admitted an amountless one refused
A zero-amount promise is admitted, an amountless one refused
Title
docs.text: A zero-amount promise is admitted, an amountless one refused

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: An expected statement with no amount at all is refused, but an expected statement whose amount is exactly zero is admitted as a promise.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The expectation door checks that an amount was stated, not what it is worth: zero passes here while the same zero statement is refused at the actual ledger door.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: For a promised movement the door asks only whether an amount was stated. Something that is not stated gets a plain refusal and nothing is stored. An amount of exactly zero, however, is a stated amount — it passes the gate and the promise is parked with it. The books treat zero differently on the two sides of today: realized movements may never carry it, promised ones may. Nothing in the promise's record marks it as odd; a zero promise looks like any other open item.

docs.title: An already committed address confirms as nothing to do
An already-committed address confirms as nothing to do
Title
docs.text: An already-committed address confirms as nothing to do

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Naming an already-committed movement's address at the confirm desk reports it as recorded and changes nothing; the confirm commit itself applies twice as once, so a repeated confirm cannot duplicate the books.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Confirming an already-actual id is a reported no-op; a repeated actual id reaches it as an idempotent re-apply, so both routes are safe to re-run.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A promise can be confirmed only once — after that the address the owner holds is the booked fact's own. Naming a committed address at the desk answers "already recorded, nothing to do" and changes nothing (confirm.py:252-259). Inside the engine the same guarantee holds at a lower level: applying the same confirmation twice returns the first result instead of inserting a second copy, so a commit cannot double itself even if it is driven twice. The promise register itself has no "confirmed" state — the row is simply gone, its identity carried on the booking's record.

docs.title: An edit that lands tomorrow leaves the books
An edit that lands tomorrow leaves the books
Title
docs.text: An edit that lands tomorrow leaves the books

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Editing a posted entry to a day after today backs the row out of the books and the corrected content re-enters as a promise for its new day.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A posted row corrected beyond today is moved out of the actual books into the promises register at its restated content, because a book row may never claim a day that has not happened.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An owner who retypes a future day onto a posted entry is not fixing the past, they are restating a promise: the correction would stop being a fact of money moved. The books therefore let the row go — it is backed out like a deletion — and the corrected content takes its place in the promises register under its new day. The back-out happens first; if registering the promise is refused, the owner is told plainly that the row is gone and that they can reserve it again themselves. A transfer touched by such a move warns that the savings side of the books was shifted too and should be checked over. The promise stays there, visible, until its real day arrives and it is confirmed like any other promise.

docs.title: An exception edit keeps its promise date honest by refusing today
An exception edit keeps its promise date honest by refusing today
Title
docs.text: An exception edit keeps its promise date honest by refusing today

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: When the owner edits a future occurrence into a one-off promise, the edited date must still lie strictly ahead of today, exactly as the promise would admit it originally — while the confirm door on the same occurrence accepts today.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Turning a future occurrence edit into a promise follows the promise's own admission rules; moving it to today is refused even though confirming the same occurrence today is legal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A future occurrence the owner reshapes — different amount, different day, next month instead — does not become a special creature. It enters the promise register under the same admission rules the owner faced when promising anything else: a real day must be stated, a full set of details is expected, and the day has to be one the money has not moved on yet. Today's date, legal on the confirm door one menu higher, is exactly what the promise refuses — the occurrence is simply not reshaped, and the owner's typing is lost.

This is the one admission asymmetry between the doors: the confirm desk accepts what the edit's exception path refuses on the very same occurrence. For the owner it is two different calendars: the booking door counts today as real, the reshaping door counts today as not yet real.

docs.text: An open item without an amount is never confirmed

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A confirmation of an open item carries a stated amount; a row with no amount recorded is refused at every confirm desk, alone or inside a group.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A movement without an amount cannot be booked; confirmations refuse amount-less rows rather than posting a blank movement.

docs.title: Description

But a realized movement always moves a sum of money, so confirming one would ask the books to record a movement that moved nothing in particular. Every confirm desk checks the amount first: a lone open item without one is refused with the reason, and a group confirmation skips its amount-less members and reports the skip. The owner resolves the gap at the edit desk, where the promise gets its real amount, before the item can become a fact.

docs.title: Confirming a group commits its landed members and keeps the group
Confirming a group commits its landed members and keeps the group
Title
docs.text: Confirming a group commits its landed members and keeps the group

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Confirming a group commits every landed member in order — oldest promise first — re-points each expected member's address to its new committed one, and leaves the group alive with its future or unresolvable members still attached.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: One group confirmation commits all landed members sequentially, re-points retired member ids, and skips ahead/future or missing members with a note.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A group gathers related promises under one address — a holiday, a tax bill paid in parts. When the owner confirms the group, every member whose day has arrived commits in date order, and the group keeps functioning afterwards: each member's address changes when it becomes a booked fact, and the group's membership list is corrected on the spot so no entry points at a retired address. Members still in the future, members whose address can no longer be resolved, and members without amounts are skipped with a note rather than blocking the rest; a committed member is already a fact and is left alone. A group with nothing landed to confirm accomplishes nothing and says so. The group itself is never retired by confirming it — it survives as the rollup over its committed and still-open members.

docs.title: Deleting a group ungroups without deleting members
Deleting a group ungroups without deleting members
Title
docs.text: Deleting a group ungroups without deleting members

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Removing a group deletes only the grouping; the member entries survive untouched in their own stores.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Group removal is an ungrouping, never a member deletion — members stay recorded after the group record is gone.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner who decides a grouping no longer helps — its label wrong, its purpose gone — removes the grouping without losing any of the entries it gathered. The group record itself goes; each member row keeps its id, its content and its place in the books or the register. The confirmation asks about the group by name and announces the members' survival afterwards, so the owner hears explicitly that the entries stay.

The distinction matters because a group is a view the owner built over real entries, not a container that owns them. Retracting entries remains possible one by one; no mass removal ever rides a group deletion.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Detecting repeating payments shows proposals only; a recurrence rule comes into existence solely through the owner reviewing proposal values and completing them.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector runs read-only: it prints candidate schedules and creates nothing. Adoption is a separate, owner-driven step — the review list itself can never put a rule into the books.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This is the trust spine of the whole flow: the owner can run detection freely, as often as they like, without ever changing what the books anticipate. The proposal table is a review surface, and its own footer tells the owner as much — nothing has been created, and naming a proposal number is what starts the adoption.

The rule earns its teeth from a concrete safeguard: the adoption reruns the detection before offering the form, and if the named number no longer sits in the fresh list, nothing happens. A list read a moment earlier can never stand in for a decision the owner has not yet made. Only after the owner has walked every field — each showing the detected value, each replaceable — and the completed rule has passed the admission checks does it enter the store.

An owner who wants a proposal rejected can simply stop; there is no accept-all door. Proposals die by inattention, one at a time, never by bulk approval.

docs.title: Every adopted value passes the owner s hands
Every adopted value passes the owner's hands
Title
docs.text: Every adopted value passes the owner's hands

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: An adopted rule is built from a form where each field starts at the detected value and exists only if the owner completes or accepts every field, with an explicit way out at each step.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Adoption is approval-by-completion, not click-through: the owner sees each detected value, Enter keeps it, typing replaces it, a quit key aborts — and nothing persists until the whole walk is done.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner never rubber-stamps a machine's guess. The adoption form opens with every field pre-filled from the detection: the payment's name, its category, the amount, the rhythm, and the day or month the rhythm lands on. Enter means the detected value was good enough; typing means the owner knows better; a quit key at any field throws the whole adoption away.

Weekly and biweekly rhythms change one question meaningfully: instead of a day of the month, the owner is asked which weekday the payment falls on, and typing the day's name snaps the schedule's start forward to that weekday. The yearly rhythm asks for its month as well. Only after the last field — the optional end date — does the form hand over a completed rule, which still has to pass the admission checks before anything is stored.

The same form serves the owner when they write a rule by hand or correct an existing one, so every way a rule's values enter the books asks the same approval walk.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A stored movement names the checking and savings balances that result after it, chained from the nearest entry on or before its date, and shifts every later entry by the same amount.

docs.title: Summary

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The running balances are not a side effect but the entry's own content: when a movement is recorded, it takes over the balances of the closest prior day, applies its own amounts, and leaves every later day's balance shifted accordingly. A movement between two dates is inserted in date order, never appended out of sequence. Each row also carries a self-check that its content is intact, so silently altered books are detectable. For the owner this means any balance read from the books is the arithmetic of the chain up to that day — and a tampered row announces itself rather than quietly agreeing.

docs.title: One admission gate for every stated movement
One admission gate for every stated movement
Title
docs.text: One admission gate for every stated movement

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A money movement enters the books only when its date reads as a real calendar day, its description is not empty, its category is on the approved list, its amount is not zero, and its date is not beyond today — the same checks on every path a movement can be stated.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Date, description, approved category, non-zero amount and no-future-date must all pass, identically for flagged, shorthand and prompted input.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Whatever way the owner states a movement — every detail spelled out, a quick shorthand breath, or one field at a time — the books accept it through one and the same door. The statement must name a real calendar day, must say what happened in words, must name a category the owner has approved for the books, must carry an amount that is not nothing, and must not be dated after today. Refuse one and the movement is not recorded, with the reason said plainly. Keeping all five checks on one path means a movement that got in through the quick door could never have been refused at the slow one.

docs.title: Only complete admissible rules are saved
Only complete admissible rules are saved
Rule Statement
docs.text: A rule is saved only when it carries a non-empty description, an approved category, a non-zero amount, a supported rhythm, day and month within their ranges, an optional start and end that parse as dates with the end never before the start.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The books never store a schedule they cannot stand behind: every field is checked against the owner's own category list and date sanity before the save happens.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The save is the only step where detection output becomes part of the books, so it carries the full admission bar. A rule without a description is refused. A category the owner has not approved anywhere in their books is refused — detection proposing an unknown category cannot smuggle it in. An amount of zero is refused, because a schedule that anticipates nothing is not a schedule. The rhythm must be one the planner knows, daily rhythm aside; a monthly or yearly rule must carry its day or month within range.

The calendar boundaries get the same scrutiny: a start or end the books cannot read as a date is refused, and an end that falls before the start is refused outright. The weekly rhythms carry their own bar — they need their start date, the weekday anchor, to be present at all.

A refused rule is announced with its reason and nothing is stored, so the owner always knows why their schedule did not take.

docs.title: Only complete future dated statements enter the expected register
Only complete future-dated statements enter the expected register
Title
docs.text: Only complete future-dated statements enter the expected register

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: A movement is parked in the expected register only when its date reads as a real calendar day, its description is not empty, its category is on the approved list, its amount is present, and its date lies after today.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The expectation door refuses an unreadable date, an empty description, an unapproved category, a missing amount and a date that is not in the future, each refusal stated in plain words.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the owner states a movement that lies ahead of today, the expectation register takes it only in complete form. The day must be a real calendar day, the description must say what is coming, the category must be one the owner has approved for the books, and the amount must be stated at all. Anything short is refused before anything is stored, and each refusal names its reason. A statement dated today or earlier is not a promise — that door points the owner back to the actual ledger, so the expectation side never collects money that has already moved.

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Detection reads only committed actual rows with a date, a description, a category and a non-zero amount; drafts and incomplete rows never shape a proposal.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A repeating pattern earns trust only from money that really moved: promised or landed-open rows, dateless, unnamed, uncategorized or zero rows are all left out of the grouping.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The proposals name real habits, so they may be mined only from real money. Rows that are still promises or promises that landed open do not count — the anticipation should not learn from itself. Rows without a date, without a name or category, or carrying a zero amount are equally invisible to the grouping, since none of them can stand for a payment that truly repeated.

The bar protects the owner in both directions: a proposal never arrives because a forgotten draft sat repeated in the intake, and a proposal never under-counts because an incomplete cousin of the same payment was thrown out. The count of times a payment repeats — the number every rhythm judgment leans on — counts only settled, fully described movements.

docs.title: Recording twice changes nothing the second time
Recording twice changes nothing the second time
Title
docs.text: Recording twice changes nothing the second time

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Stating the same movement twice stores it once: a repeat of an already-recorded movement returns the existing entry instead of a second copy.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Re-applying a recorded movement is idempotent — the original entry is returned, no duplicate row is inserted.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A movement exists once in the books even if the owner states it again. The engine checks on every landing whether the movement's identity is already present, and returns what is already there rather than recording a second copy. The identity comes from the movement's own content and creation moment, not from a counter, so the same stated movement lands as the same stored entry. A restated movement only produces a duplicate when its content differs — in which case it is a different movement by the books' reading, and it is up to the owner to notice and correct.

docs.title: Retraction re propagates the balance chain behind the removed row
Retraction re-propagates the balance chain behind the removed row
Title
docs.text: Retraction re-propagates the balance chain behind the removed row

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: After a committed entry is removed, every later row's running balances absorb the reversal of the removed entry's postings, so the books read as if the wrong entry had never posted.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Removing one row shifts every later row's balances by the inverse of the removed postings, with re-hashing, in one replay pass.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A wrong entry's damage is not confined to itself: every balance after its day was built on it. The retraction therefore carries an obligation beyond the single removal — all rows dated after the removed one receive the reversal of its account movements, each re-stamped, so the running balances stay a consistent story through time. The owner sees the effect immediately: the day's balance and every printed balance after it no longer include the wrong amount.

This is the same discipline any change to the books follows — the chain is recomputed, never patched locally. It is why a retraction of an old error heals the present numbers instead of leaving a scar.

docs.title: Suppressing a rule instance excludes one occurrence not the rule
Suppressing a rule instance excludes one occurrence, not the rule
Title
docs.text: Suppressing a rule instance excludes one occurrence, not the rule

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: Retracting a projected rule occurrence adds its date to that rule's exceptions; the rule itself keeps running and projects the remaining periods.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A wrong-looking occurrence is excluded by date — idempotent, rule preserved — while retraction of any other store entry is a true removal.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When the owner judges one projected occurrence of a standing rule wrong — a rent that month was waived, a subscription cancelled mid-cycle — the retraction must not kill the rule: future months remain projected. The occurrence's date joins the rule's exception list, so that one date disappears from the projection while the rule continues for the others. Offering the same exclusion twice changes nothing the second time.

The confirmation here is its own, lighter ritual: the occurrence is printed with rule, amount and date, and must be confirmed with an explicit typed yes. Already-excluded occurrences are reported as already handled rather than re-offered.

For every other kind of entry the same command means true removal; this distinction — suppression versus deletion — is resolved by what the id names, never asked of the owner.

docs.title: The quick statement must mean what it says
The quick statement must mean what it says
Title
docs.text: The quick statement must mean what it says

docs.title: Rule Statement
docs.text: In a quick shorthand statement, a token written like an amount is read as an amount or the whole statement is refused — it never degrades into description text.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An amount-sign or currency token that fails to parse raises a refusal of the entire shorthand, never silent absorption into the description.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The shorthand is meant for speed, and speed paths are where books go wrong quietly. So the parser holds one line: a token that starts with a sign or carries a currency mark is intended as the amount; if it cannot be read as a non-zero amount, the whole statement is refused with the reason given, rather than carrying the garbled token into the description. Relative day words are unambiguous by design — a bare signed number is money, three days back needs its letter. Amount zero is refused here too, before any check downstream.

docs.title: components
docs.text:
A structural unit of the analyzed system: one cohesive area of related functionality, named by its role, implemented within a bounded, nameable set of modules, and exposed to its consumers — other code or actors — through the interface it presents.

The components' story:

Eight components stand behind this product, and every one of them answers to one idea: the books are an append-only journal that folds into tamper-evident balances, and nothing enters a balance until the money has really moved. All eight carry the journaled-bookkeeping tag, so this is not a layered architecture story — it is one shared discipline seen from eight desks.

The discipline has three fixed points. Command mutations is the single narrow write step — every accepted change becomes one stamped mutation riding the journal — and the ledger engine folds those mutations into dated transaction rows whose running balances chain from their date-predecessor, hash-guarded against silent tampering, reloadable from checkpoint plus tail. Around that core sit the desks where the owner works: entry intake and its Dutch shorthand parser at the front door, open-entry confirmation turning landed promises into facts, entry editor and entry retraction correcting or removing what is already there, the expected register holding future-dated promises outside the balance chain entirely, and the recurrence planner turning repeated payments into anticipations that a real booking replaces.

The components cluster by what they protect. Four desks keep the owner from recording something the books cannot stand behind — intake checks and previews, confirmation refusing items ahead of today or missing amounts, the editor's field-by-field walk, and retraction demanding an explicit yes after printing the row in full. Two keep the books honest over time: the engine's chained balances and re-propagated corrections, and the register's rule that a promise never touches a balance until its day lands. The recurrence planner and the confirmation desk form the bridge between promises and facts — anticipations, confirmations and the same-day refusals that keep one truth per day.

One inconsistency travels through the set rather than being solved anywhere: the promises register can drop a promise through a standalone remove door without printing the row or demanding a yes, while every other desk protects that same owner with confirmations. The retraction component carries it openly, not as a design it defends.

The add command here builds the posting set — the checking account takes the amount, and a transfer between the two accounts mirrors it onto savings so both balances move together. When an entry retires a previously expected one, the same path builds a confirm mutation instead. Callers read back the applied entry by the mutation's identity, which is what the intake flow reports to the owner.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Resolves an entry address across the books, the promises register, groups and standing rules, and walks the owner through the correction field by field.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When a posted entry or a promise shows a mistake, this is the desk the owner works at. One address — a book id, an e-number, a group or an occurrence of a standing rule — names an entry in any of four stores, and resolution hands the row to the store's own editor: the committed row, the promised row, the group's label, or a projected occurrence with its two-option choice. On the two main desks the fields — day, description, category, amount — appear with their current values and the owner retypes what is wrong; anything confirmed unchanged stays as it stands, and three failed answers on a field abandon the whole correction. What the owner changes decides the outcome. A correction that keeps a posted row in the books lands through the mutation layer, never in place. A restated promise that stays in the register is rewritten there directly, because the register carries no balance chain to replay. A correction that moves a posted row past today backs the row out of the books and reserves the restated content in the promises register for its new day. A promise whose day has landed commits into the books exactly as restated, retiring the promise in the same mutation.

docs.title: Description

The shorthand parser keeps the quick path honest: an amount-looking token parses as an amount or fails loudly, never quieting down into description text.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Takes an entry the owner judges wrong out of the books — the committed ledger, the promises register, a group or a projected rule occurrence — after printing it and demanding an explicit yes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The desk where a wrong entry comes out. One address names the victim wherever it lives: a committed book entry, a future-dated promise, a grouping of rows, or one occurrence of a standing rule. The resolver walks the stores in turn — actual books first, then the promises register, then groups, then rule occurrences — and each answer hands the owner a different kind of retraction. Nothing is ever removed sight unseen: the row is printed in full and the owner must type an affirmative answer; a bare Enter or any other word cancels and the books stay as they were.

A committed entry does not simply vanish. Its retraction is written through the mutation layer like any other change — one record that carries the victim's prior state, so the books can be rebuilt from the journal and prove the retraction removed exactly what it claims to have removed. The balance chain then re-propagates, so later rows show the balances as if the wrong entry had never posted. A transfer removal warns the owner to re-check both accounts afterwards, since the mirrored savings leg moves with it. A projected rule occurrence is different: the occurrence is merely excluded from the projection — its date joins the rule's exclusions — so the rule keeps running for the remaining periods. Deleting a group removes only the grouping; its members survive untouched. Through the standalone remove door on the promises register, the same promise can be dropped without any printed row or stated confirmation — an inconsistency this component carries, not a design it defends.

docs.text: Folds the append-only mutation journal into transaction rows that each carry checked running balances, so every balance is recomputable and tamper-evident.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Accepts landed expected rows and rule instances into the journaled books in one step, retiring the open item behind them.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The confirmation desk is where a movement the household expected becomes a fact of the books. When money has really arrived or gone on the day it was promised, the owner calls the open item up by its address — a single expected row, one occurrence of a standing rule, or a whole group's landed members at once — and confirms it. The commit posts the movement with running balances, retires the promise behind it, and reports the new account state. A landed item confirms as-is with no questions: every detail was already stated when the promise was made. A still-future instance instead opens a prefilled question walk, so an early-landing bill can be confirmed on its real day. An address the books already record answers as a no-op. Items that cannot honestly be recorded — still ahead of today, or missing their amount — are refused with the reason. The desk also warns when a confirmation moves both accounts at once.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Reads payment history for repeating patterns, proposes standing schedules, and saves a schedule only after the owner approves it field by field.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The recurrence planner turns a repeating payment the owner keeps facing into a standing schedule the books can anticipate. It stores the owner's standing rules, proposes new rules by reading real payment history, and walks every adoption through an owner-checked form; detection alone never writes a rule.

Saved schedules never become ledger rows of their own. Each rule expands into anticipated entries only for a chosen period window, and a real payment recorded inside that window takes the scheduled entry's place, so the books keep one truth per day. An occurrence the owner never wants can be exempted by name, and a rule can pause or end without losing its history.

The owner reaches it through the product's recurrence command: review the proposals, adopt one, add a rule by hand, pause, resume, remove, edit, or correct one already-booked instance — each door running the same form and the same checks.

docs.title: concepts
docs.text:
A domain concept from the analyzed system's vocabulary, defined in plain prose and tied to the code where it is exercised.

The concepts' story:

Every concept in this family turns on one everyday question — has the money moved? The founding actual-versus-expected distinction splits a movement in two: what has happened enters the journaled books, carrying and shifting real balances, guarded against tampering; what is promised for a future day stays in a separate register, weighs nothing against those balances and can still fail to happen.

Future-day admission applies the cut to the calendar. A movement stated for today or the past is a fact, and only the fact side moves balances; stated for a future day it becomes a promise with a deliberately narrow door — nothing parks in the register until the statement is complete — while the actual ledger refuses a future date outright. The books forgive a promise of zero, but a fact of zero is a mistake by definition.

Two mechanisms share one habit: the books compute what they predict rather than store it. The confirmation backlog is the clearest case — the gap between the register and the ledger, named "geland maar niet bevestigd" (landed but not confirmed). It has no store: the open list is projected at view time, and an item leaves only when a booking supersedes, retires or excepts it. A projected occurrence of a standing rule works the same way, since its address is derived from the rule's values and the date — retrievable even after a delete, yet schedule-bound, so adjusting the rule makes addresses noted from an older forecast stop matching.

The last two concepts tell how a schedule earns its place. Detection gathers a payment that repeats often enough into a proposal, but a proposal is information, not commitment: it lives only on screen, nothing remembers it was shown, and it may stay generous — a wide observed amount range, even an unknown category — because it holds no power over forecasts. Adoption is one of two doors into the rule store; the other receives obligations the owner knows before the books ever see them, like a new subscription or a rent change, written by hand. Both doors refuse an incomplete or impossible rule, and each carries its own trust story: a hand-written rule leans wholly on the owner's judgment, an adopted one on history's evidence.

Across all six the boundary holds: a promise never looks like a fact, a projection never lands in the balance chain, and no guess becomes a rule on the books' word.

Read the full story

Fact Sheet Title Actual versus expected Future-day admission Proposal Rule provenance — written by hand or adopted from history The confirmation backlog The derivation of a projected occurrence's address

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The founding distinction: a movement that happened (journaled, balance-carrying) versus a movement promised for a future day (register-held, balance-free).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: One distinction explains most rules in this territory. A movement is either actual — it has happened, it enters the journaled books, it carries and shifts real balances, it is guarded against tampering — or expected — it is promised for a future day, it is kept in a separate register without balances, and it can still fail to happen. The admission gate's future-date refusal, the intake redirect to the register, the confirm flow that retires a promise, the empty balance fields on a promise and the mandatory balance chain on a recorded row all follow from asking one question: has the money moved, yes or no. The books deliberately refuse to let a promise look like a fact — every projection of promised money is computed at view time from the register, never stored into the balance chain.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tomorrow's money is a promise kept apart from today's money: the two sides of today each have their own door, their own idiom and their own checks.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Everything the household books do about a stated money movement splits on one line: is the day of the movement still ahead, or has it arrived? A movement stated for a future day is not money that has happened — it is an expectation, registered as an open promise that weighs nothing against the real balances and carries its own identifier. A movement stated for today or the past is a fact, and only the fact side may move the account balances. Because the whole bookkeeping leans on that cut, the admission of a future statement is deliberately narrow: the promise door demands a complete statement before it parks anything, and even the actual ledger refuses a future date outright, pointing the statement back to the expectation side. The distinction explains why a zero promise can park silently where a zero fact cannot — the books forgive a promise of nothing, but a fact of nothing is a mistake by definition.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A recurring pattern the books found in real history — offered for review, carrying values the owner may keep or replace, but never itself a rule.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A proposal is the middle thing between an observation and a schedule. When the books have seen the same payment repeat often enough, detection gathers those occurrences into a proposal: the payment's name and category, the amount to expect, the rhythm, and the calendar anchor, plus the observed spread when the amounts wandered.

The distinction that matters: a proposal is information, not commitment. It exists only on screen, only for this run of the review list, and nothing anywhere remembers it was shown. The same payment produces a fresh, freshly-computed proposal in every later detection, and the list the owner saw a moment ago has no authority over the one an adoption consults. A proposal becomes a recurrence rule only when the owner walks the adoption form to its end — until then it is the books' way of saying: this looks like a habit, decide what you want to do about it.

This is why a proposal can be generous where a rule must be strict: a proposal may carry a wide, honest range of observed amounts, an unknown category, an amount the owner would never accept — each of those is a review cost of one glance, while letting the same thing into a rule unsupervised would shape every future forecast wrongly.

docs.title: Rule provenance written by hand or adopted from history
Rule provenance — written by hand or adopted from history
Title
docs.text: Rule provenance — written by hand or adopted from history

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A standing schedule can enter the books two ways — the owner writes it the moment they recognize an obligation, or history reveals the pattern and the owner adopts a proposal — and each provenance carries its own trust story.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Two different business moments create the same kind of schedule. In one, the owner knows the obligation before the books ever see it — a new subscription, a rent change, an annual insurance — and writes the rule directly, trusting their own judgment alone. In the other, the books themselves reveal that a payment keeps repeating, a proposal is drawn from settled history, and the owner adopts it after confirming every value against what history showed. The distinction explains why the checks treat the two doors differently in spirit: a hand-written rule leans entirely on what the owner typed — the calendar anchor they chose, the amount they named — while an adopted rule leans on history's evidence and only needs the owner's blessing. Both doors end at the same form and the same store, and both refuse an incomplete or impossible rule. It also explains the detection side's caution — a proposal is never the books' word, only its guess, until the owner adopts it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The domain term for what is "geland maar niet bevestigd" — landed in real life but not yet accepted into the books; the projected open list is its only ledger.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The confirmation backlog is the working mental list of promises that came due and were not yet accepted into the books: overdue expected rows and landed-but-unconfirmed occurrences of standing rules. What the code calls the OPEN section names exactly this backlog — "Openstaand (geland maar niet bevestigd)" (ledger_view.py:215). The term matters at the boundary between two books: the promise register and the standing rules hold the promises, the journaled ledger holds the facts, and the backlog is the gap between them, always computed from the projection rather than stored. Confirming is how an item leaves the backlog: the booking supersedes it, retires it, or marks it excepted — never by editing the backlog itself, which does not exist as a store.

docs.title: The derivation of a projected occurrence s address
The derivation of a projected occurrence's address
Title
docs.text: The derivation of a projected occurrence's address

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A standing rule's occurrence carries no stored address: its identifier is always recomputed from the rule's values and the date, which makes it both permanent and schedule-bound.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When the owner names an occurrence — to confirm it, edit it, delete or suppress it — the address is not something the books store; no row was ever written. It is derived from the rule's own design: description, category, amount, rhythm, day, month and the occurrence's date hashed into a stable value. The consequences follow two ways. The address is permanent: whenever the schedule is re-expanded, the same rule on the same date yields the same address, so an occurrence the owner deleted, superseded or edited away still answers to it. And the address is schedule-bound: adjusting the rule for the future changes the addresses of every future occurrence, so addresses the owner noted from an earlier forecast stop matching.

This is why the forecast can honor a delete (hide the date) without making the address unknown (the rule's schedule still derives it), and why suppression lives in the rule's exception list rather than on the instance.

docs.text:

docs.title: Dutch register on an english language codebase
Dutch register on an English-language codebase
Convention Statement
docs.text: Every user-facing console line is written in Dutch while code identifiers, docstrings and CLI help text are English.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Rejections, confirmations and prompts speak Dutch to the owner; the programmatic layer stays English — a deliberate two-register split.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The books speak to their one reader in the reader's language: refusals ("Niet opgeslagen: …"), cancellations ("Geannuleerd — niets opgeslagen."), prompts ("Omschrijving", "Bedrag") and confirmations ("Opgeslagen als …") are all Dutch, including the domain words spaar and Overdracht, while module docstrings, function names and CLI help strings stay English. The split is consistent across the intake, command and engine territory and is itself part of the product surface: a faithful parity port that translated the refusals would change what the owner actually sees.

docs.title: One handler serves both the flagged and the walked route
One handler serves both the flagged and the walked route
Title
docs.text: One handler serves both the flagged and the walked route

docs.title: Convention Statement
docs.text: A CLI handler accepts every field as an optional keyword, prompts only for the fields left unset, and lets a provided flag ride as the default of its own interactive question.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Each interactive command is written once with optional parameters: fully specified calls never meet a question, partial calls ask only what is missing, and any given flag returns as the default inside its question.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Across the command handlers, the same writing habit repeats. Every user-visible field arrives as an optional parameter. When all are supplied, the walk is skipped entirely — a script or power user gets the exact same result without a single question. When some are missing, only those questions appear, and a field the caller did supply is offered back as that question's default rather than hidden. The effect is one implementation for two doors: the non-interactive route and the walked route cannot drift apart in what they accept or store, and the interactive questions are literally the flagged route's values offered back. This holds for the rule hand-authoring walk, and its comments explicitly preserve parity with an older seeded editing flow that follows the same question order.

docs.title: entities
docs.text:
A piece of stored information in the analyzed system's domain: data that is actually persisted and re-read — a log's lines, an index file's rows, a rules file's records — identified by its domain noun and documented with its declared fields.

Fact Sheet Name Expected entry Ledger transaction row recurrence rule

docs.title: Expected entry (model.Transaction in the expected store)
Summary
docs.text: A future-dated promised movement held in its own store with status pending, carrying no balances until it lands as an actual transaction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The promise side of the books: a rent due Friday, a salary expected next week. It shares the cashflow row's shape — date, description, category, amount — but its status marks it as expected, its balances are empty by design, and it keeps both the raw and the canonical form of its category. Each promised movement gets an identifier from its register order. When the day arrives and the movement really happens, confirming retires this entry and the realized movement enters the journaled books.

docs.title: State Management

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: One stored money movement with date, description, category, signed account postings and the resulting running balances, hash-guarded on disk.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: What the books are made of: one row per recorded movement. The row knows what moved (signed postings per account), for what purpose, on what day — and what the checking and savings balances were after it. Because balances live on the row, any point in time is readable without re-walking history. When the movement came from a promise, the row remembers which expected entries it retired. The row inherits its identity, creation timestamp and hash-scheme from the mutation that created it; its own hash covers the whole content and is recomputed whenever balances shift.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: The chain is the state. A row's checking and savings balances are derived, not stored freehand: insertion computes them from the date-predecessor row's balances plus the row's own postings, and every later row is shifted by the same postings (propagate), with a re-hash after each shift. A change to any row therefore rewrites the balance chain behind it — which is why edits and deletes go through mutation replay rather than touching rows in place.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The standing schedule the owner keeps for a repeating payment — what repeats, for how much, how often, and any dates it skips.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A recurrence rule is the owner's formal answer to a payment that keeps coming back: the same description and category every time, the amount to anticipate, and the rhythm — weekly to yearly. The rule also carries its own boundaries. A start date keeps instances from appearing too early, an optional end date retires the schedule, a pause flag silences it without erasing it, and a list of exempted dates spares single occurrences the owner already settled another way.

Rules come into existence two ways: the owner writes one directly through the add flow, or a detection proposal is adopted and each value is confirmed in the owner-checked form. Either way the rule exists only after the owner's approval. Removal takes the rule out of the store entirely; pausing keeps it but stops new anticipations. A booked occurrence keeps its identity through its rule and date, so a later correction or suppression finds exactly that one instance.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: The rule's state rides four stored parts: the schedule fields (amount, frequency, day, month), the window fields (start and end dates), the pause flag (active true or false, toggled by the pause and resume actions), and the exceptions list — dates the owner exempted from anticipation, appended by the suppress action. Removal is not a flag: the rule leaves the store outright. The store keeps every rule as one entry in the rules file, rewritten wholesale on each save.
