A spot in the analyzed code where behavior is decided but undocumented or uncertain — recorded as an open question needing a human answer, rather than a conclusion the analysis made.

Fact Sheet Title Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?

docs.title: Refused retraction on journal versus books mismatch which side should win
Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?
Title
docs.text: Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?

docs.title: Question
docs.text: When the journal's record of a retraction no longer matches the entry as it stands in the books, the rebuild refuses loudly — but who should win that standoff, and what recovery does the owner actually want: keep the live entry, or honour the recorded retraction anyway?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The pre-image guard stops a rebuild whose retraction record disagrees with the books; the business intent for resolving that conflict is not decidable from the code.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
At rebuild time, each recorded retraction is checked against the entry it claims to have removed: day, words, category, account movements, everything joined to it. Any disagreement stops the whole fold with a loud refusal, on the stated ground that silently replaying a stale retraction would corrupt the chain — the removal would land on different content than it was chosen against.

What the code does next is all it can do honestly: refuse. It cannot decide what the owner would want. Two readable outcomes pull against each other — treat the live row as the truth and somehow re-derive the journal's story, or treat the journal as authoritative and reconcile the live books to it. Nothing in the code says which the business intends, and there is no recovery door: an owner facing this refusal is left with an unfathomable error and a question only the business can answer.

The answer lives with the owner of the books, not the analysis.

docs.title: Guess
docs.text: The current behavior: a canonical-content comparison between the retraction record's snapshot and the live row; a mismatch raises a ValueError naming the target and the mismatch, aborting the fold. Unknown targets replay as nothing-to-do, so only a changed but present row triggers the conflict.

docs.title: issues
docs.text:
A point where the analyzed code and its documentation demonstrably disagree — the documented claim is quoted verbatim with its source and location, the contradicting code sits in the code-evidence links, and the finding is classified as an implementation mistake, stale documentation, or a conflict not yet attributable to either side.

  • add-flow-help-says-monthly-and-yearly-while-validation-admits-four-rhythms.md

docs.title: Add flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms
Add-flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms
Title
docs.text: Add-flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The recurrence add flag help names only monthly and yearly, but the save path and the form both accept and store weekly and biweekly rules — the documented claim demonstrably undersells what the books do.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The command surface documents its rhythm flag with a short help line naming two rhythms, written when the flow presumably offered only those. Since then the product grew weekly and biweekly schedules: the seeded form asks for a weekday anchor when the owner types those rhythms, and the shared admission checks accept and store them the same way. A fourth rhythm the help omits is not a corner case — weekly and biweekly are first-class choices in detection proposals, and an owner typing one of them by hand meets no refusal, only success.

The two cannot both be true: the help presents a two-rhythm vocabulary while the books enforce a four-rhythm vocabulary. Evidence points to docs drifting behind the code rather than the reverse — the validator and form handle all four rhythms deliberately, with anchors, snapping and day rules tuned per rhythm, none of which reads like accidental tolerance.

An owner reading the help while adding a rule by hand never learns they could formalize a weekly payment there, the exact pattern the detection flow exists to surface — the feature hides one surface away.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The claim was taken verbatim from the recurrence parser's flag help in the CLI wiring. Against it stand three independently traced sites: the seeded form's weekly branch prompting for a weekday anchor, the gap-band vocabulary producing weekly and biweekly proposals, and the admission checks validating all four frequencies with rhythm-specific rules. Classification rides the evidence: the drift side is the help text, since the code's four-rhythm handling is deliberate and heavily evidenced, while the help line reads as a leftover from a two-rhythm era. Consulted along the way: the proposal flow's rules, the form mechanism, and the command surface fact for the same program.

docs.title: Category check reads the owner s approved list date fields parse inline
Category check reads the owner's approved list; date fields parse inline
Title
docs.text: Category check reads the owner's approved list; date fields parse inline

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The admission gate runs as one inline validator that reads the owner's own category list and parses the calendar fields at the moment of saving, refusing with the reason before any write.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The rule's checks run as one function of a few dozen lines that receives the completed rule and answers with either an empty string or the reason. Each check speaks in the household's phrasing and runs in order: the description must be present, the category must appear in the list the owner has approved for their own books (read from the product's configuration at check time), the amount must be non-zero, the rhythm must be one of the four supported, day and month must sit within their ranges when the rhythm needs them, and weekly rhythms need their start anchor present. Date fields are parsed with the language's own calendar reader; a start that cannot be read and an end before the start each get their own reason. Because the function answers with reasons rather than raising, the caller shows the reason verbatim and leaves the store untouched.

docs.title: Confirm commit via the retire flavored add path and retire then drop ordering
Confirm commit via the retire-flavored add path and retire-then-drop ordering
Title
docs.text: Confirm commit via the retire-flavored add path and retire-then-drop ordering

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A confirmation is one retire-flavored mutation built by the shared add path; the ledger applies it idempotently and the promise store is rewritten only after the posting applied.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: _commit_expected (confirm.py:38-61) refuses amount-less items upstream of the engine, then calls the shared add path with retires=[t.id] — the shared builder picks ConfirmMutation when the retire list is non-empty (commands.py:108-115). ConfirmMutation. apply_on (journal.py:271-284) returns the existing entry when the mutation's identity already landed (idempotent re-apply) and otherwise inserts the transaction with linked=[*self.retires, *self.linked] — the old open item's id rides the booking's linked chain. Only after a successful apply does _commit_expected reload and rewrite the promise store without the retired row (lines 59-60) — a failed apply leaves the promise standing and nothing half-open. The group re-points expected-member ids inside a freshly reloaded membership list after each commit (confirm.py:165-170).

docs.title: Corrective rows append update and delete mutations never amend the checkpoint store
Corrective rows append Update and Delete mutations, never amend the checkpoint store
Title
docs.text: Corrective rows append Update and Delete mutations, never amend the checkpoint store

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every committed repair appends a stamped, content-addressed Update, Delete or Confirm mutation to the journal and re-folds the ledger; no code path rewrites committed rows in place.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The update command builds an update mutation carrying the full replacement of the editable fields, the delete command a delete mutation carrying the victim's content as it stood, and the landed-promise correction a retiring add in one mutation. The write step is single: it stamps the repair with a creation time, derives its content identity, appends it to the journal, re-folds the ledger from checkpoint plus the fresh tail and re-checkpoints. The folded journal, not the checkpoint store, is the truth; the checkpoint is a cache the fold can rebuild. Callers read back the applied entry by the mutation's identity to report the new balance to the owner.

docs.title: Date and amount gates inline in the confirm desks
Date and amount gates inline in the confirm desks
Title
docs.text: Date and amount gates inline in the confirm desks

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The future-day and amount refusals are inline guards comparing the item's date to today and its amount to None before any commit call.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: _confirm_expected checks t.date > date.today().isoformat() (line 68) and t.amount_eur is None (line 74) before _commit_expected; _confirm_instance routes future occurrences (occurrence_date > TODAY(), line 111) to the interactive walk whose own gate refuses confirmed_date > TODAY() (line 669), and the interactive walk refuses amount 0 at line 693. _confirm_group filters members the same way per member (lines 146, 149, 152). The refusal is a fail-stop return with a console message; nothing writes.

docs.title: Date positioned insertion and balance propagation
Summary
docs.text: Ledger.insert finds the date-predecessor via find_parent (latest row dated on or before the new date), chains balances from it, rehashes, inserts at idx+1, then propagate shifts the tail.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: find_parent scans all rows for date <= anchor and takes the last one — the balance base for the new row. The inserted row receives parent balances plus its own postings, is stamped with a fresh hash, and lands immediately after the predecessor so the list stays date-sorted even for backdated entries. propagate then walks every row after the insertion point, adding the new postings to each row's balances and rehashing each — that is the whole propagation story, a simple forward pass. When no predecessor exists (entry before the very first row), balances start from an empty dict — _validate refuses that case up front for a non-empty ledger.

docs.title: Exception recording scans all same description rules
Exception recording scans all same-description rules
Summary
docs.text: A drifted commit writes the occurrence date into the exceptions list of every rule matching the description and category; the group path re-checks coverage at confirm time with the same window constants.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: commit_instance (recurrence_cli.py:634-639) computes the covered test with AMOUNT_TOLERANCE and DAY_WINDOW; on drift it loads the recurrence store and appends the occurrence ISO date to rule.exceptions for every rule where rule.description == rule_hit.description and rule.category == rule_hit.category — a sibling-rule wide sweep, not just the hit rule — then saves. The group confirm path (_confirm_group, confirm.py:183-192) re-derives "covered" for r-members by scanning the whole ledger for a checking posting whose category, amount tolerance and day window match the occurrence, before calling commit_instance.

docs.title: Hash guards detect a silently altered entry
Hash guards detect a silently altered entry
Title
docs.text: Hash guards detect a silently altered entry

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Each stored row carries a 16-hex hash over its canonical content minus the guard itself; verify() recomputes and compares to detect tampering.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Every row's guard is a short hash over all its content excluding the guard field, so any altered field — including the stored identity, which is inside the hashed payload — mismatches on verification. The mutation identity runs the same scheme one level up: a hash over the canonical mutation minus the identity, meaning the identity doubles as an anti-corruption validator. The canonical form sorts keys and drops empty values so that equal content always produces equal bytes.

docs.title: Idempotent re apply returns the stored row unchanged
Idempotent re-apply returns the stored row unchanged
Title
docs.text: Idempotent re-apply returns the stored row unchanged

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: AddMutation.apply_on looks the mutation id up in the ledger first and returns the existing transaction when found, never inserting a second row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The content-plus-timestamp identity is assigned just before the mutation is appended, and apply_on consults it on every landing: find first, insert only when absent. This makes journal replay naturally idempotent for adds — refolding the same journal or re-applying the same mutation cannot double a balance. The same discipline is why a repeated identical statement with the same creation timestamp folds into one entry; a second capture with a different timestamp reads as a different movement.

docs.title: Instance lookup re expands the schedule so hidden dates stay resolvable
Instance lookup re-expands the schedule so hidden dates stay resolvable
Title
docs.text: Instance lookup re-expands the schedule so hidden dates stay resolvable

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: _find_instance rebuilds each active rule's occurrence dates live and hashes each candidate with the same deterministic scheme; exceptions and superseding are never consulted, so any date in the window resolves.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The resolver never looks at the view's listed rows: it takes the fresh rule store, drops inactive rules, re-expands each remaining rule's occurrences over the window (anchor date minus the 35-day lookback to today plus 400 days), and matches the owner-supplied address against a content hash recomputed from rule and date. Because expansion is pure schedule math and the hash is deterministic, the same instance yields the same address at any time — which is why dates removed from the view by exceptions or by a covering booking still resolve, while only a paused (inactive) rule disappears from matching. The window's anchor fallback (the ledger's last committed row, else today) keeps landed-but-uncommitted occurrences reachable even before an out-of-order anchor exists.

docs.title: Landed promise correction rides the retire flavored confirm commit
Landed-promise correction rides the retire-flavored confirm commit
Title
docs.text: Landed-promise correction rides the retire-flavored confirm commit

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The edit-to-actual path posts via the confirmation mutation flavor, carrying the retired promise's id with the corrected amount, and removes the promise afterwards.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The landed-promise path reuses the confirmation desk's commit: the add mutation is created in its confirm flavor, which lists the promise being retired alongside any further references, so a single journal record carries both the landed row and which promise it settles. The corrected amount and restated fields ride the same record. Only after that record has applied does the desk remove the promise from the register; a refused commit leaves the promise standing untouched. An amount-less promise is refused before the commit is attempted, with the reason named.

docs.title: Ledger.update composes delete then insert and reverses with negative postings
Ledger.update composes delete-then-insert and reverses with negative postings
Title
docs.text: Ledger.update composes delete-then-insert and reverses with negative postings

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An edit applies as full remove-then-reinsert with negatives reversing the old postings; a delete removes the row and shifts its negatives over the tail; propagate shifts every later row and rehashes each.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The engine has only two balance-moving primitives, removal and insertion, and every higher-level repair composes them. An edit is remove-then-reinsert, so a moved day simply inserts at the new date position; the row's stable identity rides along and every reference to it elsewhere keeps pointing at the same row. Removing a row applies its postings negated over the entire later tail, then the reinsertion applies the new balance effects and shifts the tail after it — leaving the whole chain re-derived and freshly rehashed. A plain removal shifts only the negated old postings. No path edits balances directly; the propagated chain is the only state.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: postings_for puts the rounded amount on 'checking' and — for the Overdracht category only — its rounded negation on 'savings'; apply_postings shifts both balance chains.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The transfer is not a special engine path: it is an ordinary posting set with two accounts in it. The category name is checked literally ('Overdracht'), and the mirror is computed at build time and stored in the mutation, so replay needs no category knowledge. Ledger.apply_postings adds each posting to the matching account's balance, which is how one entry moves both accounts and how propagate shifts every later row's copy of both balances.

docs.title: Pre image delete mutation with live row verification
Pre-image delete mutation with live-row verification
Summary
docs.text: cmd_delete reads the victim from the live ledger before appending, copies its full content into the DeleteMutation (date, description, category, postings, linked, target), and fails closed with an unappended zero-value mutation when the target is unknown.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
cmd_delete (commands.py:152-176) resolves the target against the live ledger first. Unknown target: a sentinel DeleteMutation is returned without ever being appended — the (mutation, False) pair lets the caller distinguish "nothing happened" from a real delete. A real delete: DeleteMutation(date=victim.date, description, category, postings=dict(victim.postings), linked=list(victim.linked), target=target) rides append_and_apply. The pre-image discipline is the delete's own data layout — the docstring (journal.py:312-319) states date/description/category/postings/linked ARE the victim's content, not the deletion's execution data.

At fold time apply_on (journal.py:323-346) re-resolves the target, returns None for a still-unknown target (replay idempotence), and compares canonical(preimage) == canonical(live) across date, description, category, postings, linked; any difference raises ValueError("delete : pre-image mismatch — journal snapshot does not match the live row; refusing to delete"). The guard makes a replay of a stale retraction fail loudly instead of deleting a row whose current content differs from the snapshot the journal holds.

docs.title: Prompt walk collects changed fields and fails closed after three tries
Prompt walk collects changed fields and fails closed after three tries
Title
docs.text: Prompt walk collects changed fields and fails closed after three tries

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: All four fields prompt pre-filled; a retry cap abandons the correction; a future-dated actual row warns early; change-only diffs feed the mutation, and an all-Enter walk on a landed promise is the confirm.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The desk shows every editable field with its current value; Enter keeps it, so untouched fields never carry a retype mistake into the repair. Three failed answers on one field (a bad date or a bad amount) abandon the whole correction with nothing stored. The day field warns while collecting when a posted row is being corrected to a future day, so the owner knows before committing that the row will transfer to the promises register. The walk returns only genuinely changed fields: confirming everything unchanged produces no repair at all. Amount prompting enforces the non-zero rule at the desk for real rows but lets a promise keep a deliberate zero. On a promise whose day has landed, confirming everything unchanged IS the confirmation — the walk's outcome doubles as the owner's "this happened as promised".

docs.title: The gap band classifier reads rhythm from date gaps
The gap-band classifier reads rhythm from date gaps
Title
docs.text: The gap-band classifier reads rhythm from date gaps

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Rhythm classification sorts a payment's dates, measures the day gaps between consecutive occurrences, and returns the first band — weekly, biweekly, monthly or yearly — holding at least the required gap count.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The classification is a band table applied to the gaps between consecutive occurrence dates: weekly accepts gaps of five to nine days, biweekly eleven to seventeen, monthly twenty-six to thirty-eight, yearly three hundred sixty to three hundred seventy-two. The bands never overlap, and they are judged most-specific first, so a payment that mostly shows week-long gaps with one skipped week (a gap near fourteen days) still reads as weekly rather than biweekly.

The pass bar is one fewer than the occurrence minimum — three occurrences need two in-band gaps — and when no band holds enough gaps the payment produces no rhythm at all. This one function is the sole timing authority: both detector tiers hand it their sorted dates, and every proposal's frequency came from it.

docs.title: The seeded field loop with quit at any field abort
The seeded field loop with quit-at-any-field abort
Title
docs.text: The seeded field loop with quit-at-any-field abort

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The adoption form is one linear prompt walk where every answer carries its detected default; a quit key at any prompt discards the whole walk and returns nothing.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The form walks its prompts in a fixed order — description, category, amount, frequency, then the frequency-specific question (weekday anchor for weekly or biweekly, day-of-month otherwise, month for yearly), then start date, then optional end date. Each prompt carries its current value as the default: Enter keeps it, typed text replaces it.

The abort path is mechanical, not a mode: typing the quit key as an answer terminates the walk immediately and returns nothing, regardless of how far into the walk the owner is. The category question routes through the shared category asker rather than a free-text prompt, and the amount answer is parsed separately so an unparseable or zero amount ends the walk as a refusal. The weekly and biweekly branch snaps a typed weekday name forward onto the start date — the weekday aliases cover both Dutch and English day names — turning a bare day word into a concrete calendar anchor.

The form returns a completed rule value or nothing; the saving decision — checks then store — lives one layer up, so this form alone can never put a rule into the books.

docs.title: Tier a falls back to tier b inside the detector
Tier A falls back to Tier B inside the detector
Title
docs.text: Tier A falls back to Tier B inside the detector

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The detector runs the steady-amount tier first and falls through to the timely-varying tier over all rows when the steady occurrences' dates fail to classify.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Both detector tiers live in one function on the recurrences module. The grouping pass buckets committed actual transactions by their description-category pair, skips rows with no date or a zero amount, and drops any pair already named by an existing rule. For each surviving group it computes the amount median and the inlier band — amounts within max(5% of |median|, 0.50) — then attempts Tier A: dates of the inlier rows go through the gap-band classifier, and a classification yields a proposal carrying the median.

When the inlier dates do not classify, control deliberately falls through to Tier B: the gap classifier runs again, this time over ALL rows' dates, with the median as nominal amount and \[min(amounts), max(amounts)\] attached as amount_range. Two guards sit in front of Tier B — the single-sign check (mixed ± groups continue silently) and the minimum-occurrence floor — and a proposal dict carries frequency-specific keys: day for monthly, month+day for yearly, none for weekly/biweekly.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Journal-native command mutations (roadmap step 6): every mutating command (add / edit / delete / fixes) builds a mutation, appends it to the canonical journal, and persists the checkpoint. There is no intermediate store: the journal IS the store of record, the ledger's engine owns balance chaining and date ordering, and ledger.json is the snapshot the next boot hydrates from.

Mutation ids are content hashes (one hash scheme end-to-end); machine paths stamp a monotonic ts so identical content still yields distinct ids (the Q8 lesson). Command failures happen BEFORE the append: a rejected command leaves no journal line, so every line records a change that actually happened.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Confirm an open entry in one step (financials confirm).

The fast path for the view's OPEN section: a landed-but-unconfirmed expected row (e####) or rule instance (r:-hash) is committed into the journaled ledger with the zero-prompt idiom — the stored values are taken as-is, no field prompts. The adjust path stays 'edit ' (prefilled prompts); a wrong confirm is recoverable via delete/edit, and the commit is journaled either way.

Resolver chain (same shape as edit/delete, exact ids only): t#### (committed hash) -> already actual: idempotent no-op (exit 0) e#### (expected) -> ConfirmMutation retires the e-row and the actual lands in one mutation; the expected row is dropped only after the confirm applied r:-hash (rule instance) -> AddMutation with the rule's own values; a covering commit supersedes the instance automatically, a drifted one is excepted Bare 'confirm' shows the OPEN section (the confirmation backlog) and asks which row to confirm. Anything unresolvable exits 2 with the standard 'Onbekende id' message.

Resolves the id in the committed ledger (hash id, full or unambiguous prefix) or the expected register (e####), shows the row, and requires an explicit confirmation (bare Enter is NOT yes). Actual rows are applied as one DeleteMutation carrying the victim's full pre-image (the engine verifies it against the live row and refuses loudly on mismatch). Expected rows are removed from the expected register (no balance chain).

There is no undo; the journal IS the audit trail of what was removed.

docs.text:
Change-set engine (roadmap step 6): apply reviewed fix files against the journaled ledger.

The change-set is an in-memory list of dicts (the internal contract); financials fix --file loads a JSON/TOML document and routes it through this engine. Field ops re-point at the committed ledger: each op becomes one UpdateMutation carrying the target's FINAL row state (idempotent, final-state semantics — the from-guard still prevents stale edits from clobbering newer values). remove_row emits a DeleteMutation targeting the victim's journal id (pre-image from the ledger). add_expected_row and e-targeted remove_row keep operating on the expected register (hypotheticals, overlay — never committed facts).

Every mutation is applied through the single write step (commands.append_and_apply): append → boot (replay) → checkpoint. A guard violation aborts BEFORE any append, so every journal line records a change that actually happened.

docs.text:
Groups: named rollups of projected/committed rows (financials group).

A group bundles related rows into one virtual row in the view — the credit-card statement case: every purchase of one statement is a member (e####, committed hash id, or r: rule instance) and the statement shows as a single "Mastercard" row with the summed amount on the payment date.

Groups are organization metadata, NOT money movement: they are not journaled (journal = committed money; expected + rules + groups = forecast inputs), they live in their own groups.json overlay, and membership edits never touch the member rows themselves. The projection is a VIEW: hiding members and rolling them up happens at render/walk time, and a group's members keep their ids — group add/remove only edits the membership list.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Quick-add shorthand parser for financials add "...".

Grammar (left to right, whitespace-separated): [date] [amount] [Category:]description

  • date: ISO (2026-09-12), vandaag/today, morgen/tomorrow, overmorgen, gisteren/yesterday, eergisteren, or ±Nd relative days (e.g. -3d). Relative days REQUIRE the d suffix — bare "-25" is always an amount.
  • amount: signed (+/-) or currency-marked (€/eur) number, comma decimal allowed, 0 rejected. A bare unsigned number is NEVER an amount — it stays part of the description ("25 jaar jubileum" keeps its text).
  • rest: description, optionally "Category: description" where Category case-insensitively matches an approved category.

Anything omitted is prompted afterwards by the caller (date defaults to today via Enter); nothing is ever silently assumed.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
The TUI's step-3 add dialog: a native Textual form (modal screen) for financials tui's a key.

One source of truth for the RULES: validation, projection and the save mutations are imported from the CLI modules (entry._validate / _validate_amount, commands.projected_checking / cmd_add, expected.add_expected) — only the PROMPTING is native widgets. The same dispatch as the CLI applies: a future date saves to the expected register instead of the journal (no balance chaining — expected rows have no balances), and the CLI's future-date rejection inside entry._validate is bypassed by dispatching BEFORE it (CLI parity: entry.add_transaction dispatches before _validate too).

Form: Datum / Omschrijving / Categorie / Bedrag / checking-saldo confirmation. Enter walks the fields (Tab works natively too); on the saldo field Enter submits. Esc cancels (dismiss(None)).

The category is a FUZZY AUTOCOMPLETE (textual-autocomplete), not free text: the approved categories (config-driven, call time) are offered in a dropdown the moment the field takes focus — an empty input shows ALL of them (questionary-style), typing narrows fuzzily. Enter completes the highlighted match and advances to the next field (the library intercepts Enter/Tab while the dropdown is visible; a mouse click completes too). Esc with the dropdown open only hides it — a second Esc cancels the dialog. Enter on a hidden dropdown accepts an EXACT approved category; anything else is refused inline (submit re-validates every value, so a Tab-past is caught at the gate too). A bare 'q' in any field cancels (CLI parity).

The saldo confirmation shows the live projection for the typed date+amount; blank accepts the projection (the data-quality gate is "you saw the number", the typed value is never stored — balances are engine-computed). Enter-driven — no per-keystroke ledger boots.

Tests: pilot-pressable. Validation errors render inline (a Static line) instead of rich console output.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
The TUI (steps 1–3): a scrollable ledger view — Textual App + DataTable, consuming build_view (the same composition as list; one composition, two renderers) — the step-2 readonly detail dialog, and the step-3 add dialog (a, implemented in tui/add.py).

Keys: up/down (j/k) move the row cursor one row; pageup/pagedown by page; home/end jump to the first/last row; q or escape quits; a opens the add dialog; enter opens the detail dialog on an entry row. The DataTable clamps at the first/last row by itself (no offset math here) and auto-scrolls the viewport when the cursor reaches a screen edge. The table holds the FULL committed history above the actuals window; the initial view is positioned on the projection: the PROJECTIE row at the bottom of the viewport with the 10 rows above it starting at the top, so the forecast's near future is what you see first.

Row design: every entry row is TWO lines tall — the Datum column holds the date; the merged second column holds the id (line 1, dim) and "description / category" (line 2); the amount and the two balances are their own single-line columns. Section separators stay one line (label in the merged column). The merged column FILLS: the other columns stay content-sized and it takes every remaining cell (fit_columns — DataTable has no flex columns), so the numbers end flush at the right edge. Rows are mixed-height (add_row height=2); only the initial-position scroll math needs line offsets — cursor, keys and dialogs stay row-based.

Step 2: Enter on an entry row opens the readonly DetailScreen (the row's full data + a provenance status line); Esc/q closes it. The screen composes from the entry tuple so the editable step reuses it.

Step 3: a opens the AddScreen form (native widgets; the validation and save rules are imported from the CLI modules). On save the table rebuilds from a fresh build_view and the cursor lands on the newly added row; a toast confirms the new id.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time bootstrap for the journaled ledger (roadmap step 1).

See docs/journaled-ledger.md. Reads the current stores and emits, into a STAGING directory (default: /migration — never the live store root, never overwriting existing outputs without --force):

events.jsonl append-only journal: two opening events (seed balances, derived from the first row) + one committed event per actual row, in replay order; NO sequence numbers — the row order IS the order. id = 16-hex content hash over the canonical event minus id (self-validating, idempotent appends, deterministic bootstrap) ledger.json checkpoint: folded entries + computed balances + tip (id of the last journal event — the watermark) expected.json pruned hypotheticals (balances and source_line stripped) rules.json recurrences, carried as-is (they never had balances)

Seed rule (decided 2026-09-18): opening = first row's recorded balance minus that row's own effect on the account. Worked example t0001 (2024-11-24, Huur, +350,00, recorded 3.126,47 / 20.000,00): checking opening = 3126.47 - 350.00 = 2776.47 savings opening = 20000.00 (no transfer in the first row)

Op vocabulary (final): add | update | delete | confirm. No opening op (openings are ordinary add mutations: "Opening", Inkomsten); no reconcile op — money that moved without a transaction becomes an explicit correction TRANSACTION (owner policy 2026-09-18: "I will always create a transaction implementing the mutation"); the bootstrap derives those correction rows and lists them for review.

Every mutation carries ts (creation time, part of the hashed content): identical content then yields DISTINCT ids (two Q8 rows stay two rows — the 2026-09-19 duplicate-collapse incident). Machine-minted rows get a monotonic clock (never repeats); human entries rely on manual distinctness. Ids are minted through journal.py's Mutation classes, so bootstrap and engine share one hash scheme.

Verification gate (two-tier): HARD: the folded TIP must equal the recorded tip — the one comparison that validates the entire amount chain end-to-end. On failure: report, exit non-zero, write NOTHING. SOFT: per-row balance deviations are counted and shown; after the correction pass this must be EMPTY — any survivor is an inconsistency between corrections and the fold.

Run by the owner (Makefile target: migration-boostrap): uv run python scripts/bootstrap_journal.py

Live ids e0092–e0099 (8 runs). The promotion's drift guard correctly refused: these rows exist ONLY in the live store, absent from the bootstrap baseline.

This script removes ONLY rows matching the exact signature below; any row with the id but different content REFUSES the run (owner data is never guessed away). Backup before write; post-verify the store parses.

docs.text:
One-time data promotion (roadmap step 6, phase D1–D6).

Moves the migration staging stores to their canonical locations and retires the old stores — renamed with a timestamp, never destroyed. After this, command_journal() resolves to /journal.jsonl (the staging file no longer exists) and the app boots from the promoted stores with no further change.

Moves (in order, rollback = copy the backups back): D1 data/journal.jsonl -> backups/journal.jsonl.retired- (old audit trail) D4 migration/journal.jsonl -> data/journal.jsonl (the event journal) migration/ledger.json -> data/ledger.json (its checkpoint) D2 data/transactions.json -> backups/transactions.json.retired- D3 data/expected.json -> backups/expected.json.retired- migration/expected.json -> data/expected.json (pruned baseline) D5 migration/rules.json deleted ONLY when byte-identical to data/recurrences.json (which stays put); refusal otherwise D6 migration/ removed when empty

Guards: - pre-flight: the staging journal folds cleanly and its tip is recorded; the same tip must hold after the move (the move is byte-preserving) - expected.json drift check: any row present in the LIVE store but missing from the staging baseline REFUSES the promotion loudly (rows added after the bootstrap would be lost) — the owner decides - post-verify: load_ledger() from the promoted location == the pre-flight fold (ids + balances)

Run (Makefile target: migration-promote): uv run python scripts/promote_stores.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/promote_stores.py --write # backups + move + verify

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time regeneration: rewrite the staging checkpoint to the canonical fold (roadmap step 6 boot requirement).

Why: the staged migration/ledger.json was written by the bootstrap's file-order evidence pass (step 1). Step 3 made the engine's date-positioned fold THE canonical fold (design note, 2026-09-21), so the staged checkpoint's ROW ORDER is stale wherever a journal row's date differs from its file position (the 47 known inversion rows). Balances are fine (tip holds: unchanged from the bootstrap) — only the order is stale, but load_ledger hydrates rows as persisted, so a stale order boots the ledger in non-date order until a tail replay re-derives it. This script folds the journal canonically and persists the result atomically.

Run (Makefile target: migration-recheckpoint): uv run python scripts/recheckpoint.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/recheckpoint.py --write # backup + rewrite + verify

Verification gate: after writing, hydration from the new checkpoint must equal a fresh fold exactly (ids + balances), and the tip balances must hold at the bootstrap values.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
One-time repair: re-mint stale mutation ids in the migration journal.

The step-2 observer bug (2026-09-19): four live confirm rows were appended by a writer that stamped ts into the journal line but minted the id over content WITHOUT ts. The id doubles as the row's anti-corruption validator (16-hex content hash over the canonical mutation minus the id), so those rows now fail fold()'s rehash verification — the fold refuses loudly.

This script scans the journal, re-derives the id from each mismatched row's own content (the content itself is never touched), and rewrites ONLY the affected lines. Everything else stays byte-identical.

Run (Makefile target: migration-remint): uv run python scripts/remint_journal_ids.py # dry-run: report only uv run python scripts/remint_journal_ids.py --write # backup + repair + verify

Verification gate: after writing, the full journal must fold cleanly (at the bootstrap tip balances); the script refuses to write when the scan finds nothing, and reports loudly when the post-fold check fails.

docs.title: Docstring
docs.text:
Shared test fixtures: journal + expected-store isolation.

Every test runs with the canonical journal resolved through financials.fixes.journal_file pointed at a temporary directory — so running the suite never appends to the owner's real journal — and with the expected store pointed at a tmp file too: fix flows legitimately READ the expected register (e.g. add_expected_row's id-uniqueness check), and reading the owner's real store would make tests depend on live data (or crash on its row shape). A test that wants the live stores overrides these fixtures explicitly.

docs.title: Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history
Adopting a detected recurring payment
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The ledger already holds the habit; this flow makes the books say so. Only settled, fully described payments feed the grouping — Only settled history feeds detection — so every proposal names money that actually moved. Payments the owner has already formalized stay silent (A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed), which keeps the list a to-do that shrinks as habits are adopted. And because detection is read-only (Detection never saves a rule), the owner can ask for the list as often as they like without ever changing what the books anticipate.

Two tiers of answer come back. A steady payment — the rent, the subscription whose figure barely moves — proposes its median outright (A steady-amount payment proposes its median). A budget-style payment that keeps its appointment for changing figures proposes the same middle value but carries its observed low and high openly (A timely varying-amount payment proposes its median with its spread), so the owner sees the spread at a glance. A payment that swings between income and expense is refused as one habit (A payment habit mixing income and expense is never one pattern).

Nothing is created by looking. Naming a proposal opens a form pre-filled with the detected values; the owner accepts each field or retypes it, and quitting at any point stores nothing. Only a completed walk that passes the admission checks saves the rule (Only complete admissible rules are saved) — refused rules come back with their reason and the books stay untouched. A saved rule immediately shows its next three anticipated dates, and from then on the forecast generates its instances without further typing.

docs.title: Author a standing recurrence rule by hand
Authoring a rule by hand
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The owner sometimes knows an obligation before the books ever see it: a fresh subscription, a rent change, a yearly insurance premium. Authoring a rule turns that knowledge into a standing schedule directly — one complete statement of description, category, amount and rhythm, or a walk whose questions ask only for what is missing, where pressing Enter keeps the offered answer.

Two quiet mechanics shape what gets stored. A weekly or biweekly rhythm named by weekday moves the start forward to the first matching day, and every occurrence then lands on that weekday for the schedule's life. No bar compares the start with today: a blank start becomes the authoring day, and a readable past start passes just as freely as a future one — the owner may backdate a rule that was truly running before it was written down.

Before anything stores, the rule meets the same admission bars as an adopted schedule: a non-empty description, a category the owner approved, a non-zero amount, one of four rhythms, sane day and month ranges, readable dates, and an end never before the start. A refusal names its bar, and the store stays untouched. The saved schedule then confirms itself with the cadence in plain words and the next three dates the forecast will anticipate — yet books nothing. The ledger carries no entry for a rule until a real payment or an explicit confirmation touches it.

Later life runs through the same store's doors, with the same care. Pause silences a schedule while every field and its history stay stored, and resume brings it back as it stood (paused rules keep their place); removal ends the rule permanently, and only after the owner sees the exact rule and types yes (removal waits for a stated yes). One habit to watch: pressing Enter on the anchor question keeps a silent default, pinning a weekly schedule to whatever weekday the authoring day fell on — the printed cadence line is the only place that shows it.

docs.title: Commit a recurring rule instance into the ledger
Process story — booking a standing rule's month
docs.text:
process-story · for client

A standing rule promises the same bill every month; this is where one month's promise becomes money. The owner brings the projected occurrence to a door, and the plain case is the confirmation desk: hand it an occurrence whose day has landed and it posts the movement exactly as the rule promised, no questions. A day still ahead can be walked through first, every value offered prefilled, the day shifted to when the money actually landed. Two doors reshape rather than book. An occurrence that will differ becomes a one-off promise of its own while the rule skips just that month — but the reshaping door refuses a promise dated today, the one date the doors disagree on, so an owner moving the day to today loses the typing. For a month that should never book at all, a waived rent or a dead subscription, one typed yes is enough and the forecast goes quiet. The desk then scores the posting against the rule's mark — the right category, essentially the promised amount, near the promised day — and either the month counts as handled or the drift is recorded as the rule's exception and stops nagging. Suppression itself leaves no trail in the books, only silence; and a suppressed occurrence still answers to its own address, so the same month can walk back through the booking door.

docs.title: Confirm a landed open entry into the books
Process story — confirming landed entries
docs.text:
process-story · for client

Money has moved, and the books must now say so. The owner accepts a landed entry — named by its address, or picked from the desk's open list when nothing was named — and it commits without a single prompt, because every detail was settled when the promise was made (a landed open item confirms as promised). The posting enters as a real journal entry with running balances on both accounts, and the promise retires behind it, its old address kept on the booking's own record.

Some doors stay shut. Money that has not moved yet is refused and left open — a promise cannot become history ahead of its day (confirmation never lands ahead of the real day), and a movement with no stated amount cannot be booked at all (no amount, no confirmation). An address the books already hold confirms as a quiet no-op, safe to re-run with no double entry (already committed confirms as nothing to do), and a transfer confirmation warns that both accounts moved together.

Whole groups clear in one pass. Landed members commit in day order, each retired member's address re-pointing to its committed one, while still-future members are skipped with a note and the group itself stands (a group commits its landed members and keeps the group). When the landed item traces to a standing rule, a booking that drifted from the rule's mark — a different amount, or a day outside the window — is recorded as an exception for the owner to judge; an on-mark booking supersedes the occurrence (off-mark bookings count as exceptions). The owner hears the outcome with the new account state.

docs.title: Correct a posted entry through the journal
Entry correction
docs.text:
process-story · for client

A posted entry shows a mistake — an amount typo, the wrong category, a day from another month — and the owner picks the entry by address, or from the last ten rows when no address springs to mind. The editor reads that address first: it may name a committed book row, a promise for the future, one occurrence of a standing rule, or a whole group. Groups and rule occurrences are corrected in another editor entirely, so this walk serves only the books and the promises register; an address matching nothing ends in an unknown-address refusal, and nothing changed. On a committed row the fields come one at a time — day, description, category, amount — each pre-filled with the value standing now. Enter keeps a value; three failed answers on a field abandon the whole correction, again with nothing changed. Correcting a row to a day after today moves it out of the books: the row is backed out and its corrected content is reserved as a promise for the new day, and the owner is told plainly when that reservation is refused — the tomorrow rule. A promise whose day has already arrived commits into the books in the same act and retires from the register — the landed-promise rule. Every committed repair keeps history intact: the fix lands as a new appended record behind the old content — the record-not-typed rule — and the balance chain re-applies past it, so every later row reflects the fix while the books still show what the entry said before. The owner leaves with the new checking balance; a transfer touched along the way warns that the savings side moved with it.

docs.title: Record a money movement in the journaled ledger
Recording a money movement
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The owner notices money has moved — a bill paid, income arrived — and states it in whatever precision the moment gives: fully flagged, a quick shorthand breath like "gisteren -25 Kafe", or field by field when asked. However the statement arrives, one admission gate stands before anything is stored — a real calendar day, words saying what happened, a category on the approved list, a non-zero amount, and no date after today — One admission gate for every stated movement — and a refusal is spoken plainly, the books left exactly as they were. The quick statement is held to mean what it says: a token written like an amount either reads as one or the whole line is turned down, never quietly absorbed into the description — The quick statement must mean what it says. A statement dated ahead of today is never recorded as fact; it redirects to the expected register as a promise — Future promises never enter the balance chain — and Registering a future payment picks that thread up from there. When fields stay open, the intake shows the checking balance the movement would produce and asks for agreement; three disagreements abandon the whole movement, and a quit, an abort or an interrupt records nothing — Backing out leaves the books untouched. A rehearsal behaves the same way in miniature, showing the entry and its projected balances while storing nothing — A rehearsal stores nothing. An accepted movement lands as an entry the books stand behind: the row slots into date order, takes over the balances of the nearest prior day, and shifts every later day by the same amount, so any balance read from the books is the arithmetic of the chain up to that day — Every entry lands with balances it stands behind. Stating the same movement twice within one creation moment stores it once; the second telling returns the first entry — Recording twice changes nothing the second time. Money moved between the owner's own accounts rides a single entry that touches both accounts, so the household total stands still while the split follows the real move — A transfer moves both accounts. The owner hears back the stored identity and the running balances — or the plain reason nothing changed.

docs.title: Register a future payment in the expected register
Registering a future payment
docs.text:
process-story · for client

The rent lands next Tuesday, the salary is on its way, and the owner wants both visible without touching the real balance. Stating a future movement — amount, day, and what it is for — parks a promise in the expected register: every view shows it as an open item, actual money stays untouched, and the promise waits for its day. Two doors lead there. The expect command takes a fully stated movement on purpose, and the ordinary add command funnels into the same register whenever the stated day lies ahead of today — the books will not record a future movement as if it had already happened. Only a complete statement is parked. The register checks that the day reads as a real calendar day, the description says what is coming, the category is on the approved list, and an amount was stated at all; any shortfall earns a plainly worded refusal with nothing stored — Only complete future-dated statements enter the expected register — while a promised zero passes exactly where the actual ledger would refuse one — A zero-amount promise is admitted, an amountless one refused. The today-boundary runs double-stranded too: the register wants a promise ahead of today and the ledger enforces the same divide from its side, so money that has already moved can never end up posing as a promise. Nothing is written blind — a rehearsal shows precisely what would be stored and stores nothing. Once parked the promise carries its own identity and awaits its day; confirmation, told in a story of its own, turns it into a real ledger entry and the cycle closes there.

docs.title: Retract a wrong entry from the books with confirmation
Retract a wrong entry
docs.text:
process-story · for client

An owner catches an entry that should never have hit the books — a duplicate, or something that simply is not real. The delete command takes the id by name, or offers the last ten posted rows to pick from. The chosen row prints first, and nothing moves until the owner types a clear yes; a bare Enter or any other word leaves the books untouched.

The kind of wrongness sets the shape. A committed entry never vanishes in place: its removal lands in the journal as one record carrying the entry's full prior state, so the books can be built up again and prove exactly what left — and every later balance re-reads as if the row had never posted. A promised future payment is dropped from its register, since it never weighed on the books. A deleted group takes only the grouping with it, the member entries staying put. A projected occurrence goes quiet for one date while its rule keeps running. An address the books cannot resolve ends the attempt with nothing written at all.

When the removed entry moved money between two accounts, the retraction warns the owner to re-check both sides. One neighbouring door stays unguarded: the promises register's standalone remove action drops a promise without printing it or asking.

docs.title: Archetype mapping
docs.text:
archetype-mapping · for client

The product is a personal bookkeeping journal — one keeper's recurring answers to "did the money move, and what is left?" — built so every recorded answer can be proven rather than trusted. The founding distinction is actual versus expected (Actual versus expected): a movement that happened enters the journaled books, carries and shifts real balances, and is guarded against tampering; a movement promised for a future day weighs nothing, lives in its own register, and can still fail to happen. Nearly every rule in the territory follows from asking that one question.

The distinction organizes the component map. The journal engine (Ledger engine) folds each accepted change into dated transaction rows whose running balances chain from the row before, so the books are always a recomputation of recorded changes, never a state edited in place; the command pipeline (Command mutations) is the narrow write step every change passes. Intake (Entry intake) gates statements before anything lands, and the future-day cut (Future-day admission) sends tomorrow's money to the promise register (Expected register) instead of the books. The confirmation desk (Open-entry confirmation desk) is where a promise becomes a fact — the confirmation backlog (The confirmation backlog) is the gap between the two calendars, computed fresh at every view and never stored.

The repair side honours the same proven-over-trusted stance: the retraction desk (Entry retraction) takes a wrong entry out as its own written record that carries what was removed, and the editor (Entry editor) resolves one address across all four stores — books, promises, groups, rule occurrences — walking the keeper field by field before deciding where the corrected content belongs.

Anticipation is a second promise machinery. The recurrence planner (Recurrence planner) turns repeating history into standing schedules, but every detection result stays a proposal — information on screen, never commitment (Proposal) — and an occurrence carries no stored address at all: the same rule on the same date always derives the same address (The derivation of a projected occurrence's address), which is why a suppressed occurrence can still answer when named. A rule enters the books two ways — written by hand the moment the keeper recognizes an obligation, or adopted from history the books themselves reveal (Rule provenance — written by hand or adopted from history) — and both doors end at the same owner-checked form, so no way in skips the keeper's hands.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
executive-summary · for client

One household's cashflow books, built so every recorded fact can be proven rather than trusted — an evidence-first journal where changes are appended and balances are recomputation, never edited states.

The books prove themselves: every correction and removal is its own appended record carrying what changed, each row carries a hashed self-check, and re-landing the same movement stores it once (A correction is recorded, not typed) — judge any change near the journal against this property first.

Rule-occurrence confirmation can double-book: a group confirm skips an occurrence a real booking already covers, while the same occurrence confirmed by its own address commits again (A covered rule occurrence double-books when confirmed directly by its own address) — aligning that check across both confirm doors is the highest-value fix.

The removal ritual is not uniform: the expect remove door takes an id and deletes without showing the row or asking for a yes (The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming), one door away from the identical guarded operation.

Which side wins when a retraction record no longer matches the live books is decided nowhere (Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?) — an owner ruling is pending, and until then the keeper facing the refusal has no recovery door.

Next: read the SWOT analysis for the evidence behind each point and the product summary for the capability map. Verification: six objections were raised during the analysis and all six carry resolved markers at their target versions — no fact stands contested; the vault holds no separate coverage or run record.

docs.title: Product summary
docs.text:
product-summary · for client

The product keeps one household's cashflow books for a single keeper: it turns stated money movements into recorded facts the books stand behind, and every later question — what is left, what was wrong, what is still owed — reads from those facts rather than from an edited state. Recording a movement is one appended change; the books recompute a balance for any day from the change chain, each recorded row carries a self-check over its own content, and a hand-altered book fails verification instead of agreeing quietly (Every entry lands with balances it stands behind). Stating the same movement twice stores it once (Recording twice changes nothing the second time), and a transfer between the household's two accounts shifts both running balances through one entry (A transfer moves both accounts).

Movements are stated in three precisions — every detail flagged, a Dutch quick shorthand in one breath, or field by field — and all three pass the same admission gate: a real calendar day, words that say what happened, a category the keeper approved, an amount that is not zero, no date beyond today (One admission gate for every stated movement). A rehearsal shows the would-be balances and stores nothing (A rehearsal stores nothing); backing out at any prompt leaves the books untouched (Backing out leaves the books untouched); and a shorthand token that looks like an amount must parse as one or the whole statement is refused (The quick statement must mean what it says).

Money promised for a future day never enters the balance chain (Future promises never enter the balance chain): it parks in a separate register of open promises until its day arrives. Confirming then turns the promise into a booked fact exactly as it was promised, with no further questions (A landed open item confirms as it was promised); related promises confirm as one group, oldest first, each member re-pointed as it becomes a fact (Confirming a group commits its landed members and keeps the group), and a promise without an amount is refused everywhere (An open item without an amount is never confirmed).

When something is wrong, three repair desks take over. The correction desk records the fix rather than retyping it: one appended written record, nothing overwritten (A correction is recorded, not typed); an entry restated for a future day leaves the books and re-enters the promise register (An edit that lands tomorrow leaves the books). The retraction desk prints the victim row first and writes only on a typed affirmative answer (A retraction only writes after a stated yes), as one record carrying the removed content (A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood). No undo or restore comes after a retraction (No undo or restoration door after a retraction) — the shown-then-confirmed ritual is the safety, by design.

For payments that repeat, the product reads real payment history and proposes standing schedules; detection alone never saves a rule (Detection never saves a rule): every adopted value passes the keeper's hands in a form walk (Every adopted value passes the owner's hands), and only complete, admissible rules are saved (Only complete admissible rules are saved). A standing schedule never books anything by itself — it only makes the forecast anticipate (Hand-writing a rule never books anything); a real payment recorded in its window takes the scheduled entry's place, so a day never carries two truths.

docs.title: SWOT analysis
docs.text:
swot · for client

Evidence snapshot: the fact base was captured in a single pass on 2026-11-11 over a roughly thirteen-thousand-line Python codebase (47 modules, 637 symbols per financials); no separate coverage or run record exists in the vault, and all six recorded objections carry resolved markers at their target versions, so no fact is excluded here as contested.

Strengths: admission is one gate, not three — flagged, shorthand and prompted statements all pass the same five checks, so a movement admitted through the quick door could never have been refused at the slow one (One admission gate for every stated movement). What the books show rests on recomputation: every recorded movement chains its running balances from its date-predecessor and shifts every later day, so any balance is verifiable arithmetic rather than a stored claim (the balance-chain rule, with the date-positioned insertion and propagation pass behind it, Date-positioned insertion and balance propagation). Each row fails verification when its content is hand-altered (Hash guards detect a silently altered entry), which is what makes a quiet book-tamper impossible. Restating a movement stores it once, so replays cannot double a balance (Recording twice changes nothing the second time, Idempotent re-apply returns the stored row unchanged). Corrections are recorded, not retyped (A correction is recorded, not typed), and a retraction is one appended record carrying the removed content (A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood), so the books keep a replayable account and a rebuild proves a removal removed exactly what it claims. Removal writes only after the printed row and a typed affirmative (A retraction only writes after a stated yes), and the deliberate boundaries close the frame: no undo door after a retraction (No undo or restoration door after a retraction), and a standing schedule never books money by itself (Hand-writing a rule never books anything).

Weaknesses: the all-Enter gesture changes meaning by desk — a pure review on a posted row, but a finished confirmation on a promise whose day has arrived, with no signal at the moment of acting (All-Enter keeps a posted row but confirms a landed promise), so a booked money fact can commit by reflex. The already-covered booking check lives on one door only: a rule occurrence confirmed inside a group is skipped when a booking already covers it, while the same occurrence confirmed by its own address commits unconditionally (Group-skip check versus direct-commit when one rule occurrence is confirmed twice in one pass), so money that moved once can post a second time. One removal door takes an id and deletes with no printed row and no stated yes (The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming) — the trust the confirmation ritual builds fails at exactly that door. The same stated date is legal at the confirm desk and refused at the occurrence reshape, losing the keeper's typed work (Booking today wins through confirm but loses through the occurrence reshape). An unknown rule-instance address exits the confirm desk in silence, unlike every other unknown address (An unknown rule-instance address fails the confirm in silence). One knowledge gap stands where a business decision belongs: when a retraction record no longer matches the live books, the rebuild refuses loudly — but which side should win is undecided (Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?, question cited; the code's guess is pending human judgment), and the keeper facing that refusal has no recovery door. The add-help documentation names two payment rhythms while validation admits four (Add-flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms), so the weekly rule hides from the one input path built to write it.

Opportunities: the open decision above awaits an owner of the books — once ruled, the journal-versus-books standoff becomes specifiable behavior instead of a live dead end (the same hotspot, its guess pending). And the counterparty side of every promise is already a documented party with a stake: the anticipated payer keeps pending deliveries visible as open items in the register (Anticipated payer), which is precisely where the confirmation workflow concentrates the keeper's attention. This quadrant is thin by capture — exactly one hotspot and two actors were recorded.

Threats: the external exposure that is documented is delivery uncertainty itself — a promised movement may simply never happen, and the books hold it as an open item until the keeper confirms, so anticipated flow rests on the keeper working the backlog (Anticipated payer), bounded by the design that keeps promises out of the balance chain (Future promises never enter the balance chain). The sensitivity census carries eleven documented hazards, and every one describes a hazard inside the product's own doors rather than an external compliance or security exposure, so under the internal-versus-external frame none stands as a threat point: they are the weaknesses above seen from the keeper's side of the desk. The threats quadrant is correspondingly thin — one external dependency, stated without padding.

docs.title: The actors' story
docs.text:
family-story · for client

Only two named parties move through this product, and their difference is the whole design. The owner keeps the books; the anticipated payer stands on the other side of every promise the books are not allowed to record. One is a role, the other an external counterparty — and the product treats them so differently that the split explains the register, the confirmation desk and the future-date refusals all at once.

The owner is the single pair of hands: she states payments and income in whatever precision the moment allows, and every guard in the product exists to protect her. Rejections before an entry is accepted, the rehearsal run that previews balances without storing, the confirmations and retractions that ask for a stated yes — all of it shields one accountable person from a balance she cannot stand behind. Her care-about links run across the ledger, the register, the confirmation desk, corrections, retractions and the standing rules; no other actor touches any of that ground.

The anticipated payer is deliberately less visible. A rent due Friday or a salary expected next week is a promise, not a fact, and the counterparty may never deliver — so the promise parks in the expected register as an open item while the books stay quiet. When an owner statement carries a future date, the intake redirects it there rather than booking it as if the money had already moved. The payer appears in the movement, confirmation and correction processes precisely as that open promise, and keeps its own date honesty rules.

What the two facts agree on: nothing reaches the journaled books without the owner's action. The payer never records anything alone; their role is to be the reason promises exist, and to stay visible as an open item until the money lands and the owner confirms it. The census is complete — 2 actor facts, both read this pass.

docs.title: The components' story
docs.text:
family-story · for client

Eight components stand behind this product, and every one of them answers to one idea: the books are an append-only journal that folds into tamper-evident balances, and nothing enters a balance until the money has really moved. All eight carry the journaled-bookkeeping tag, so this is not a layered architecture story — it is one shared discipline seen from eight desks.

The discipline has three fixed points. Command mutations is the single narrow write step — every accepted change becomes one stamped mutation riding the journal — and the ledger engine folds those mutations into dated transaction rows whose running balances chain from their date-predecessor, hash-guarded against silent tampering, reloadable from checkpoint plus tail. Around that core sit the desks where the owner works: entry intake and its Dutch shorthand parser at the front door, open-entry confirmation turning landed promises into facts, entry editor and entry retraction correcting or removing what is already there, the expected register holding future-dated promises outside the balance chain entirely, and the recurrence planner turning repeated payments into anticipations that a real booking replaces.

The components cluster by what they protect. Four desks keep the owner from recording something the books cannot stand behind — intake checks and previews, confirmation refusing items ahead of today or missing amounts, the editor's field-by-field walk, and retraction demanding an explicit yes after printing the row in full. Two keep the books honest over time: the engine's chained balances and re-propagated corrections, and the register's rule that a promise never touches a balance until its day lands. The recurrence planner and the confirmation desk form the bridge between promises and facts — anticipations, confirmations and the same-day refusals that keep one truth per day.

One inconsistency travels through the set rather than being solved anywhere: the promises register can drop a promise through a standalone remove door without printing the row or demanding a yes, while every other desk protects that same owner with confirmations. The retraction component carries it openly, not as a design it defends.

docs.title: The concepts' story
docs.text:
family-story · for client

Every concept in this family turns on one everyday question — has the money moved? The founding actual-versus-expected distinction splits a movement in two: what has happened enters the journaled books, carrying and shifting real balances, guarded against tampering; what is promised for a future day stays in a separate register, weighs nothing against those balances and can still fail to happen.

Future-day admission applies the cut to the calendar. A movement stated for today or the past is a fact, and only the fact side moves balances; stated for a future day it becomes a promise with a deliberately narrow door — nothing parks in the register until the statement is complete — while the actual ledger refuses a future date outright. The books forgive a promise of zero, but a fact of zero is a mistake by definition.

Two mechanisms share one habit: the books compute what they predict rather than store it. The confirmation backlog is the clearest case — the gap between the register and the ledger, named "geland maar niet bevestigd" (landed but not confirmed). It has no store: the open list is projected at view time, and an item leaves only when a booking supersedes, retires or excepts it. A projected occurrence of a standing rule works the same way, since its address is derived from the rule's values and the date — retrievable even after a delete, yet schedule-bound, so adjusting the rule makes addresses noted from an older forecast stop matching.

The last two concepts tell how a schedule earns its place. Detection gathers a payment that repeats often enough into a proposal, but a proposal is information, not commitment: it lives only on screen, nothing remembers it was shown, and it may stay generous — a wide observed amount range, even an unknown category — because it holds no power over forecasts. Adoption is one of two doors into the rule store; the other receives obligations the owner knows before the books ever see them, like a new subscription or a rent change, written by hand. Both doors refuse an incomplete or impossible rule, and each carries its own trust story: a hand-written rule leans wholly on the owner's judgment, an adopted one on history's evidence.

Across all six the boundary holds: a promise never looks like a fact, a projection never lands in the balance chain, and no guess becomes a rule on the books' word.

docs.title: The processes' story
docs.text:
family-story · for client

Eight processes tell one story about this ledger: the owner states what happened or what is coming, and the books either change as agreed or stay untouched with the reason said plainly. Every process starts at the owner's noticing — money moved, money will move, a number repeats, a row is wrong — never with a decision the books take on their own.

The main arc runs through three processes. Recording a movement accepts whatever precision the moment gives — full detail, a Dutch quick-shorthand, or bare and prompted — and holds it behind one admission gate: a real calendar day, words for what happened, an approved category, a non-zero amount. A statement dated after today never lands as a fact; it becomes a promise in the expected register, weighing nothing against balances yet visible in every forecast view. Registering a future payment parks that promise deliberately, and confirming a landed entry closes the cycle when the day arrives — committing the item exactly as it was promised and refusing without exception to book money that has not actually moved.

Two more processes keep mistakes from staining history. Correcting a posted entry re-presents each field with its current value and appends an update record rather than rewriting a row; a correction that would move an entry to tomorrow backs the row out and reserves it as a promise instead. Retracting a wrong entry removes a row only after the owner's typed confirmation, writing one record that carries the entry's full prior state — so the books can be rebuilt and prove exactly what left. Both re-propagate the balance chain, so every later row reads as if the fix had always been true.

Repetition has two entrances. Authoring a rule serves the obligation the owner already knows; adopting detected rules mines real payments for habits and hands back an inert review list that stores nothing on its own. Both entrances pass the same admission bars, and in both the owner's hands finish the rule — a completed statement, or a completed field-by-field walk. Once standing, every occurrence meets the commitment doors with three outcomes: book it as the rule promised, reshape this month into a one-off promise, or suppress the date with a typed yes while the rule keeps running.

The eight agree on more than they disagree. Quitting, failed answers and refused confirmations leave the books untouched; every accepted change goes through one journaled write; a promise crosses into the books only at a confirmation. The named exceptions are small: the reshaping door refuses a promise dated today while the booking door takes today or earlier as landed, and suppression silences only the forecast — the hidden occurrence still books by its own address.
