docs.title: Hand writing a rule never books anything
Hand-writing a rule never books anything
Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The system deliberately does not record a ledger entry, change any balance or store an instance when a standing schedule is written — the schedule only ever shows up as anticipation the forecast presents.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Writing a standing rule saves the rule and nothing else: no money movement is recorded against it, by design.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The moment a standing rule is saved, the household's real balances are untouched. The rule exists so the forecast can anticipate the payment — and only so the forecast can. The module that stores rules states this boundary explicitly: rules are never materialized into the transaction store; each repeats only as a virtual expected entry during a viewing window, and a real recorded payment in that window takes its place so a day never carries two truths. Whatever the owner later wants booked must still travel the normal recording doors; a rule is a promise, not a payment.

docs.title: No undo or restoration door after a retraction
No undo or restoration door after a retraction
Title
docs.text: No undo or restoration door after a retraction

docs.title: Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: The system deliberately provides no restore or undo for a removed entry — recovery means re-registering, and only the journal's own records preserve what the retraction carried.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Nothing re-enters a removed entry; the journal's pre-image records are the only recoverable trace, surfaced through replay — no restoration command exists.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Once an entry is retracted, nothing offers to put it back. There is no restore command, no trash, no second-chance door. The deliberate boundary shows in the design everywhere else: retraction demands a printed row and a typed yes precisely because there is no take-back afterwards; the retraction record itself carries the removed content so the journal COULD reconstruct what was removed, but the product exposes no command that does so for the owner.

The owner's recovery path is the general one: re-register what was wrongly removed (through the intake or the promises register, whichever fits), accepting that a fresh registration is a new record, not the old one restored. A projected occurrence excluded by mistake can be brought back by editing the rule's exceptions — again through the rules machinery, not a restore door.

The boundary holds because the confirmation ritual makes the no-undo stance liveable: the owner was shown and asked, twice over on the recent-picker, before anything was written.

docs.title: Non-Goal Statement
docs.text: Deleting a projected occurrence writes nothing that remembers the suppression — no flag, note or row — it only adds the date to the rule's exception list, so the forecast stops expecting money it silently no longer shows.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The books keep no record of which occurrences were suppressed or why; only the forecast silence and the rule's exception date remain.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When the owner deletes a projected occurrence, the stores change in one way only: the date joins the rule's exempted dates. No suppression flag rides the rule, no note explains the decision, and no entry in any book names the suppressed occurrence. Whoever later asks "why is there no rent in March?" — the owner months on, or anyone reading the books — finds nothing: the rule simply projects everything except the dates it was told to skip.

The boundary is deliberate within this door: suppression is forecast-silencing, not bookkeeping. A decision that must be explainable later has to take a different door (booking the real movement, or reshaping the occurrence into a promise with its own record).

docs.title: An unknown address still leaves a record behind
An unknown address still leaves a record behind
Title
docs.text: An unknown address still leaves a record behind

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The recorded-not-typed rule overstates its own guarantee — an edit of an unknown address does write a record, because the write layer appends the update mutation before it ever checks that the row exists.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The contested rule promises that only a genuine act of repair leaves a mark, and names three paths that supposedly write nothing — a failed edit, an abandoned walk, an unknown address. Two of the three hold. When the owner cancels at the prompts or leaves every field unchanged, the editing code returns before any write happens and no record appears anywhere. The third path leaks, and the leak is visible in the code this rule itself anchors to.

When an edit targets a row that has already gone, the editing code never inspects for that case before writing. It hands the change to the update command at the anchored span, and that command stamps and appends its mutation unconditionally — the shared write step puts the record in the journal first and only afterwards loads the ledger to look up the entry. The target-row-vanished reply the owner then sees comes after the fact — the attempted repair is already part of the records.

By the rule's own measure this fails. The rule defines auditability through the records, saying the books can show what changed from the records alone, and a repair record that matched nothing is precisely what the rule asserts cannot happen. The rule's core survives: corrections do append as their own records and no row is rewritten in place. The defect lives in the description's absolute nothing-written claim — the honest wording simply drops the unknown-address case from that list, or acknowledges that the attempt itself is still recorded.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Payload contradicts source — the description claims a failed edit, an abandoned walk or an unknown address writes nothing at all, but the code this rule anchors to appends the update mutation to the journal before the target-row lookup happens, so an unknown address does write a record; only two of the three enumerated paths are silent.

docs.title: Corrective rows mechanism misclaims how callers read back the applied entry
Corrective rows mechanism misclaims how callers read back the applied entry
Title
docs.text: Corrective rows mechanism misclaims how callers read back the applied entry

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Contests Corrective rows append Update and Delete mutations, never amend the checkpoint store: its closing clause says callers read back the applied entry by the mutation's identity, but the update command reads back by the target entry's id and the delete command returns no readback at all.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The corrective rows mechanism closes its account with: "Callers read back the applied entry by the mutation's identity to report the new balance to the owner." That holds on the add and confirm paths, where the readback looks the entry up under the mutation's own content id (commands.py:124). It does not hold on the update path the fact itself anchors to: cmd_update resolves the readback with find(target) (commands.py:148), that is by the entry's stable id, not by the update mutation's id. The journal's design note (journal.py:14-16) says a transaction keeps the id its creating mutation assigned and never recomputes it, so an update mutation's id cannot resolve the updated entry — the two ids only coincide for the entry an add or confirm created. The delete path generalizes even less: cmd_delete returns just the mutation and a success flag (commands.py:176), no readback, because the removed entry is no longer resolvable. The clause reads as borrowed from the intake flow's add behavior rather than as a property of every corrective command.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The code evidence at the fact's own anchored span does not support the claim: commands.py:148 reads the applied entry back by the target's id, the by-mutation-identity readback exists only on the add path (commands.py:124), the delete path returns no readback at all, and journal.py:11-17 confirms an entry's id stays its creating mutation's.

docs.title: Proposed Replacement
docs.text:
{
  "description": "The update command builds an update mutation carrying the full
replacement of the editable fields, the delete command a delete
mutation carrying the victim's content as it stood, and the
landed-promise correction a retiring add in one mutation. The
write step is single: it stamps the repair with a creation time,
derives its content identity, appends it to the journal, re-folds
the ledger from checkpoint plus the fresh tail and re-checkpoints.
The folded journal, not the checkpoint store, is the truth; the
checkpoint is a cache the fold can rebuild. Callers read back the
landed entry after the repair — the add and confirm paths by the
mutation's own identity, the update path by the target entry's
id; the delete path returns the mutation and its success flag
because the deleted entry is no longer resolvable.
"
}

docs.title: Detection is not shielded from future dated rows as the summary claims
Detection is not shielded from future-dated rows as the summary claims
Title
docs.text: Detection is not shielded from future-dated rows as the summary claims

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The sensitivity's summary asserts the shared ledger view excludes future-dated rows from what detection sees; the view projects every committed row with no date filter and the write path imposes no future-date guard, so such a row reaches the detector as an ordinary occurrence.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The core claim is sound and stands: the detector consumes the shared view's rows directly, so it inherits whatever selection the view applies. The summary sharpens that core into one specific assertion — the view "excludes future-dated rows" — and that assertion does not hold.

The view's projection copies every committed transaction into its row shape in one pass, converting dates and mirroring categories, with a single date test nowhere among the steps. The detector receives exactly that list: the detection command's very next line hands the view's rows to the proposal engine, unfiltered.

The write path cannot supply the missing shield either. The booking command builds the stored mutation from whatever ISO date the entry names, and the single write step appends it and boots the ledger without examining whether the date lies ahead of today. A future-dated committed row is a first-class row, ordered like any other; the only date test on the view side picks the balance anchor for the projection walk, not the rows handed to detection.

A reader taking the summary at its word would believe a payment booked ahead of its date can never feed a proposal. It can: the detector groups and classifies it like any other occurrence.

docs.title: Pausing a rule does not resurface its payment in detection

Title
docs.text: Pausing a rule does not resurface its payment in detection

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The fact A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed promises the owner that a removed or paused rule lets the payment resurface in later detection runs; the exclusion check consults only the name-category pair, so a paused rule silences the payment exactly like an active one. Removal alone resurfaces it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The contested statement is exactly what the detector does: a payment whose name and category already sit on an existing rule earns no new proposal. The trouble lives in the description's closing sentence, which asserts that removal and pausing both resurface the payment.

Three reads from this pass close the chain. The exclusion set is built from every rule handed in and reads only the description-category pair — no query touches the active flag (recurrences.py 204-207). The command that renders the proposal table passes the rules file as loaded, and the loader returns every recorded row without an activeness filter (recurrences.py 40-46, recurrence_cli.py 860-862). Pausing is a real, persisted state right next door: the toggle sets the row's active flag to false and saves the file (recurrence_cli.py 492-504).

So after a pause the row still sits in the rules file under the same name and category, and detection keeps the payment quiet; the promised resurfacing never comes. The removal half of the sentence is untouched by this challenge — the proposed payload keeps the accurate statement and summary and corrects the description, extending the statement so the pause behavior is spelled out rather than guessed.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The description's claim that a paused rule resurfaces its payment is contradicted at the fact's own anchor and by the pause-to-detection chain: the exclusion set consults only name and category, the loader filters nothing, and pausing persists an inactive row the detector still reads.

  "classifiers": [
    "business-value",
    "implicit",
    "stable"
  ],
  "description": "Once the owner has formalized a repeating payment, the detector stops suggesting it. The comparison is deliberately simple \u2014 the payment's name and its category together decide whether a rule already covers that ground \u2014 so a rule adopted weeks ago keeps its payment quiet in every later detection run, even as the payment keeps arriving.\n\nThe practical effect is that the proposal list stays a to-do list. It shrinks as the owner adopts, and it never grows back with items they have already handled. An owner who removed a rule will see the payment resurface in detection again \u2014 without the formalization, the repeating payment is once more an observation, not a schedule. Pausing is different: the paused row stays in the rules file, the detector counts it as existing cover, and the payment remains silent until the rule is removed or detection learns to skip inactive rules.",
  "statement": "A payment whose description and category already name an existing recurrence rule produces no detection proposal, regardless of how regularly it still repeats \u2014 whether that rule is active or paused; only a removed rule lets the payment resurface.",
  "summary": "Detection excludes what the books already anticipate: an existing rule for the same payment silences any new proposal for it, so the owner is never offered a duplicate schedule.",
  "title": "A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed"

docs.title: Stored process script drops its final end event below the process body
Stored process script drops its final end event below the process body
Title
docs.text: Stored process script drops its final end event below the process body

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The recurrence adoption process's stored BPMN script still fails validation after its two recorded repair cycles: its last end event is dedented to column 0, so the parse refuses the document. Restoring the body indent makes the same script pass.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This challenges Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history, whose note records that the stored script was left failing two repair cycles ago. Refinement grade binds that script to compose, so this pass ran bpmn_tools:validate on the exact stored text and it refused the document — the verbatim finding sits in the reason below.

The break is mechanical and single-line. Line 39 of the stored script is the second process's closing end event, and it sits at column 0 while every other line of that process body carries the two-space indent; the parser therefore treats the document as closed before it and refuses the bare end construct. The first process's own end event carries the body indent correctly, which makes the inconsistency easy to see by eye. The fact's narrative held up everywhere else this pass: the two-tier detection with median amounts and gap bands (detect_candidates, _classify_frequency and _proposal in src/financials/recurrences.py 185-303), the review-only table (detect_recurrences in src/financials/recurrence_cli.py 854-911), and the seeded field loop with its admission bar and next-three-dates ending (_seeded_field_loop 280-356, _validate 150-183, take_proposal 914-952).

Re-validating the stored script with that one line restored to the body indent returns valid, so the repair is mechanical. The proposal below carries the full corrected payload — script fixed, note updated to the validated wording so the failure marker does not go stale — and touches nothing else in the fact's content.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: Refinement grade requires the stored script to pass bpmn_tools:validate; the run this engagement refused it with this parse finding, quoted verbatim: line 39: expected a process block, the message flows section or the end of the script, found end (parse) — a document opens with process "Name"; the message flows section comes after all processes, e.g. process "Order" ... message flows ... The break is the single line 39 of the stored script: the second process's closing end event dedented to column 0, outside the process body, while the same script's first process end event carries the body indent. The fact's own note agrees the script was left failing (the unvalidated marker matches the live refusal, so it is honest rather than stale) — but agreeing does not clear a refinement-grade script. No other defect worth contesting surfaced at the anchors.

docs.text:
The fact's third outcome sentence covers two correction kinds in one breath — a correction that keeps the row in the books, and one that restates the promise — and assigns both to the mutation layer. The books half matches the code: a kept posted row updates as one command mutation (src/financials/edit.py lines 255-262).

The module's own docstring states this is deliberate: expected rows are edited in the register because no balance chain replays there (src/financials/edit.py lines 10-11). The entry retraction process script fails the BPMN validation its note claims it passed
Title
docs.text: The entry retraction process script fails the BPMN validation its note claims it passed

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Contests the entry retraction process — its stored script refuses bpmn_tools:validate with a parse error, while the fact's own note states the script validated as valid.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The process fact stores its script at refinement grade — its note carries neither a draft marking nor an unvalidated marker — and that note states the script was validated with bpmn_tools:validate and came back valid. Re-running the validator on the stored script this pass refused it verbatim:

line 21: expected a process block, the message flows section or the end of the script, found end (parse)

Line 21 is the second process's closing end event, stored at column zero while every other line of that process body is indented two spaces. A one-line A/B pin narrows the whole failure to that single line: re-validating the identical script with only that end line indented two spaces returns valid. The note's validation claim is therefore stale, and the script behind the process is not composed.

Everything else in the process fact held up at its primary anchor. The resolver the description narrates reads exactly in delete.delete_transaction 95-143 — committed entry first, then expected register entries, then a group id, then a projected rule occurrence, with an unknown id ending on an error and nothing written — and all five detail spans the note cites exist at their cited def lines on the codebase. The challenge stops at the script's validity and the stale note.

Correction is one line: indent the second process's end line two spaces; the re-validated form is proven to parse by the A/B run.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The script gate — a CLEAN-note process is refinement grade, and its stored script must pass bpmn_tools:validate. The stored script fails with the parse refusal (line 21: expected a process block, the message flows section or the end of the script, found end (parse)) quoted verbatim above, no unvalidated marker is present in the note, and the note's "Script validated with bpmn_tools:validate (valid)" claim is stale — a failing script under a clean note is exactly the defect this gate exists to catch.

docs.title: The rule authoring process claims a future start gate the validator does not have
The rule authoring process claims a future-start gate the validator does not have
Title
docs.text: The rule authoring process claims a future-start gate the validator does not have

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The rule authoring process says validation refuses rules without a future start; the validator it anchors to has no such gate and accepts any parseable start, past included. One sentence of the description misstates what the code enforces.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The rule authoring process describes its safety net as two refusal gates: validation refuses a rule without a future start, and it refuses an unsound amount. The amount half matches the code — the validator rejects a zero amount outright. The future-start half does not. The validator's gates, read verbatim, are a non-empty description, an approved category, a nonzero amount, a frequency inside the known vocabulary, a day of month in range, a month for yearly rules, a present start for weekly and biweekly rules, parseable date strings, and an end date not before the start. No line in it compares the start with today. The authoring flow instead lets a missing start default to today's date and lets any parseable start pass — including past ones, which are deliberately includable: the detection flow builds proposals with the first historical occurrence as the start and pushes them through this very validator before saving, so a future-start refusal there would make adoption impossible. The fix is small — describe the validator by its real gates, and keep the today-default where it belongs, as a default rather than a gate.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The description claims validation refuses rules without a future start; the anchored validator contains no date-today comparison and accepts any parseable start, past or future, while the detection adoption flow relies exactly on past first-occurrence starts passing that same validator.

docs.title: Proposed Replacement
docs.text:
{
  "description": "Some obligations are known before the ledger ever sees them: a new subscription, a rent change, a yearly insurance. The owner spells the rule with flags or walks the interactive prompts \u2014 missing fields are asked, a weekly or biweekly rule gets its weekday snapped to the anchor date, and a start left blank defaults to today's date \u2014 and every instance is generated from the rule's start date onward, optionally bounded by an end date. Validation refuses an empty description, a category outside the approved list, a zero amount, a frequency outside the four supported ones, out-of-range day or month figures, and an end date before the start, because a malformed rule would poison every projection it touches. The saved rule immediately shows its next three instances so the owner sees what the forecast now expects. Pausing, resuming and removing the rule later keep the same store healthy.\n"
}

docs.title: Summary

docs.title: The zero refusal for new entries is anchored to the booking step
The zero refusal for new entries is anchored to the booking step
Title
docs.text: The zero refusal for new entries is anchored to the booking step

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Contests the corrected-to-zero sensitivity on its intake-door evidence alone: the cited span is the silent booking step, while the actual zero refusal sits one decision earlier in the intake path's validation gate, which the fact does not cite. The business claim itself checks out.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The corrected-to-zero sensitivity claims that a promise confirmed at the correction desk can land in the books at zero, an amount the intake door refuses before recording. The story's substance survived this engagement's reads: the desk treats zero as a legal placeholder for an unconfirmed promise, a landed promise commits the amount as it last stood, and the books accept the resulting posting without a murmur. The challenge is narrower than the claim — it is about where the door evidence points.

The fact anchors the door half of its claim to one span of the intake path, and that span is the silent booking step: it takes whatever amount it receives, builds the postings, applies the mutation, zero included. A verifier expanding the fact's door evidence finds the opposite of a refusal — a step with no gate at all.

The refusal the fact speaks of does exist, one decision earlier: the intake path's validation turns a stated movement of zero away before any booking is attempted. The evident correction is a re-anchor — trade the booking-step span for the validation gate's refusal lines, and on the placeholder side prefer the amount prompt's zero-allowance span over the single field-collection line the fact cites today.

docs.title: Reason
docs.text: The fact's intake-door anchor carries no zero check: the booking step applies whatever amount it receives, so the claim's support at that anchor fails. The zero refusal the fact describes lives in the intake path's validation gate, code the fact never anchors. The claim itself verified; only the door-side evidence is mislaid — a wrong provenance floor on an otherwise-true fact.

docs.title: processes
docs.text:
One business process the analyzed codebase carries out, captured as a process-diagram document with its business trigger — tied to the business rules it realizes and the code that carries the evidence.

The processes' story:

Eight processes tell one story about this ledger: the owner states what happened or what is coming, and the books either change as agreed or stay untouched with the reason said plainly. Every process starts at the owner's noticing — money moved, money will move, a number repeats, a row is wrong — never with a decision the books take on their own.

The main arc runs through three processes. Recording a movement accepts whatever precision the moment gives — full detail, a Dutch quick-shorthand, or bare and prompted — and holds it behind one admission gate: a real calendar day, words for what happened, an approved category, a non-zero amount. A statement dated after today never lands as a fact; it becomes a promise in the expected register, weighing nothing against balances yet visible in every forecast view. Registering a future payment parks that promise deliberately, and confirming a landed entry closes the cycle when the day arrives — committing the item exactly as it was promised and refusing without exception to book money that has not actually moved.

Two more processes keep mistakes from staining history. Correcting a posted entry re-presents each field with its current value and appends an update record rather than rewriting a row; a correction that would move an entry to tomorrow backs the row out and reserves it as a promise instead. Retracting a wrong entry removes a row only after the owner's typed confirmation, writing one record that carries the entry's full prior state — so the books can be rebuilt and prove exactly what left. Both re-propagate the balance chain, so every later row reads as if the fix had always been true.

Repetition has two entrances. Authoring a rule serves the obligation the owner already knows; adopting detected rules mines real payments for habits and hands back an inert review list that stores nothing on its own. Both entrances pass the same admission bars, and in both the owner's hands finish the rule — a completed statement, or a completed field-by-field walk. Once standing, every occurrence meets the commitment doors with three outcomes: book it as the rule promised, reshape this month into a one-off promise, or suppress the date with a typed yes while the rule keeps running.

The eight agree on more than they disagree. Quitting, failed answers and refused confirmations leave the books untouched; every accepted change goes through one journaled write; a promise crosses into the books only at a confirmation. The named exceptions are small: the reshaping door refuses a promise dated today while the booking door takes today or earlier as landed, and suppression silences only the forecast — the hidden occurrence still books by its own address.

docs.title: Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history
Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history
Title
docs.text: Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Mines the real payment history for repeating patterns, shows them as a review-only proposal list, and turns a proposal into a standing schedule only when the owner walks the adoption form to its end.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The same bill keeps arriving and retyping it is waste. The owner asks the books which payments look like habits, and the books answer with a list built from money that actually moved: payments of the same name and category, grouped, their rhythm judged from the spacing of their dates, their amount taken from the middle of what was really paid. Payments that already sit under a standing rule pause silently — the list never grows back.

There are two tiers of answer. The steady ones — subscriptions, rent — propose their middle value with nothing more said. The wanderers — budget-style payments that arrive on time for changing figures — propose the same middle value but carry their observed low and high openly, so the owner sees the spread at a glance. A payment that swings between income and expense is refused as one habit in either tier.

The list itself is inert: nothing anywhere is created by looking. Adopting means naming a number, and the books open a form with that payment's values already filled in — the owner accepts each field with Enter or replaces it by typing, and may quit at any point, which stores nothing. Only the completed walk passes the admission checks (approved category, non-zero amount, sane dates), and only then does the rule enter the books; its next three anticipated dates are shown straight after, so the owner sees the schedule sitting in the forward calendar. From that point the forecast generates its instances without further typing.

docs.text: Repeating payments have accumulated in the ledger history and the owner acts on them — surface: the recurrence detect and recurrence take commands

Author a standing recurrence rule by hand
Title
docs.text: Author a standing recurrence rule by hand

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Creates a recurring rule directly — description, category, amount, frequency and anchor date — so the forecast carries the repeating entry without waiting for history to prove it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Some obligations are known before the ledger ever sees them: a new subscription, a rent change, a yearly insurance. The owner who recognizes one writes the standing rule directly — in one complete statement or by answering the walk's questions one by one, with the questions asking only for what is missing and offered answers standing if the owner presses Enter. A weekly rhythm gets its weekday applied to the start date, so every occurrence lands on the named weekday for the schedule's life. A start left blank defaults to today's date, and a readable start in the past is accepted just as freely as one in the future — no bar compares the rule's beginning with the current day. Before anything is stored, the rule passes the same admission bars as an adopted schedule: a non-empty description, a category the owner has approved, a non-zero amount, one of the four rhythms, sane day and month ranges, readable dates and an end never before the start — a refusal names the bar and the store is left untouched.

The saved schedule confirms itself with its cadence in plain words and the next three dates the forecast will anticipate, so the owner sees immediately what their books now expect — and nothing is booked: the ledger keeps no entry for a rule until a real payment or an explicit confirmation touches it. Later life of the rule runs through the same store's doors: pause silences a schedule while keeping everything for later, resume brings it back as it stood, and remove ends it permanently — only after showing the owner the exact rule and taking a typed yes. One habit to watch: an anchor question answered with Enter keeps the silent default, anchoring a weekly schedule to whatever weekday the authoring day fell on; the printed cadence line is the only place that shows it.

docs.title: Commit a recurring rule instance into the ledger
Commit a recurring rule instance into the ledger
Title
docs.text: Commit a recurring rule instance into the ledger

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Brings a standing rule's projected occurrence into the books — as the rule promised it, as a reshaped one-off promise, or as a deliberately silenced date — while the rule keeps anticipating every other period.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The forecast shows every active standing rule's upcoming occurrences, and the owner meets them through a booking door. When a recurring bill's day arrives, the owner can take the occurrence straight to the confirmation desk: it books the money exactly as the rule promised — no questions — unless the owner walked a still-future occurrence first, where every value is offered prefilled and the day may be shifted to when the money actually landed. After posting, the books either count the occurrence as handled — the movement matched the rule's mark: same category, essentially the same amount, near the planned day — or the booking had drifted, and the occurrence is kept off the forecast as an exception so nothing keeps nagging.

The other doors reshape instead of booking. An occurrence that will differ from the standing rule — a different amount, a moved day — becomes a one-off promise of its own, admitted under the promise register's rules, and the original occurrence steps aside for that one month while the rule keeps running; a promise dated today or earlier is refused here, the one calendar the doors disagree on. An occurrence that should never book at all — a waived rent, a cancelled subscription — is suppressed after a typed yes: its date joins the rule's excepted days and the forecast goes quiet.

Suppression is forecast-silencing only. The occurrence's derived address stays alive everywhere else, so the very occurrence the owner deleted can still be booked by its address later — nothing at either door recalls the earlier delete. The books record neither the suppression nor its reason; only the forecast silence remains.

docs.title: Confirm a landed open entry into the books
Confirm a landed open entry into the books
Title
docs.text: Confirm a landed open entry into the books

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Turns a landed expected entry or rule occurrence into a real ledger posting, closes the open item behind it, and reports the new account state — refusing any item whose money has not actually moved.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Money has moved at (or before) the day it was promised — the moment every forecast lives for — and the owner brings the movement into the books. The item is named by address, or picked from the desk's open list when nothing is named; a no-op answer follows when the books already record the address. A landed item commits exactly as it was promised, without a single question: the posting enters as a real journal entry with running balances on both accounts, and the promise behind it is retired — its old address carried on the booking's own record, so no open entry lingers. When the item is a whole group, every landed member commits in day order, each member's address is re-pointed to its new committed one, and the group keeps its still-future members. A booking that drifted from its standing rule (different amount, or too far from the planned day) records the occurrence as an exception; a booking that matches supersedes the occurrence on its own. Money that has not moved yet is never confirmed — a future item is refused and left open, an item without an amount is refused outright, and a group quietly skips such members with a note. A transfer confirmation warns that both accounts moved together. The outcome returns to the owner with the new account state.

docs.title: Correct a posted entry through the journal
Correct a posted entry through the journal
Title
docs.text: Correct a posted entry through the journal

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Fixes date, description, category or amount of an entry after posting, by appending corrective mutations instead of rewriting history.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A posted entry turns out wrong — a typo in the amount, the wrong category, a date that belongs to another month. The owner picks the entry by its address, or from the last ten rows when no address springs to mind. The desk resolves the address first: the address may name a committed row, a promise for the future, one occurrence of a standing rule, or a whole group — and the same correction walk is not even used for the last two, the books hand over to the matching editor instead. An address matching nothing ends with an unknown-address refusal and nothing has changed. On a committed row the fields — day, description, category, amount — appear one at a time, each filled with the current value. Enter keeps the value; three failed answers on a field abandon the whole correction, again with nothing changed. Correcting a row to a day after today does not keep it in the books: the row is backed out and its corrected content is reserved as a promise for its day, and the owner is told plainly when that reservation is refused. A correction that keeps the entry in the books appends an update record; the balance chain re-applies from that record so every later row reflects the fix, and the owner sees the new checking balance. The promises register has its own two outcomes. A promise whose day has arrived commits into the books as the restated content — one retiring bookkeeping record, then the open entry leaves the register. A promise still in the future is simply restated where it stands. Transfers in either desk warn that the savings side moved too. Every committed repair goes through one write step — the record is stamped, appended to the journal and the books re-folded — so a correction never rewrites history and stays auditable later.

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text: A posted or expected entry shows a mistake and the owner revises it — surface: the edit command (id, or pick from the last ten rows)

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Steps live in edit.py (resolver 274-319, walk 66-113, desks 165-271), the write step in commands.py, the engine mechanics in journal.py; script composed and validated this pass.

docs.title: Record a money movement in the journaled ledger
Record a money movement in the journaled ledger
Title
docs.text: Record a money movement in the journaled ledger

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Takes a realized payment or income into the books: one journaled entry that sets the running checking and savings balances.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The owner notices money moved — a bill was paid or income arrived — and states the movement in whatever precision the moment gives: all details flagged, a Dutch quick-shorthand such as "gisteren -25 Kafe", or bare and prompted. One admission gate stands before anything is stored: a real calendar day, words saying what happened, a category on the approved list, a non-zero amount, and no date after today; refusing one means the movement is not recorded and the reason is said plainly. A statement dated in the future becomes a promise in the expected register instead of a fact in the books. When the statement leaves fields open, the tool asks for them and shows the checking balance the movement would produce; the owner must agree with that projection — three disagreements abandon the whole movement — and any quit, abort or Ctrl-C leaves the books untouched. A rehearsal shows the entry and its projected balances and stores nothing. An accepted movement is handed over and landed: its row slots into date order among the existing rows, takes over the balances of the nearest prior day, and every later day shifts by the same amount, so the running checking and savings balances follow the real movement of money. A transfer between the owner's own accounts moves both accounts with that one entry — the checking amount is mirrored onto savings. Stating the same movement twice within one creation moment stores it once. The owner hears back the stored identity and the two running balances, or the plain refusal.

docs.text: A payment or income became known to the owner and must enter the books — surface: the add command (flagged, shorthand or bare interactive)

docs.title: Register a future payment in the expected register
Register a future payment in the expected register
Title
docs.text: Register a future payment in the expected register

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An upcoming payment or income is stated ahead of its day and the books park it as an open promise — invisible to actual balances, visible to the forecast — until confirmation turns it into a real movement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A bill or a payment the owner already knows will come — a rent due next week, a salary on its way, a tax bill — should be visible in the forecast before the money actually moves. The owner states the amount, the day, and what it is for. There are two doors for this. The expectation door is where a fully stated future movement goes on purpose. The ordinary statement door is just as good: whatever the owner states in pieces gets completed first, and any completed statement dated after today is shown the way to the expectation door — the books refuse to record a future movement as if it had happened. The expectation door checks the statement completely: the day must be a real calendar day, the description must say what is coming, the category must be approved, an amount must be stated. Each shortcoming is refused with a plainly worded reason, nothing is stored. A promise must also lie ahead of today — the actual ledger enforces the same border from its side, so money that has already moved can never end up as a promise. On approval the promise gets its own identity and is parked: it weighs nothing against real balances, shows up as an open item in every view, and awaits its day. The owner can rehearse the registration first — a rehearsal shows exactly what would be stored and stores nothing. Confirmation, once the day has come, turns the promise into a real ledger entry and the cycle closes there.

docs.text: An upcoming payment or income became known and lies ahead of today — surface: the expect command, or the add command when the entered date is in the future

docs.title: Retract a wrong entry from the books with confirmation
Retract a wrong entry from the books with confirmation
Title
docs.text: Retract a wrong entry from the books with confirmation

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Removes an entry that should never have been there, with explicit confirmation and suppression of rule instances.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An entry turns out to be duplicate or simply not real — it must come out of the books. The owner names or picks the row from the last ten posted entries, sees it printed, and must answer an explicit typed confirmation before anything is written; a bare Enter or any other word cancels with the books untouched.

What kind of wrongness the owner is fixing decides the shape. A committed entry does not vanish in place: the retraction is written through the journal as one record carrying the entry's full prior state, so the books can be rebuilt and prove the retraction removed exactly what it claims. The balance chain then re-propagates, so every later row reads as if the wrong entry had never posted — a transfer removal warns the owner to re-check both accounts. A future-dated promise is simply dropped from its register — it was never in the books, so no journal record is owed. A group deletion removes only the grouping; members survive untouched. A projected rule occurrence is not deleted but suppressed: its date joins the rule's exceptions and the rule keeps running for the remaining periods. An unknown address ends the attempt with an error and nothing written.

One gap the owner should know: the expect command's standalone remove action drops a promise without printing or asking — the unguarded door beside this process.

docs.text: An owner judges an entry or projected instance wrong and retracts it — surface: the delete command (id, or pick from the last ten rows)

docs.title: A confirmed correction can greet the owner with yesterday s balances
All-Enter keeps a posted row but confirms a landed promise
Title
docs.text: All-Enter keeps a posted row but confirms a landed promise

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The same gesture — confirming every field unchanged — silently finishes a confirmation on a landed promise while doing exactly nothing on a posted row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The editor's fields all keep their current value when confirmed unchanged, which reads as a pure review gesture: look, leave everything as it stands, move on. On a posted row that reading is right — confirming everything answers "nothing changed" and no record is written. On a promise whose day has already arrived the same gesture IS a confirmation: the books ask no further question and the row is committed as a landed fact as the owner steps out of the walk. The identical action thus means "I changed nothing" on one desk and "this happened as promised" on the other, with no signal at the moment of acting that the second case is a commit at all.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: A parity port must reproduce the dual meaning exactly and preserve the no-second-question character of the landed-promise path; making the confirm explicit would change an owner-visible flow.

docs.title: An identical restatement depends on when it was entered
An identical restatement depends on when it was entered
Title
docs.text: An identical restatement depends on when it was entered

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Two statements of the same movement produce one entry only if both carried the same creation timestamp; a later restatement of identical content gets a new timestamp and is stored as a second row.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The deduplication the owner might assume from 'recording twice changes nothing' only holds within one timestamp. The mutation's identity mixes content with its creation moment, deliberately — the comment on the field says as much: uniqueness is a human discipline, the timestamp exists only to separate identical content. So re-adding the same café visit an hour later is honest from the tool's reading — identical content, different creation moment, therefore a different movement. The owner who meant to correct and accidentally re-added now has the movement twice, and only the later delete/edit flow repairs it.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: Idempotency tests must control timestamps: the same payload with the same ts folds, with a different ts duplicates.

docs.title: An incomplete add statement keeps its future dispatch hidden until prompted complete
An incomplete add statement keeps its future dispatch hidden until prompted complete
Title
docs.text: An incomplete add statement keeps its future dispatch hidden until prompted complete

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An add statement with a future date given only in pieces is not redirected at once: the owner first answers the interactive questions, and a future date inside --checking is never dispatching at all.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A future-dated movement stated in one breath — every field given — is redirected to the expectation register immediately, before anything else happens. But when the owner states the movement only in pieces, the redirect waits hidden behind the interactive questions: the owner first answers every field, and only the completed statement decides which door takes it. During those questions a future date handed to the checking balance position is treated as a balance number, not as a date — nothing about the statement hints that the register is where it will end up. The owner answers the usual prompts and the entry parks as a promise only after the last answer.

docs.title: An unknown rule instance address fails the confirm in silence
An unknown rule-instance address fails the confirm in silence
Title
docs.text: An unknown rule-instance address fails the confirm in silence

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An r:-prefixed id that matches no standing rule exits the confirm with the failure code and prints nothing — the code expects a caller to report it, but the caller does not.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Naming the confirmation desk with an address from the rule-instance family that matches no standing rule produces no visible answer at all — no explanation, no refusal note, only a failure exit. The code's own remark says the unknown id is the caller's business to report, yet the address reaches the desk through exactly that caller, which delegates and returns without a word. Every other unknown address greets the owner with a clear refusal. The gap is invisible in the direct case and untested; a typo in a remembered instance address simply looks like the confirm did nothing.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: A parity re-implementation that reports unknown r: ids like every other unknown id would differ observably from this desk (exit code matches, user-visible output does not).

docs.title: Backdated entries are inserted later ones rewritten
Backdated entries are inserted, later ones rewritten
Title
docs.text: Backdated entries are inserted, later ones rewritten

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Recording a movement dated before existing rows lands it in date position and rewrites every later row's balances; the entry itself keeps no trace that the owner stated it late.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Add 'yesterday's café' a week after the fact and the row slots between its neighbors, shifting each later day's balances by the posting — the chain never shows the recording moment on the row itself. The creation timestamp of the mutation preserves the stating order in the journal, but the ledger rows read as if the movement had always been in date order. That is the intended bookkeeping behavior, but a reader comparing two books rebuilt at different times will find balances that match per-row yet disagree if the earlier rebuild predates a backdated insert: the checkpoint carries the rewrite, and the journal carries the true order of statements.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: A reimplementation must reproduce insert-position semantics and balance rewriting, not append-order — tests that only append will pass both designs and hide the difference.

docs.title: Entering nothing keeps today s calendar position as the recurring anchor
Entering nothing keeps today's calendar position as the recurring anchor
Title
docs.text: Entering nothing keeps today's calendar position as the recurring anchor

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: On a hand-written rule, every anchor question answered with a bare Enter keeps the silent default the old non-interactive path used — today's day-of-month, today's month, today's date, no end — so a guided run can still end on an anchor the owner never deliberately chose.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: An owner walking the add questions sees each one offered, yet Enter at the day question keeps the current day of the month as the schedule's recurring day, Enter at the month question on a yearly rhythm keeps the current month, and Enter at the start question keeps today. The same silent fallback also stands behind the flag route: a fully specified hand rule without an explicit day or month still picks up the current calendar position. The save confirmation states the resulting cadence in plain words — which day, which month — so a watchful owner catches a wrong anchor the moment it is confirmed; a day past the 28th even earns a spoken warning that short months will skip it. But nothing asks twice or refuses: an owner who answers every question with Enter walks away with a schedule anchored to the day they happened to write it on.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: The code's own comments mark these questions as gap fixes that must keep Enter-compatibility with the older seeded flow ("Enter keeps the old silent default", "mirroring day defaulting to today's day-of-month") — re-implementing the add flow must reproduce the Enter-keeps-default behavior or the interactive scripts that drive it change what gets stored.

docs.title: The dry run confirmation names an id the entry never keeps
The dry-run confirmation names an id the entry never keeps
Title
docs.text: The dry-run confirmation names an id the entry never keeps

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Rehearsing a future statement with --dry-run prints a confirmation naming the e-number the entry would get next, but a rehearsal stores nothing — the real run days later is free to hand the same id to a different promise.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Rehearsing an expectation shows the owner exactly what would be parked, down to an identifier the entry would carry. Nothing is stored, yet the message reads like a completed booking: the owner can walk away believing the promise is registered. When the statement is actually parked afterwards — often days later — the register hands out identifiers by current order, so another promise entered in between may take the very id the rehearsal displayed. The number in the rehearsal message is a preview of a moving target, not a binding commitment.

docs.title: The dry run projects only the checking account
The dry run projects only the checking account
Title
docs.text: The dry run projects only the checking account

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The rehearsal preview shows the projected checking balance only — a transfer's savings movement is never shown in the dry-run line.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A rehearsal of a transfer of, say, €250 shows the checking side (−250) and its projected result, but not the mirrored +250 on savings, although the real landing would move both. The dry-run line the owner sees is built from the checking posting and the projected checking balance alone. The rehearsal still stores nothing, so nothing is wrong in the books — but the owner weighing the rehearsal against reality sees half of the movement.

docs.title: Parity Relevance
docs.text: A faithful reimplementation should either mirror this preview asymmetry exactly or knowingly fix it; a dry-run parity test with a transfer category would expose the difference.

docs.title: The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming
The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming
Title
docs.text: The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A promise can be removed from the register with a single command that neither shows the row nor asks for a yes — while the identical removal through the retract command prints and demands confirmation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The observable surprise: an owner who has learned that every removal in this product first shows the entry and demands a typed yes meets one door where none of that happens. Removing a future-dated promise through the expect command's remove action takes the id and deletes — no row printed, no confirmation asked — announcing only the success after the fact; even a wrong id gets only the same bare unknown-id error the guarded doors print.

The same promise removed through the retract command instead goes through the full ritual: printed row, explicit 'ja' or cancel. Two doors, one operation, two different guarantees. The register's own add side refuses incompleteness and the past loudly, so the asymmetry is not a general laxness of the register but a one-door-only gap.

docs.title: The projection hides a suppressed occurrence but its address stays bookable
The projection hides a suppressed occurrence but its address stays bookable
Title
docs.text: The projection hides a suppressed occurrence but its address stays bookable

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: After deletion, the projected row is gone yet the instance resolves and commits at the confirm desk — the suppression only affects the forecast, never the booking doors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner deletes an occurrence and sees it vanish — the forecast keeps its word. Nothing, though, was recorded about the address: it derives from the rule's schedule only, and no suppression flag exists to find. So the same address, typed later at the confirm desk or the edit desk, still resolves to rule and occurrence and offers the same booking or reshaping walk as before. A suppressed occurrence can therefore be confirmed after all, entering the books on a date the projection had already given up.

The code documents this deliberately: the resolver's own note says suppressed instances stay resolvable and the delete door never warns that the disappearance is forecast-only. For the owner the oddity is exactly the double-booking shape of the covered-occurrence sensitivity, reachable after a deliberate delete.

docs.title: Weekly proposals anchor on the first occurrence s weekday
Weekly proposals anchor on the first occurrence's weekday
Title
docs.text: Weekly proposals anchor on the first occurrence's weekday

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A weekly or biweekly proposal never names a day of month: its schedule starts at the first occurrence, and the weekday of that earliest date silently becomes the anchor every future instance snaps to.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner sees weekly proposals shown with a weekday in brackets — that weekday is not asked, not chosen, and not stored per instance: it is inherited from the very first date the detection trusted. Adoption seeds the same date as the start, so accepting everything keeps that weekday forever, and the instance calendar repeats it from then on.

The surprise cuts in when history was irregular: the earliest recorded occurrence may sit on a different weekday than the payment's current habit (a payment that fell on Friday the first time and Tuesday since). The proposal carries the Friday, and nothing in the review or adoption names the difference as a warning. Only typing a bare weekday name in the form's anchor question moves the schedule off that inherited day.

This is why the form asks a weekday at all for weekly rhythms — the anchor question exists to let the owner override exactly this inherited value, and Enter silently ratifies whatever the first occurrence decided.

docs.title: 1. Executive summary
docs.text:
One household's cashflow books, built so every recorded fact can be proven rather than trusted — an evidence-first journal where changes are appended and balances are recomputation, never edited states.

The books prove themselves: every correction and removal is its own appended record carrying what changed, each row carries a hashed self-check, and re-landing the same movement stores it once (A correction is recorded, not typed) — judge any change near the journal against this property first.

Rule-occurrence confirmation can double-book: a group confirm skips an occurrence a real booking already covers, while the same occurrence confirmed by its own address commits again (A covered rule occurrence double-books when confirmed directly by its own address) — aligning that check across both confirm doors is the highest-value fix.

The removal ritual is not uniform: the expect remove door takes an id and deletes without showing the row or asking for a yes (The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming), one door away from the identical guarded operation.

Which side wins when a retraction record no longer matches the live books is decided nowhere (Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?) — an owner ruling is pending, and until then the keeper facing the refusal has no recovery door.

Next: read the SWOT analysis for the evidence behind each point and the product summary for the capability map. Verification: six objections were raised during the analysis and all six carry resolved markers at their target versions — no fact stands contested; the vault holds no separate coverage or run record.

docs.title: 2. Archetype mapping
docs.text:
The product is a personal bookkeeping journal — one keeper's recurring answers to "did the money move, and what is left?" — built so every recorded answer can be proven rather than trusted. The founding distinction is actual versus expected (Actual versus expected): a movement that happened enters the journaled books, carries and shifts real balances, and is guarded against tampering; a movement promised for a future day weighs nothing, lives in its own register, and can still fail to happen. Nearly every rule in the territory follows from asking that one question.

The distinction organizes the component map. The journal engine (Ledger engine) folds each accepted change into dated transaction rows whose running balances chain from the row before, so the books are always a recomputation of recorded changes, never a state edited in place; the command pipeline (Command mutations) is the narrow write step every change passes. Intake (Entry intake) gates statements before anything lands, and the future-day cut (Future-day admission) sends tomorrow's money to the promise register (Expected register) instead of the books. The confirmation desk (Open-entry confirmation desk) is where a promise becomes a fact — the confirmation backlog (The confirmation backlog) is the gap between the two calendars, computed fresh at every view and never stored.

The repair side honours the same proven-over-trusted stance: the retraction desk (Entry retraction) takes a wrong entry out as its own written record that carries what was removed, and the editor (Entry editor) resolves one address across all four stores — books, promises, groups, rule occurrences — walking the keeper field by field before deciding where the corrected content belongs.

Anticipation is a second promise machinery. The recurrence planner (Recurrence planner) turns repeating history into standing schedules, but every detection result stays a proposal — information on screen, never commitment (Proposal) — and an occurrence carries no stored address at all: the same rule on the same date always derives the same address (The derivation of a projected occurrence's address), which is why a suppressed occurrence can still answer when named. A rule enters the books two ways — written by hand the moment the keeper recognizes an obligation, or adopted from history the books themselves reveal (Rule provenance — written by hand or adopted from history) — and both doors end at the same owner-checked form, so no way in skips the keeper's hands.

docs.title: 3. Product summary
docs.text:
The product keeps one household's cashflow books for a single keeper: it turns stated money movements into recorded facts the books stand behind, and every later question — what is left, what was wrong, what is still owed — reads from those facts rather than from an edited state. Recording a movement is one appended change; the books recompute a balance for any day from the change chain, each recorded row carries a self-check over its own content, and a hand-altered book fails verification instead of agreeing quietly (Every entry lands with balances it stands behind). Stating the same movement twice stores it once (Recording twice changes nothing the second time), and a transfer between the household's two accounts shifts both running balances through one entry (A transfer moves both accounts).

Movements are stated in three precisions — every detail flagged, a Dutch quick shorthand in one breath, or field by field — and all three pass the same admission gate: a real calendar day, words that say what happened, a category the keeper approved, an amount that is not zero, no date beyond today (One admission gate for every stated movement). A rehearsal shows the would-be balances and stores nothing (A rehearsal stores nothing); backing out at any prompt leaves the books untouched (Backing out leaves the books untouched); and a shorthand token that looks like an amount must parse as one or the whole statement is refused (The quick statement must mean what it says).

Money promised for a future day never enters the balance chain (Future promises never enter the balance chain): it parks in a separate register of open promises until its day arrives. Confirming then turns the promise into a booked fact exactly as it was promised, with no further questions (A landed open item confirms as it was promised); related promises confirm as one group, oldest first, each member re-pointed as it becomes a fact (Confirming a group commits its landed members and keeps the group), and a promise without an amount is refused everywhere (An open item without an amount is never confirmed).

When something is wrong, three repair desks take over. The correction desk records the fix rather than retyping it: one appended written record, nothing overwritten (A correction is recorded, not typed); an entry restated for a future day leaves the books and re-enters the promise register (An edit that lands tomorrow leaves the books). The retraction desk prints the victim row first and writes only on a typed affirmative answer (A retraction only writes after a stated yes), as one record carrying the removed content (A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood). No undo or restore comes after a retraction (No undo or restoration door after a retraction) — the shown-then-confirmed ritual is the safety, by design.

For payments that repeat, the product reads real payment history and proposes standing schedules; detection alone never saves a rule (Detection never saves a rule): every adopted value passes the keeper's hands in a form walk (Every adopted value passes the owner's hands), and only complete, admissible rules are saved (Only complete admissible rules are saved). A standing schedule never books anything by itself — it only makes the forecast anticipate (Hand-writing a rule never books anything); a real payment recorded in its window takes the scheduled entry's place, so a day never carries two truths.
