docs.title: Record a money movement in the journaled ledger
docs.text:
Trigger: A payment or income became known to the owner and must enter the books — surface: the add command (flagged, shorthand or bare interactive)

The owner notices money has moved — a bill paid, income arrived — and states it in whatever precision the moment gives: fully flagged, a quick shorthand breath like "gisteren -25 Kafe", or field by field when asked. However the statement arrives, one admission gate stands before anything is stored — a real calendar day, words saying what happened, a category on the approved list, a non-zero amount, and no date after today — One admission gate for every stated movement — and a refusal is spoken plainly, the books left exactly as they were. The quick statement is held to mean what it says: a token written like an amount either reads as one or the whole line is turned down, never quietly absorbed into the description — The quick statement must mean what it says. A statement dated ahead of today is never recorded as fact; it redirects to the expected register as a promise — Future promises never enter the balance chain — and Registering a future payment picks that thread up from there. When fields stay open, the intake shows the checking balance the movement would produce and asks for agreement; three disagreements abandon the whole movement, and a quit, an abort or an interrupt records nothing — Backing out leaves the books untouched. A rehearsal behaves the same way in miniature, showing the entry and its projected balances while storing nothing — A rehearsal stores nothing. An accepted movement lands as an entry the books stand behind: the row slots into date order, takes over the balances of the nearest prior day, and shifts every later day by the same amount, so any balance read from the books is the arithmetic of the chain up to that day — Every entry lands with balances it stands behind. Stating the same movement twice within one creation moment stores it once; the second telling returns the first entry — Recording twice changes nothing the second time. Money moved between the owner's own accounts rides a single entry that touches both accounts, so the household total stands still while the split follows the real move — A transfer moves both accounts. The owner hears back the stored identity and the running balances — or the plain reason nothing changed.

docs.title: Register a future payment in the expected register
docs.text:
Trigger: An upcoming payment or income became known and lies ahead of today — surface: the expect command, or the add command when the entered date is in the future

The rent lands next Tuesday, the salary is on its way, and the owner wants both visible without touching the real balance. Stating a future movement — amount, day, and what it is for — parks a promise in the expected register: every view shows it as an open item, actual money stays untouched, and the promise waits for its day. Two doors lead there. The expect command takes a fully stated movement on purpose, and the ordinary add command funnels into the same register whenever the stated day lies ahead of today — the books will not record a future movement as if it had already happened. Only a complete statement is parked. The register checks that the day reads as a real calendar day, the description says what is coming, the category is on the approved list, and an amount was stated at all; any shortfall earns a plainly worded refusal with nothing stored — Only complete future-dated statements enter the expected register — while a promised zero passes exactly where the actual ledger would refuse one — A zero-amount promise is admitted, an amountless one refused. The today-boundary runs double-stranded too: the register wants a promise ahead of today and the ledger enforces the same divide from its side, so money that has already moved can never end up posing as a promise. Nothing is written blind — a rehearsal shows precisely what would be stored and stores nothing. Once parked the promise carries its own identity and awaits its day; confirmation, told in a story of its own, turns it into a real ledger entry and the cycle closes there.

docs.title: Confirm a landed open entry into the books
docs.text:
Trigger: An expected or projected movement has landed in the account and the owner accepts it into the books — surface: the confirm command (bare, e-number, rule instance or group id)

Money has moved, and the books must now say so. The owner accepts a landed entry — named by its address, or picked from the desk's open list when nothing was named — and it commits without a single prompt, because every detail was settled when the promise was made (a landed open item confirms as promised). The posting enters as a real journal entry with running balances on both accounts, and the promise retires behind it, its old address kept on the booking's own record.

Some doors stay shut. Money that has not moved yet is refused and left open — a promise cannot become history ahead of its day (confirmation never lands ahead of the real day), and a movement with no stated amount cannot be booked at all (no amount, no confirmation). An address the books already hold confirms as a quiet no-op, safe to re-run with no double entry (already committed confirms as nothing to do), and a transfer confirmation warns that both accounts moved together.

Whole groups clear in one pass. Landed members commit in day order, each retired member's address re-pointing to its committed one, while still-future members are skipped with a note and the group itself stands (a group commits its landed members and keeps the group). When the landed item traces to a standing rule, a booking that drifted from the rule's mark — a different amount, or a day outside the window — is recorded as an exception for the owner to judge; an on-mark booking supersedes the occurrence (off-mark bookings count as exceptions). The owner hears the outcome with the new account state.

docs.title: Correct a posted entry through the journal
docs.text:
Trigger: A posted or expected entry shows a mistake and the owner revises it — surface: the edit command (id, or pick from the last ten rows)

A posted entry shows a mistake — an amount typo, the wrong category, a day from another month — and the owner picks the entry by address, or from the last ten rows when no address springs to mind. The editor reads that address first: it may name a committed book row, a promise for the future, one occurrence of a standing rule, or a whole group. Groups and rule occurrences are corrected in another editor entirely, so this walk serves only the books and the promises register; an address matching nothing ends in an unknown-address refusal, and nothing changed. On a committed row the fields come one at a time — day, description, category, amount — each pre-filled with the value standing now. Enter keeps a value; three failed answers on a field abandon the whole correction, again with nothing changed. Correcting a row to a day after today moves it out of the books: the row is backed out and its corrected content is reserved as a promise for the new day, and the owner is told plainly when that reservation is refused — the tomorrow rule. A promise whose day has already arrived commits into the books in the same act and retires from the register — the landed-promise rule. Every committed repair keeps history intact: the fix lands as a new appended record behind the old content — the record-not-typed rule — and the balance chain re-applies past it, so every later row reflects the fix while the books still show what the entry said before. The owner leaves with the new checking balance; a transfer touched along the way warns that the savings side moved with it.

docs.title: Commit a recurring rule instance into the ledger
docs.text:
Trigger: A recurring bill's occurrence lands in the account and the owner books it — surface: the confirm command on a rule instance id, edit on the instance, or delete as suppression

A standing rule promises the same bill every month; this is where one month's promise becomes money. The owner brings the projected occurrence to a door, and the plain case is the confirmation desk: hand it an occurrence whose day has landed and it posts the movement exactly as the rule promised, no questions. A day still ahead can be walked through first, every value offered prefilled, the day shifted to when the money actually landed. Two doors reshape rather than book. An occurrence that will differ becomes a one-off promise of its own while the rule skips just that month — but the reshaping door refuses a promise dated today, the one date the doors disagree on, so an owner moving the day to today loses the typing. For a month that should never book at all, a waived rent or a dead subscription, one typed yes is enough and the forecast goes quiet. The desk then scores the posting against the rule's mark — the right category, essentially the promised amount, near the promised day — and either the month counts as handled or the drift is recorded as the rule's exception and stops nagging. Suppression itself leaves no trail in the books, only silence; and a suppressed occurrence still answers to its own address, so the same month can walk back through the booking door.

docs.title: Author a standing recurrence rule by hand
docs.text:
Trigger: The owner recognizes a repeating obligation and formalizes it as a standing rule — surface: the recurrence add, pause, resume and remove commands

The owner sometimes knows an obligation before the books ever see it: a fresh subscription, a rent change, a yearly insurance premium. Authoring a rule turns that knowledge into a standing schedule directly — one complete statement of description, category, amount and rhythm, or a walk whose questions ask only for what is missing, where pressing Enter keeps the offered answer.

Two quiet mechanics shape what gets stored. A weekly or biweekly rhythm named by weekday moves the start forward to the first matching day, and every occurrence then lands on that weekday for the schedule's life. No bar compares the start with today: a blank start becomes the authoring day, and a readable past start passes just as freely as a future one — the owner may backdate a rule that was truly running before it was written down.

Before anything stores, the rule meets the same admission bars as an adopted schedule: a non-empty description, a category the owner approved, a non-zero amount, one of four rhythms, sane day and month ranges, readable dates, and an end never before the start. A refusal names its bar, and the store stays untouched. The saved schedule then confirms itself with the cadence in plain words and the next three dates the forecast will anticipate — yet books nothing. The ledger carries no entry for a rule until a real payment or an explicit confirmation touches it.

Later life runs through the same store's doors, with the same care. Pause silences a schedule while every field and its history stay stored, and resume brings it back as it stood (paused rules keep their place); removal ends the rule permanently, and only after the owner sees the exact rule and types yes (removal waits for a stated yes). One habit to watch: pressing Enter on the anchor question keeps a silent default, pinning a weekly schedule to whatever weekday the authoring day fell on — the printed cadence line is the only place that shows it.

docs.title: Adopt detected recurring rules from ledger history
docs.text:
Trigger: Repeating payments have accumulated in the ledger history and the owner acts on them — surface: the recurrence detect and recurrence take commands

The ledger already holds the habit; this flow makes the books say so. Only settled, fully described payments feed the grouping — Only settled history feeds detection — so every proposal names money that actually moved. Payments the owner has already formalized stay silent (A schedule with an existing equal is never re-proposed), which keeps the list a to-do that shrinks as habits are adopted. And because detection is read-only (Detection never saves a rule), the owner can ask for the list as often as they like without ever changing what the books anticipate.

Two tiers of answer come back. A steady payment — the rent, the subscription whose figure barely moves — proposes its median outright (A steady-amount payment proposes its median). A budget-style payment that keeps its appointment for changing figures proposes the same middle value but carries its observed low and high openly (A timely varying-amount payment proposes its median with its spread), so the owner sees the spread at a glance. A payment that swings between income and expense is refused as one habit (A payment habit mixing income and expense is never one pattern).

Nothing is created by looking. Naming a proposal opens a form pre-filled with the detected values; the owner accepts each field or retypes it, and quitting at any point stores nothing. Only a completed walk that passes the admission checks saves the rule (Only complete admissible rules are saved) — refused rules come back with their reason and the books stay untouched. A saved rule immediately shows its next three anticipated dates, and from then on the forecast generates its instances without further typing.

docs.title: Retract a wrong entry from the books with confirmation
docs.text:
Trigger: An owner judges an entry or projected instance wrong and retracts it — surface: the delete command (id, or pick from the last ten rows)

An owner catches an entry that should never have hit the books — a duplicate, or something that simply is not real. The delete command takes the id by name, or offers the last ten posted rows to pick from. The chosen row prints first, and nothing moves until the owner types a clear yes; a bare Enter or any other word leaves the books untouched.

The kind of wrongness sets the shape. A committed entry never vanishes in place: its removal lands in the journal as one record carrying the entry's full prior state, so the books can be built up again and prove exactly what left — and every later balance re-reads as if the row had never posted. A promised future payment is dropped from its register, since it never weighed on the books. A deleted group takes only the grouping with it, the member entries staying put. A projected occurrence goes quiet for one date while its rule keeps running. An address the books cannot resolve ends the attempt with nothing written at all.

When the removed entry moved money between two accounts, the retraction warns the owner to re-check both sides. One neighbouring door stays unguarded: the promises register's standalone remove action drops a promise without printing it or asking.

docs.title: No undo or restoration door after a retraction
docs.text:
Statement: The system deliberately provides no restore or undo for a removed entry — recovery means re-registering, and only the journal's own records preserve what the retraction carried.

Rationale: Once an entry is retracted, nothing offers to put it back. There is no restore command, no trash, no second-chance door. The deliberate boundary shows in the design everywhere else: retraction demands a printed row and a typed yes precisely because there is no take-back afterwards; the retraction record itself carries the removed content so the journal COULD reconstruct what was removed, but the product exposes no command that does so for the owner.

The owner's recovery path is the general one: re-register what was wrongly removed (through the intake or the promises register, whichever fits), accepting that a fresh registration is a new record, not the old one restored. A projected occurrence excluded by mistake can be brought back by editing the rule's exceptions — again through the rules machinery, not a restore door.

The boundary holds because the confirmation ritual makes the no-undo stance liveable: the owner was shown and asked, twice over on the recent-picker, before anything was written.

docs.title: Suppression stores no suppression record
docs.text:
Statement: Deleting a projected occurrence writes nothing that remembers the suppression — no flag, note or row — it only adds the date to the rule's exception list, so the forecast stops expecting money it silently no longer shows. Rationale: When the owner deletes a projected occurrence, the stores change in one way only: the date joins the rule's exempted dates. No suppression flag rides the rule, no note explains the decision, and no entry in any book names the suppressed occurrence. Whoever later asks "why is there no rent in March?" — the owner months on, or anyone reading the books — finds nothing: the rule simply projects everything except the dates it was told to skip.

The boundary is deliberate within this door: suppression is forecast-silencing, not bookkeeping. A decision that must be explainable later has to take a different door (booking the real movement, or reshaping the occurrence into a promise with its own record).

docs.title: Hand-writing a rule never books anything
docs.text: Statement: The system deliberately does not record a ledger entry, change any balance or store an instance when a standing schedule is written — the schedule only ever shows up as anticipation the forecast presents. Rationale: The moment a standing rule is saved, the household's real balances are untouched. The rule exists so the forecast can anticipate the payment — and only so the forecast can. The module that stores rules states this boundary explicitly: rules are never materialized into the transaction store; each repeats only as a virtual expected entry during a viewing window, and a real recorded payment in that window takes its place so a day never carries two truths. Whatever the owner later wants booked must still travel the normal recording doors; a rule is a promise, not a payment.

docs.title: The dry run projects only the checking account (parity)
docs.text:
Description: A rehearsal of a transfer of, say, €250 shows the checking side (−250) and its projected result, but not the mirrored +250 on savings, although the real landing would move both. The dry-run line the owner sees is built from the checking posting and the projected checking balance alone. The rehearsal still stores nothing, so nothing is wrong in the books — but the owner weighing the rehearsal against reality sees half of the movement.

Parity Relevance: A faithful reimplementation should either mirror this preview asymmetry exactly or knowingly fix it; a dry-run parity test with a transfer category would expose the difference.

docs.title: An identical restatement depends on when it was entered (integrity)
docs.text:
Description: The deduplication the owner might assume from 'recording twice changes nothing' only holds within one timestamp. The mutation's identity mixes content with its creation moment, deliberately — the comment on the field says as much: uniqueness is a human discipline, the timestamp exists only to separate identical content. So re-adding the same café visit an hour later is honest from the tool's reading — identical content, different creation moment, therefore a different movement. The owner who meant to correct and accidentally re-added now has the movement twice, and only the later delete/edit flow repairs it.

Parity Relevance: Idempotency tests must control timestamps: the same payload with the same ts folds, with a different ts duplicates.

Impact: file/src/financials/journal.py/Mutation#62-65, file/src/financials/journal.py/AddMutation.apply_on#251-254

docs.title: Backdated entries are inserted, later ones rewritten (lineage)
docs.text:
Description: Add 'yesterday's café' a week after the fact and the row slots between its neighbors, shifting each later day's balances by the posting — the chain never shows the recording moment on the row itself. The creation timestamp of the mutation preserves the stating order in the journal, but the ledger rows read as if the movement had always been in date order. That is the intended bookkeeping behavior, but a reader comparing two books rebuilt at different times will find balances that match per-row yet disagree if the earlier rebuild predates a backdated insert: the checkpoint carries the rewrite, and the journal carries the true order of statements.

Parity Relevance: A reimplementation must reproduce insert-position semantics and balance rewriting, not append-order — tests that only append will pass both designs and hide the difference.

During those questions a future date handed to the checking balance position is treated as a balance number, not as a date — nothing about the statement hints that the register is where it will end up. The owner answers the usual prompts and the entry parks as a promise only after the last answer.

docs.title: An unknown rule-instance address fails the confirm in silence (ux)
docs.text:
Description: Naming the confirmation desk with an address from the rule-instance family that matches no standing rule produces no visible answer at all — no explanation, no refusal note, only a failure exit. The code's own remark says the unknown id is the caller's business to report, yet the address reaches the desk through exactly that caller, which delegates and returns without a word. Every other unknown address greets the owner with a clear refusal. The gap is invisible in the direct case and untested; a typo in a remembered instance address simply looks like the confirm did nothing.

Parity Relevance: A parity re-implementation that reports unknown r: ids like every other unknown id would differ observably from this desk (exit code matches, user-visible output does not).

docs.title: All-Enter keeps a posted row but confirms a landed promise (ux)
docs.text:
Description: The editor's fields all keep their current value when confirmed unchanged, which reads as a pure review gesture: look, leave everything as it stands, move on. On a posted row that reading is right — confirming everything answers "nothing changed" and no record is written. On a promise whose day has already arrived the same gesture IS a confirmation: the books ask no further question and the row is committed as a landed fact as the owner steps out of the walk. The identical action thus means "I changed nothing" on one desk and "this happened as promised" on the other, with no signal at the moment of acting that the second case is a commit at all.

Parity Relevance: A parity port must reproduce the dual meaning exactly and preserve the no-second-question character of the landed-promise path; making the confirm explicit would change an owner-visible flow. docs.title: The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming (ux)
docs.text:
Description: The observable surprise: an owner who has learned that every removal in this product first shows the entry and demands a typed yes meets one door where none of that happens. Removing a future-dated promise through the expect command's remove action takes the id and deletes — no row printed, no confirmation asked — announcing only the success after the fact; even a wrong id gets only the same bare unknown-id error the guarded doors print.

The same promise removed through the retract command instead goes through the full ritual: printed row, explicit 'ja' or cancel. Two doors, one operation, two different guarantees. The register's own add side refuses incompleteness and the past loudly, so the asymmetry is not a general laxness of the register but a one-door-only gap.

docs.title: Weekly proposals anchor on the first occurrence's weekday (format)
docs.text:
Description: The owner sees weekly proposals shown with a weekday in brackets — that weekday is not asked, not chosen, and not stored per instance: it is inherited from the very first date the detection trusted. Adoption seeds the same date as the start, so accepting everything keeps that weekday forever, and the instance calendar repeats it from then on.

The surprise cuts in when history was irregular: the earliest recorded occurrence may sit on a different weekday than the payment's current habit (a payment that fell on Friday the first time and Tuesday since). The proposal carries the Friday, and nothing in the review or adoption names the difference as a warning. Only typing a bare weekday name in the form's anchor question moves the schedule off that inherited day.

This is why the form asks a weekday at all for weekly rhythms — the anchor question exists to let the owner override exactly this inherited value, and Enter silently ratifies whatever the first occurrence decided.

docs.title: The projection hides a suppressed occurrence but its address stays bookable (ux)
docs.text:
Description: The owner deletes an occurrence and sees it vanish — the forecast keeps its word. Nothing, though, was recorded about the address: it derives from the rule's schedule only, and no suppression flag exists to find. So the same address, typed later at the confirm desk or the edit desk, still resolves to rule and occurrence and offers the same booking or reshaping walk as before. A suppressed occurrence can therefore be confirmed after all, entering the books on a date the projection had already given up.

The code documents this deliberately: the resolver's own note says suppressed instances stay resolvable and the delete door never warns that the disappearance is forecast-only. For the owner the oddity is exactly the double-booking shape of the covered-occurrence sensitivity, reachable after a deliberate delete.

docs.title: 1. Issues
docs.text:
Note

While analyzing the codebase, our agents often encounter issues. Although not strictly part of the analysis, we report them because they often hold valuable information where the current implementation fails.

We identify four kinds:

  • code-bug: the implementation has a mistake that hinders the intended functionality
  • docs-drift: the documentation does not match the implementation and the documents are the stale side
  • docs-code-conflict: the mismatch is demonstrated but neither side is attributable yet
  • functional-mistake: the implemented behavior contradicts the established functional facts with no documented claim involved

docs.title: Add-flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms
docs.text:
Classification: docs-drift

Summary: The recurrence add flag help names only monthly and yearly, but the save path and the form both accept and store weekly and biweekly rules — the documented claim demonstrably undersells what the books do.

Claim: --frequency monthly | yearly (add)

Rationale: The claim was taken verbatim from the recurrence parser's flag help in the CLI wiring. Against it stand three independently traced sites: the seeded form's weekly branch prompting for a weekday anchor, the gap-band vocabulary producing weekly and biweekly proposals, and the admission checks validating all four frequencies with rhythm-specific rules. Classification rides the evidence: the drift side is the help text, since the code's four-rhythm handling is deliberate and heavily evidenced, while the help line reads as a leftover from a two-rhythm era. Consulted along the way: the proposal flow's rules, the form mechanism, and the command surface fact for the same program.

docs.title: 2. Hotspots
docs.text:
Note

Sometimes our agents encounter a bump in the road, an implementation that is so obscure or a comment that is so incomprehensible, that they need your ruling to make sense out of it.

These situations are reported as hotspots because they probably cover a dark secret that, when resolved, not only improved the analysis, but might also help to improve the implementation if needed.

In contrast to issues, hotspots deal with functional uncertainty, yet the answer to their questions might result in a new issue.

docs.title: Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?
docs.text:
Summary: The pre-image guard stops a rebuild whose retraction record disagrees with the books; the business intent for resolving that conflict is not decidable from the code.

Description: At rebuild time, each recorded retraction is checked against the entry it claims to have removed: day, words, category, account movements, everything joined to it. Any disagreement stops the whole fold with a loud refusal, on the stated ground that silently replaying a stale retraction would corrupt the chain — the removal would land on different content than it was chosen against.

What the code does next is all it can do honestly: refuse. It cannot decide what the owner would want. Two readable outcomes pull against each other — treat the live row as the truth and somehow re-derive the journal's story, or treat the journal as authoritative and reconcile the live books to it. Nothing in the code says which the business intends, and there is no recovery door: an owner facing this refusal is left with an unfathomable error and a question only the business can answer.

The answer lives with the owner of the books, not the analysis.

Question: When the journal's record of a retraction no longer matches the entry as it stands in the books, the rebuild refuses loudly — but who should win that standoff, and what recovery does the owner actually want: keep the live entry, or honour the recorded retraction anyway?

A case stays open until a resolution names it. This report follows the cases; the full statement behind each case lives on the fact pages every heading links to.

docs.title: SWOT Analysis
docs.text:
Note

The engagement closes with a SWOT analysis — what the product does well, where its doors still leak, what the captured findings open up, and what outside pressure the design acknowledges. Every claim in the quadrants carries its evidence as a fact reference, and each reference links to the full fact behind it on the fact pages.

docs.title: 1. Evidence snapshot
docs.text: The fact base was captured in a single pass on 2026-11-11 over a roughly thirteen-thousand-line Python codebase (47 modules, 637 symbols per financials); no separate coverage or run record exists in the vault, and all six recorded objections carry resolved markers at their target versions, so no fact is excluded here as contested.

docs.title: 2. Strengths
docs.text: Admission is one gate, not three — flagged, shorthand and prompted statements all pass the same five checks, so a movement admitted through the quick door could never have been refused at the slow one (One admission gate for every stated movement). What the books show rests on recomputation: every recorded movement chains its running balances from its date-predecessor and shifts every later day, so any balance is verifiable arithmetic rather than a stored claim (the balance-chain rule, with the date-positioned insertion and propagation pass behind it, Date-positioned insertion and balance propagation). Each row fails verification when its content is hand-altered (Hash guards detect a silently altered entry), which is what makes a quiet book-tamper impossible. Restating a movement stores it once, so replays cannot double a balance (Recording twice changes nothing the second time, Idempotent re-apply returns the stored row unchanged). Corrections are recorded, not retyped (A correction is recorded, not typed), and a retraction is one appended record carrying the removed content (A retraction is one record carrying the entry as it stood), so the books keep a replayable account and a rebuild proves a removal removed exactly what it claims. Removal writes only after the printed row and a typed affirmative (A retraction only writes after a stated yes), and the deliberate boundaries close the frame: no undo door after a retraction (No undo or restoration door after a retraction), and a standing schedule never books money by itself (Hand-writing a rule never books anything).

docs.title: 3. Weaknesses
docs.text: The all-Enter gesture changes meaning by desk — a pure review on a posted row, but a finished confirmation on a promise whose day has arrived, with no signal at the moment of acting (All-Enter keeps a posted row but confirms a landed promise), so a booked money fact can commit by reflex. The already-covered booking check lives on one door only: a rule occurrence confirmed inside a group is skipped when a booking already covers it, while the same occurrence confirmed by its own address commits unconditionally (Group-skip check versus direct-commit when one rule occurrence is confirmed twice in one pass), so money that moved once can post a second time. One removal door takes an id and deletes with no printed row and no stated yes (The expect remove door drops promises without printing or confirming) — the trust the confirmation ritual builds fails at exactly that door. The same stated date is legal at the confirm desk and refused at the occurrence reshape, losing the keeper's typed work (Booking today wins through confirm but loses through the occurrence reshape). An unknown rule-instance address exits the confirm desk in silence, unlike every other unknown address (An unknown rule-instance address fails the confirm in silence). One knowledge gap stands where a business decision belongs: when a retraction record no longer matches the live books, the rebuild refuses loudly — but which side should win is undecided (Refused retraction on journal-versus-books mismatch — which side should win?, question cited; the code's guess is pending human judgment), and the keeper facing that refusal has no recovery door. The add-help documentation names two payment rhythms while validation admits four (Add-flow help says monthly and yearly while validation admits four rhythms), so the weekly rule hides from the one input path built to write it.

docs.title: 4. Opportunities
docs.text: The open decision above awaits an owner of the books — once ruled, the journal-versus-books standoff becomes specifiable behavior instead of a live dead end (the same hotspot, its guess pending). And the counterparty side of every promise is already a documented party with a stake: the anticipated payer keeps pending deliveries visible as open items in the register (Anticipated payer), which is precisely where the confirmation workflow concentrates the keeper's attention. This quadrant is thin by capture — exactly one hotspot and two actors were recorded.

docs.title: 5. Threats
docs.text: The external exposure that is documented is delivery uncertainty itself — a promised movement may simply never happen, and the books hold it as an open item until the keeper confirms, so anticipated flow rests on the keeper working the backlog (Anticipated payer), bounded by the design that keeps promises out of the balance chain (Future promises never enter the balance chain). The sensitivity census carries eleven documented hazards, and every one describes a hazard inside the product's own doors rather than an external compliance or security exposure, so under the internal-versus-external frame none stands as a threat point: they are the weaknesses above seen from the keeper's side of the desk. The threats quadrant is correspondingly thin — one external dependency, stated without padding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The challenge said the contested fact pointed its door evidence at the wrong span, and the code agreed on every read. The booking step the fact anchored — cmd_add in the command module — takes whatever amount it receives, builds the postings and applies the mutation, zero included; a verifier expanding that span finds no refusal anywhere in it. The actual refusal lives one decision earlier, in the entry module's shared validation, lines 80 to 81, which turns a stated movement of zero away before any booking is attempted.

The placeholder half needed re-evidence too. The single field-collection line the fact cited is a bare call that shows nothing about zero; the real zero allowance is the amount prompt's flag for expected rows — reserve the promise now, fill in the real amount when it lands. Both halves of the sensitivity's story therefore verify, but the fact was standing on spans that do not carry them.

The correction re-words the statement so the intake-door half rests on the validation gate's refusal, and re-words the description to name the amount prompt's zero allowance on the placeholder side and the booking step's silence as the reason zero passes at commit time. The commit leg was re-checked as well: the confirmation path hands the promise's standing amount to the booking step untouched, which is why zero lands in the books at all.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Correction landed as version 2 of the contested fact; the objection was stamped with that version, and this resolution settles the rest. Links on the contested fact only carry forward — the verifier should note the residual re-point it names: the door-side anchor should become the validation gate's refusal span rather than the booking step.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The objection against the rule authoring process stands — its validation claim overstated what the code enforces, and the process gained both the true gate list and the now explicit past-and-future start latitude plus the today default.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Re-checked every anchor the objection rests on. The validator _validate in src/financials/recurrence_cli.py lines 150 to 183 holds nine bars — a non-empty description, an approved category, a non-zero amount, one of four rhythms, a day of month in range, a month for yearly rules, a present start for weekly and biweekly rules, parseable date strings, and an end date not before the start — and not one line compares the start with today. The authoring flow add_recurrence defaults a missing start to today's date and hands any parseable start to the validator, so past starts pass. The adoption path take_proposal pushes detector proposals through the same validator before saving, and the proposal builder _proposal in src/financials/recurrences.py seeds every start from the first historical occurrence — a future-start refusal there would break adoption itself, exactly as the challenge argued.

The challenged fact carried the false sentence only in its first capture; a later rewrite had already swapped it for the real gate list. The objection's second half still lacked a home — the today-default stated as a default rather than a gate — so the correction ordered here adds that half to the process description as its next version, while keeping the rewritten gates text intact.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Correction landed as version 4 of the rule authoring process; the stamp on the objection names that same version.

docs.text: Checked three facts against src/financials/journal.py and the entry flow around them: the timestamp-dependent restatement quirk, the backdated-insert rewriting quirk and the shared-predecessor sensitivity. All three held up.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The brief assigned a bucket over src/financials/journal.py#144-310 with three facts. Two quirk facts and one sensitivity fact, all carter-written, so all three were judged at full tier-1 depth: display contract, payload keys, link targets, and the primary anchors read this engagement.

The restatement quirk rests on the Mutation timestamp field whose comment says identical content needs distinct ids, and on content_hash hashing that timestamp into the id; add's apply_on deduplicates strictly by id, so a same-content restatement entered later carries a different id and lands as a second row. I chased the inferred claim that the later restatement gets a fresh timestamp at entry time and confirmed it in the commands layer: add minting fills an empty creation time at entry, from a monotonic microsecond clock whose docstring states the exact purpose the quirk describes.

The backdated-insert quirk matches insert and propagate exactly: a transaction dated before later rows slots into date position, every later row's balances is rewritten and rehashed, and the row itself carries no statement-order trace. The peripheral sentence about the carrying of rewritten balances also checks out — the checkpoint persists the fold's recomputed rows, so a rebuild made before a backdated insert disagrees with one made after it.

The sensitivity fact claims the projected balance the owner confirms and the stored balance come from one find_parent call. The projector indeed calls find_parent on the same date and projects from that predecessor's checking balance, the engine chains from the same lookup at write time, and nothing cross-checks the two. Its inferred three-strikes presentation detail also verified: the interactive prompt loop allows three agreement attempts and cancels the movement after the third mismatch, and the TUI dialog mirrors a single-mismatch rejection of the same projection.

No within-set twins. No tier-2 re-trace remained after tier 1; all objections stayed empty for lack of grounds, the pass ran green.

Title

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Deep-reviewed the money-movement intake process as a refined fact of version three — script validation, anchor reads and a full mechanic trace from the add branch down to the journal engine. Every claim held against the code that carries the flow; no objection was needed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This pass judged the intake process at refinement grade: its clean-marked refined script, its primary anchors, and one load-bearing mechanic at a time. The BPMN composition passes bpmn_tools:validate verbatim — five pools from the owner through entry intake, command mutations, the ledger engine and the expected register, wired by twelve message flows including the future promise parked outside the balance chain. The script's gate order mirrors the code's execution order: the shorthand parse refusal comes before the prompts, the prompts before the future-date dispatch, the admission gate before the rehearsal choice, and storage comes last — the same sequence the add branch of cli.main (275-290), the intake function and the command module carry.

Every admission-gate clause in the description matched its line in the validator the fact anchors to (entry.py 63-91): a real calendar day, words that say what happened, a category on the approved list, a non-zero amount, no date after today — and each refusal is printed plainly and returns with the books untouched. The rehearsal path shows the projected checking number and stores nothing (261-267); backing out at a question aborts cleanly (240-242), and the command layer turns Ctrl-C into the same nothing-stored outcome (288-290). The future-dated statement with all fields known rides to the expected register at two dispatch points (220-232 and 245-253), so promises never enter the balance chain.

Two claims needed deeper stitching than one anchor read. The transfer mirror is genuine: the posting builder puts a savings mirror beside the checking amount for the transfer category (commands.py 88-95), so one entry really moves both accounts. The double-statement guard is narrower than the prose might suggest — it is the idempotent re-apply by mutation id (journal.py 252-254), and because the timestamp clock deliberately mints distinct stamps for identical content re-entered fresh (commands.py 34-37), the guard binds precisely within one creation moment, which is the qualifier the description itself carries.

The balance mechanics checked out at the engine: rows land at their date position and take the nearest prior day's running balances (journal.py 212-217), every later row shifts by the same posting set (220-225), and the description's three-disagreement abandonment matches the retry constant of three at entry.py line 31. One limit stands: the rehearsal path's stores-nothing claim was verified down to the intake function's early return — the single write step in append_and_apply (72-85) is reachable by no rehearsal branch in the code read this pass, but the rehearsal end state was not observed at runtime.

docs.title: List level validation of the eight detection phase ledger processes
List-level validation of the eight detection-phase ledger processes
Title
docs.text: List-level validation of the eight detection-phase ledger processes

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Reviewed the eight initial process identifications at detection grade — names, scope, overlaps, gaps — alongside tier-1 anchor reads of each process's primary code. Seven held up; one description misstates its validator and carries an objection with a proposed replacement.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This pass judged the eight processes as the high-level identifications the exploring phase left behind, not as finished analyses. At the mechanical level the set is clean and uniform: every fact names itself as a draft script pending deep analysis, and every script in the set opens with its process declaration and closes with a single end line. Tracing each draft task against execution order surfaced one thing worth naming, though: the register process drafts its dry-run preview after the storing step, while the code appends, previews, and then saves. The order still matches what the anchored code actually does — nothing in the draft asserts an execution fact — so that stays a detailed-review remark, not a defect. Every one of the eight scripts declares exactly one business task per traced step, and the tasks read as business operations the anchoring modules genuinely carry.

The naming and scope work came out well. Each name sits at the right altitude: intake and register name a life phase rather than a command, confirmation and correction name the transition, and the three recurrence processes split cleanly by intent — mining rules from history, committing a projected instance, authoring a rule by hand. Every process anchors to the module that actually implements its flow: the dispatch behavior of the register process, its future-date gate and approved-category check, the multi-store resolvers behind the edit and delete commands, and the seeded adoption loop of the detection process all read true against the primary anchors.

The overlap analysis deserves its own paragraph because there is a genuine knot here. Registering a future payment and committing a recurring instance both describe putting money expectations into the books, and the delete and removal processes both describe retraction. Reading the four together shows the divisions are deliberate: the register process keeps expected entries and the instance process keeps projected rule occurrences apart — a covering transaction on a committed instance supersedes the projection rather than creating an expected row, so the two streams genuinely do not trade content. Retraction similarly splits its subject: the removal process owns book-out transactions and suppression of a projected instance, the correction process keeps in-book fixes and the future-date escape that flips an entry into the expected register. The remaining knot — editing a projected instance is claimed by both the confirmation process and the instance commitment process — is the same split, and resolving it belongs to the deep pass that will draw those two processes' boundaries in full.

The gap check leans on the surface inventory of the command line. Eight processes cover adding, expecting, confirming, correcting, retracting, grouping, and the recurrence rule surface. No process mentions reading — the ledger view, the interactive window, and the monthly report are the owner's daily visibility surface, and their absence is conspicuous next to processes that repeatedly reference what 'financials list' shows. Grouping is partially present (a confirmation group confirm and member-preserving group deletion), but group creation and membership management have no process of their own. Data repair is entirely invisible: the command line carries reviewed-fix application machinery, yet no process mentions it. One more observation: every fact in the set carries business-value as its value class, which at this uniform level says more about phase conventions than about differentiation between the processes.

For the process claiming a future-start validation gate, the tier-1 read found a real problem and raised an objection with a proposed replacement: the validator in that process' primary anchor has no such gate and accepts any parseable start, and the detection flow depends exactly on that openness, since proposals carry their first-historical-occurrence start through the same validator before saving. That the objection was raised does not reflect on the review's course — it is this pass's normal defect channel.

Title
docs.text: Re-read of the two open-confirmation sensitivity facts

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Both confirm-path sensitivities were checked claim by claim against freshly read anchor code, and both held up: the direct instance commit really lacks the cover check its group twin carries, and the open picker really offers every landed promise without an amount filter.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Each of the two confirmation sensitivities was re-read against its own code this pass. The anchored function bodies came back verbatim, and the reads extended to the two functions the anchors delegate to — the shared commit core and the walk behind the open list — so both halves of every claim had evidence behind it.

The double-booking claim stands. The group path consults the ledger first: it skips a rule instance already covered by a real commit when category, amount and date sit inside the superseding window, and the skip is announced in a note. The direct instance path hands the same values straight to the commit core, and the core posts the booking with no look back at what the ledger already holds — its covered logic runs the other way, deciding whether the fresh commit supersedes the rule's period in the projection, never whether the movement was already paid. One movement, two doors, one guard.

The second claim survives on different lines. The projection keeps expected rows by date alone, the walk over it adds no amount check, and the picker prints every survivor, formatting each amount as a signed number. A promise that landed without its amount reaches that format and the render breaks there — before the prompt that asks which id to confirm.

One limit worth naming: the intake door that lets an amount-less promise into the register was taken from the fact's own account, not re-traced here. The anchors do not rest on it, and nothing between landing and render filters on amount, so the visible pipeline already carries the claim.

docs.title: Condition
docs.text: The owner gives today as the date on a future standing-rule occurrence — legal as a real landing through the confirm door, refused when the same date is typed to reshape the occurrence into a promise.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: On the reshape path the promise admission rule governs and refuses today; the confirm door's same-day permission never materializes there.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Both rules speak on the same case — a future occurrence and the date today. The confirm desk holds that once the owner states the true landing day, a movement may be booked, and today counts as landed; its code refuses only the day after today. The reshape path holds that a promise keeps the promise calendar and refuses the day money has already moved on. When the owner picks the reshape option on an occurrence and types today, the code's branching gives the case to the promise calendar: the reshape is refused, the occurrence keeps its projected shape, and nothing enters the books on that door. The confirm-door permission is not overridden in the abstract — each door keeps its own calendar — but on the reshape path the refusal wins and the same-day booking simply cannot be reached there.

For the owner this reads as: to book today's edition of the occurrence, leave the edit door and take it to the confirm desk instead; the edit door records only days still to come.

docs.title: Visible Effect
docs.text: The reshape is refused with no store change and the owner's typed work is lost — the same occurrence booked today remains available only through the confirm door.

Title

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Confirming a standing-rule occurrence by its own address commits unconditionally, while the same occurrence inside a group is first checked against bookings that already cover it — the double-booking guard exists on one door only.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The group confirm path skips occurrences already covered by a real booking; the direct instance confirm path has no such check, so money already booked can be posted a second time.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the owner books a movement by hand that a standing rule also promises — the rent paid on the actual day, say — the rule's occurrence for that period stops showing as open, because a real booking covers it. Confirming the occurrence as part of a group respects that: the desk looks for a booking that already covers the occurrence and skips it with a note. But calling the same occurrence up by its own address commits straight away, with no look at what has already been booked for it. Money that moved once can therefore enter the books again through the second door — the balance claims the movement twice, and nothing at either door warns the owner. The quiet case is the direct one, which is exactly the door an owner reaching for a remembered address uses.

docs.title: A promise corrected to zero lands in the books worth nothing
A promise corrected to zero lands in the books worth nothing
Title
docs.text: A promise corrected to zero lands in the books worth nothing

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Through the entry editor a promise can be confirmed into the books at an amount of zero, a value the intake door's checks refuse before recording.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The correction desk lets a landed promise commit at 0.00 where the intake desk would refuse — a difference in door checks, not in what the books want recorded.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The houses hold different opinions about zero. When an owner reserves money that has not been decided yet, the amount prompt treats zero as a legal placeholder — reserve the promise now, fill in the real amount when it lands. The intake side is stricter. Before a new entry is recorded, its checks turn a stated movement of zero away, and only complete statements reach the books.

The correction desk sits between these two opinions. It lets the zero placeholder stand right up to the moment the promise's day arrives, and then commits the promise exactly as it was last corrected — zero included, if that is what stood — because the booking step takes whatever amount it is handed. A payment worth nothing is thus a legal fact of the books through one door and an impossible statement through the other.

The owner believes their books reflect money moved. In this case the books carry a movement that never had a real amount, and every balance built on it is right only if the true amount really was zero.

docs.text: A future-dated expense stated as zero is admitted by the expectation door and weighs nothing in every forecast, while the same zero statement would have been refused with a plain message at the actual ledger door.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: An owner who slips a zero where an amount belongs hears nothing: the promise parks cleanly, and the shortfall only becomes visible when the promised day has passed unpaid.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The two doors of the books disagree about zero. At the actual ledger a movement worth zero is refused outright, because zero money moving is a mistake by definition. At the expectation door the same zero is treated as a stated amount and the promise parks silently. So an owner who fat-fingers a rent as zero gets a clean confirmation, an open item that reads like any other, and a forecast that quietly understates the outflow. Nothing marks the entry for attention; the mistake surfaces only when the day arrives and the money does not, and by then the promise may already have been confirmed as-is.

docs.title: An amount less promise can reach the open picker and break the offer to confirm
An amount-less promise can reach the open picker and break the offer to confirm
Title
docs.text: An amount-less promise can reach the open picker and break the offer to confirm

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The open list offers every landed promise for confirmation regardless of whether its amount was ever recorded, so one amount-less promise silently poisons the very screen the owner uses to confirm everything else.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The open confirmation list does not filter out amount-less promises; the first bare confirm after one lands can fail instead of showing the backlog.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Promises are allowed into the register without their amount — a deliberate door elsewhere in the intake. Confirmation is the door that refuses them, and the refusal is polite when the owner names the item directly. But the moment the owner confirms bare, the backlog is the gatekeeper: it lists what is owed confirmation without checking each item can actually be confirmed. One amount-less promise in that list and the whole offer to confirm can fail — before the owner has picked anything, before any refusal message can explain why. Every other landed promise stays invisible behind it, and the only workaround is naming an item by address directly. Nothing warns that the two doors disagree.

docs.title: Deleting an occurrence reads as a booking decision but books nothing
Deleting an occurrence reads as a booking decision but books nothing
Title
docs.text: Deleting an occurrence reads as a booking decision but books nothing

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The owner can trust the forecast's disappearance as proof an occurrence is handled, while the deleted instance remains bookable through its own address — the money can enter the books twice from the owner's point of view.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The owner's delete means "this occurrence must never be booked", but the books treat it as "hide it from the forecast" — a silently violated agreement, since the address still commits.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When the owner deletes a projected occurrence — a rent waived that month, a subscription cancelled mid-cycle — the visible result, one row gone from the forecast, reads like a done decision: this occurrence will never enter the books. The stores hold nothing of that decision; the only permanent trace is the forecast silence. Nothing stops the same occurrence's address from committing later, and nothing at that door recalls the earlier delete. A month later, working from a remembered address or an old list snapshot, the owner can book exactly what they had ruled out — and the forecast cannot warn, because it was told to be quiet.

The silent agreement: the delete door and the booking doors must stay consistent about what suppression means. Breaking that agreement harms the balance the owner trusts, without any visible notice at either end.

docs.title: The adoption re derives the list the owner reviewed
The adoption re-derives the list the owner reviewed
Title
docs.text: The adoption re-derives the list the owner reviewed

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The proposal list the owner reviews and the list the adoption consults are two separate detections — a value change in the ledger between review and adoption changes what the adoption offers without ever saying so.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The owner reviews numbered proposals, then names a number to adopt: the adoption reruns detection fresh and takes that number from the new list, so what the form seeds may not be what the table showed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The review table presents numbered proposals; adoption takes a number, not a payment's identity. Between the owner reading the table and naming the number, money may have been recorded, a rule added or removed elsewhere, or the history itself grown — and the adoption silently re-derives the whole list and takes the numbered slot from whatever is in front of it at that moment.

The owner believes they are filling in proposal seven as they saw it. If the list reshuffled or shrank, they are instead confirming a different payment's values — and only the fields they actually read catch the difference. The seeded defaults are designed to be accepted quickly, which is precisely what makes an unnoticed substitution easy to complete.

The mismatch is never announced: there is no check that proposal seven still shows the same description when adopted. The owner's protection is their own glance at the form's title line, which does show the proposal's name before any value is accepted.

docs.title: The detector and the view must agree on what a repeating payment is
The detector and the view must agree on what a repeating payment is
Title
docs.text: The detector and the view must agree on what a repeating payment is

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Proposals are computed over the ledger view's rows, so the detector's notion of a settled payment inherits every filtering and naming rule the view layer applies silently.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Detection reads history through the shared ledger view, which excludes future-dated rows and applies its presentation logic — detection never sees that filtering happen, so a change in the view changes proposals with no signal in the recurrence code.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The detector does not read the books directly; it reads the same presentation the owner browses, which assembles committed rows through the shared view. That view exists for display purposes — it filters what counts and how rows present — and detection leans on it wholesale.

The fragile property: proposals are only as complete and only as honest as the view's selection. If the view's notion of a settled movement shifts — a filtering rule tightens, a naming rule changes — the detection output shifts with it, and nothing in the recurrence side notices, because the two sides share the computation rather than a contract.

The owner sees the consequence only in the list's shape: a payment that used to propose stops proposing, or proposes differently, with no explanation because the cause lives outside the recurrence code entirely.

docs.title: The fixes repair door writes promises without the intake checks
The fixes repair door writes promises without the intake checks
Title
docs.text: The fixes repair door writes promises without the intake checks

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: An expected entry created through a cleanup-fixes repair enters the register with no future-date, approved-category, or amount check, so a mis-stated repair lands where the commands would have refused it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The register has a second entry door with none of the intake gates: only its date, category, amount and description as written in the reviewed fix file are taken over verbatim.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Besides the expect command there is a repair path that recreates a promised movement from a cleanup-fixes file. That path takes over the date, category, amount and description exactly as the file states them and parks the entry — no question asked about whether the date lies ahead of today, whether the category is approved, or whether an amount is there at all. Even a date that is not a real calendar day would slip in. The fix files are meant to be reviewed by hand before use, which is the only protection this door has; a single mis-stated line in an otherwise sound repair file lands a broken promise in the register without any refusal, and nothing flags it afterwards.

docs.title: The projection preview and the real write share one predecessor
The projection preview and the real write share one predecessor
Title
docs.text: The projection preview and the real write share one predecessor

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: The checking balance the owner is asked to agree with, and the balance the stored entry will actually carry, both come from the same date-predecessor computation — if that ever diverges, the owner signs off on a balance the books will not hold.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The interactive balance agreement and the engine's chain both derive from find_parent; their agreement is by shared computation, not independently checked.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: At entry time the owner sees a projected checking balance and must agree with it for the statement to proceed — three disagreements and the movement is abandoned. That projection exists so a discrepancy between the owner's own administration and the tool is caught before storing. But the projection's number and the stored entry's number come from the same predecessor lookup: nothing cross-checks the stored entry against what was shown, because they cannot disagree by construction. The fragile part is the shared source — any change to how a predecessor is chosen updates both, so a wrong chain base would be confirmed by the owner at entry time and carried into every later balance without ever looking wrong on screen.

docs.title: The same add walk on different days stores different weekly schedules
The same add walk on different days stores different weekly schedules
Title
docs.text: The same add walk on different days stores different weekly schedules

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: An owner who completes the weekday question with Enter gets a schedule anchored to whatever weekday the authoring day happened to be, so re-typing a lost rule on another day silently produces a different schedule than the original.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Keeping the start's own weekday looks like a harmless default, but it welds the schedule's repeating day to the calendar day of authoring — identical wording on two different weekdays yields two different schedules.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: A householder replacing a lost weekly rule types the same words they used the first time, answers the questions the same way, and takes the offered weekday default — the rule keeps whatever weekday the first run fell on. The books make no complaint and the confirmation reads like the same schedule, yet every anticipated date now falls on a different day of the week than before. Nothing in the add walk flags the difference; only the printed cadence line betrays it, and only to a reader who checks. Anyone re-authoring rules from memory, and any tooling that replays the same answers to rebuild a rule set, shares this fragile equality: sameness of wording does not mean sameness of schedule.

docs.title: The unguarded remove door drops the wrong promise silently
The unguarded remove door drops the wrong promise silently
Title
docs.text: The unguarded remove door drops the wrong promise silently

docs.title: Sensitivity Statement
docs.text: Anyone removing a promised entry through the unguarded remove door can delete the wrong id with no preview and no confirmation, and hear only a success or a bare unknown-id error — the mistake is silent on both sides.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The expect remove door's missing print-and-confirm makes a wrong id a silent wrong deletion, one door away from the guarded retract command that would have prevented it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner relies on the product's promise that removals are shown before they happen. On the expect command's remove action that promise silently fails: a mistyped or misremembered id removes a different promised entry than intended, with no printed row to catch the mistake and no confirmation to stop it. The owner learns of the removal only after it has happened.

The harm is bounded — a dropped promise is recoverable by re-registering it, and promises never touch the balance chain — but it is silent: nothing distinguishes "removed what I meant" from "removed something else" at the moment of removal. The guarded retract command sits one door away and would have printed the victim first.

Escalated from the quirk about the two-door asymmetry: the quirk states what the two doors do; this names who is hurt — the owner who trusts uniformity of the removal ritual.

Fact Sheet Name Journaled bookkeeping

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The intake flow, the mutation layer and the ledger engine that together turn a stated money movement into a checked, chained ledger entry.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Three components jointly deliver the personal books. The entry-intake flow captures a movement the owner states, in whatever precision the moment allows, and checks it before anything is stored. The command mutations layer stamps and lands each accepted change as one journal mutation. The ledger engine replays mutations into rows that carry their own running balances, guarded by hashes against silent corruption. Forward-dated promises never reach these books: the expected register keeps them apart until they land as facts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The confirmation desk's command. Confirms an expected entry, a rule instance or a whole group whose movement has landed: the commit posts the movement as a real journal entry with running balances and closes the open item. Landed items confirm as-is with no prompts; a future-dated rule instance opens the prefilled question walk; an already-committed address is a no-op; bare confirm shows the open list to pick from. Unknown ids are refused with a message (except the silent rule-instance case). What the id turns out to be decides the retraction: a committed or promised entry is printed and removed after an explicit typed yes; a group id removes only the grouping; a rule-occurrence id excludes that occurrence from the rule's projection. docs.title: Description
docs.text: The owner types or omits one address; the rest is a walk. Committed rows (t-addresses) open the actual-entry editor; promise addresses open the promise editor with a move-to-promise option; group addresses open the group editor; and an occurrence of a standing rule (its r-address) opens the occurrence menu — reshape this occurrence into a promise or adjust the standing rule itself. Omitting the address offers the ten most recent actual rows to pick from. An address none of the doors recognize is refused with Onbekende id. Cancel inside any walk is a full undo. docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Writes a standing rule in one typed command — description, category, amount, rhythm and anchor — or walks the owner through the missing pieces question by question.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The add door is how an owner formalizes a repeating obligation without waiting for history to prove it. Reached as the add action of the product's recurrence command, it takes the payment's name, its category, its amount (negative for outgoings), how often it repeats, and the anchor — the day of the month, the month for a yearly rhythm, or the weekday for a weekly rhythm — plus an optional start and an optional end date. Leave pieces out and the door asks for them one question at a time; answer everything up front and it saves silently. The saved schedule is confirmed with its cadence and the next three dates the forecast will anticipate.

Non-interactive pieces, as the door accepts them: --description, --category, --amount (decimal), --frequency (monthly, yearly, weekly or biweekly), --day (day of month, 1-31), --month (month, 1-12), --start (ISO date the rule begins), --end (ISO date it lapses, empty = never), --weekday (ma, di, wo, do, vr, za or zo for weekly rhythms).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Silences a standing schedule's anticipation without erasing it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The pause door stops the forecast from anticipating a schedule the owner still wants to keep. The owner names the rule by a fragment of its description; if it is already silenced, the door says so rather than pretending a change happened. Resuming brings it back exactly as it stood.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Retires a standing schedule permanently after showing it to the owner and taking a typed yes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The remove door ends a schedule's life in the forecast. The owner names the schedule by any unique fragment of its description; the door shows the exact rule about to go — name, amount, category, rhythm and starting point — and waits for a typed yes before erasing it. Nothing else short of that word removes anything, and a no leaves the schedule standing untouched. Pausing and resuming share this naming style without the finality: those doors only silence or reawaken a schedule.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Reawakens a paused standing schedule so the forecast anticipates it again.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The resume door is the pause door's mirror: the owner names the schedule by a fragment of its description and the schedule anticipates again from its stored window and rhythm. A schedule that was never paused is simply reported as already active, with no store rewrite.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Adopts a numbered proposal from the detection list by walking the owner through its values — every field pre-filled, Enter keeps it, typing replaces it, quitting aborts.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The adoption door: the owner names the proposal number from the review table, and the form opens with that proposal's values already in place. What they see seeded is the payment's name, category, amount, rhythm and calendar landing; accepting every field with Enter stores a rule exactly as the history suggested it, and typing over any field takes the owner's version instead.

The saved rule's next three anticipated dates are shown immediately, so the owner sees their schedule in the books' forward calendar before they leave the command. Quitting at any prompt stores nothing and says so.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The owner opens this to see what the books would formalize: one row per detected pattern, showing the payment's name and category, the amount (with its observed range when the amounts varied), the rhythm, when in the cycle the payment lands, how often it was seen, and when it first appeared.

Running it is safe by design — read-only, repeatable at will. The table's own footer says what to do next: adopt a proposal through the product's recurrence add flow, or name a number to adopt it directly with the same command.

Fact Sheet Title Open confirmation list screen

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The bare confirm picker: the backlog of landed-but-unconfirmed open items shown as one table, from which the owner picks an item to confirm.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: When the owner calls the confirmation desk with nothing in hand, the desk answers with the backlog itself — every open item whose day has arrived but is not yet recorded as real, computed fresh from what the register and the standing rules owe confirmation today. The list shows each item's address, day, description, category and amount. Choosing an item (or leaving the pick empty to cancel) hands that entry to the same confirm path an explicit address would. An empty backlog answers that there is nothing to confirm, and the owner walks away without changing anything. The list is never a store of its own.
